Publisher: Medical Hall Year of Publication: 1905 City of Publication: Varanasi
Place of Publication: India Title: Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā Author: Śrī Nandikeśvara Śivācārya
The *Śaradā* commentary composed by Śrī Śivakumāra Śāstrī,
published by the Medical Hall,
Vārāṇasī.
Salutation to Śrī Gaṇeśa;
salutation to the venerable one who is worshipped by the universe.
The Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā composed by Nandikeśvara;
the first part.
He who, in the form of the *haṃsa*, was Śiva within the entire assembly of cakras beginning with the *ādhāra*,
became known as Bhāvādi through the power of the grace of the eternal bliss-guru;
furthermore, through the distinctions of conduct (*ācāra*) and so forth, he became the sixfold *liṅga*.
To him, the embodiment of the illustrious Guru and the husband of the Daughter of the Mountain, we offer our salutations. || 1 ||
The Vedas, Śāstras, and Āgamas were composed by Him for the attainment of the desired goals of men,
being differentiated into various forms according to the distinctions of ritual action (karma), meditative worship (upāsti), and knowledge (jñāna).
To him who proclaims the causes in the world, homage! || 1 ||
Whose son was Bāṇa? Whose son was the lotus-eyed Padmanayana? Whose son was Padmabhū? Whose son was Mahīratha, whose wings were the Vedas?
He drank the Hālāhala poison, which spread like the fire of the dissolution of the three worlds.
And who else but Śambhu, the god of the world's welfare, should be resorted to? || 2 ||
In the Śrauta rituals, Vedic words are established in the sacrificial rites (vaitānika),

and in the Smārta rituals as well, the many Smṛtis composed by the great seers have been examined; however, through careful attention, one must perceive the intended meaning of these [texts] within the heart.
The ultimate intent is established solely in the practice of pleasing the Supreme Lord. || 3 ||

Let there be a kingdom adorned with the happiness of sovereignty over the entire circle of the earth; let the vassal kings be conquered and enemies subdued; let the treasury be like that of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera);
and likewise, let the Vedas, honored by the knowledge of their limbs and secret portions, be brought under the control of one's speech.
If the mind is not fixed upon the pair of lotus feet of Piśāna, what then?
Therefore, having reflected that a person should constantly bring about the gratification of the Lord alone through mind, speech, and body, the sages of old, such as Vāmadeva and others,
cast off the worldly latent impressions residing in the mind by means of dispassion.
Having restrained their minds through constant practice, they became absorbed in that meditation with their intentions fixed upon it.
Although supreme knowledge is the primary cause for attaining Great Lordship,
and selfless actions are likewise sufficient for purifying the mind,
yet both of these depend upon the feet of Him who is an ocean of infinite compassion.
The ancient sages have said that [even the most learned] does not deserve even a sixteenth part of devotion. || 6 ||
Furthermore, devotion is said here to be both supreme and non-supreme; the former is declared to be primary.

Its primacy consists in the absence of desire for fruits, or in being love directed toward that alone, or in possessing detachment from all enjoyment whatsoever—these three being characterized by love itself.
The eminent sage Dvaipāyana has declared its ninefold divisions.
I perpetually worship the lotus-foot of Śāraṅga upon my own young lotus-heart, which is like the orb of the sun to the darkness of obstacles. || 2 ||
He whose splendor of speech is woven through the entire collection of scriptures investigating karma and Brahman;
who, by producing words that reveal the reality of the *liṅga*, the limbs, and the sacred sites, acts like the six-faced Lord Kārttikeya;
and who possesses the roar of a lion for crushing the temples of the intoxicated lordly elephants of the learned.
I bow my head to the Guru named Malleśvara, who is the sun to the darkness of obstacles.
Without having reflected upon the Vedas and the Shastras, some who considered themselves scholars, out of resentment, did not accept the wearing of the Shiva-linga. || 4 ||

But that [love] devoid of the aforementioned qualifiers, yet endowed with exactly those same distinctions, becomes love as the substantive reality (dharmibhūta); like a thread, it pervades everything.
That love [manifests] in remembrance, hearing, prostration, glorification, and service.
In such acts as the offering of one's entire self, he likewise joins [the devotee] with intense [devotion].
This being so, reflect within your own mind with boundless love, desiring never to be separated from the remembrance of the Lord; thus,
through the constant maintenance of the *liṅga* manifested as having that very nature, you should strive for eternal union.
Like one filled with intense longing, will he not repeatedly captivate the heart of his devotee? (9)
"Grant me a boon at my svayaṃvara; by your command, I shall compose the *Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā* for the purpose of refuting them. (5)
For when the heart is made one-pointed through devotion, a person considers the positions of Indra, Kubera, and others to be trivial,
and remains solely attached to his own desired goal.
Day and night, he extends a continuous stream of meditation.
Thus, through the observation of the devotee’s state and by means of various logical arguments, the establishment of Śambhu’s great *jyotirliṅga* within one's own body is easily accomplished;
for that which Jaimini established— that Dharma is accessible solely through the Word— is [thus validated].
Therefore, even the words of the Vedas have been cited by the Śaivas for the purpose of establishing that [reality]. || 10 ||
They indeed say this: "The wearing of the sectarian marks (*liṅgadhāraṇa*) is certainly not to be accepted by the followers of the Veda, because it is non-Vedic.

For if it were Vedic, its being expounded in the sentences of the Vedas and Vedāntas would be the determining factor; yet we do not perceive either of those in this case. Alternatively, it is not something to be understood through Smṛti and other texts rooted in the Veda."
Because no scriptural statements supporting that [practice] are seen in the Smṛtis of Manu and others,
the *Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā* was composed to prevent those texts from being interpreted as having a different intent, and to establish one's own desired purport. (11)
This [work] primarily relies upon the Kāmika, the Vātula, the one known as the Mukuṭa-vīra, and the Skānda-liṅga Āgamas. (12)
In order to bring supreme satisfaction to Śambhu, who is with Ambā, this commentary named *Śan* is composed and offered at the feet of Śambhu. (13)
Although worldly desire indeed acts as the motivator here, nevertheless, the thought remains in his mind: "May Gaurī’s Lord be somewhat pleased. (14)

If you think that, like the practice of auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) and so forth, the wearing of the sectarian mark (*liṅga*) has its root in the Veda as something to be inferred, that too is mere wishful thinking; for since the wearing of the mark is practiced by all cultured people (*śiṣṭas*), it is not the practice of a few individuals that serves as the means for inferring a Vedic basis. And thus:

How can the wearing of the *liṅga*, which falls outside the scope of all means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), be accepted by the Vedic tradition? To this we reply: it is because the wearing of the *liṅga* has been declared with certainty in the Vedas, Śāstras, Purāṇas, and in the Āgamas such as the Kāmika, specifically for the Vīraśaiva.
Like the moonlight upon the moon shining on the head of Śambhu, she,
having reached this autumn season, will attain supreme brilliance.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the hosts (Śiva), Gaurī together with her Lord (Śiva), and the great [deity] Sarasvatī,
she prayed for awakening from those who know the reality of Śiva.
Its commentary is now commenced today.

Thus it is stated in the Siddhānta. The meaning of this is as follows: "Vedas" refers to the *Ṛg* and the other [Vedas]. By this, the *Mahābhārata* is also implied, based on the statement of the learned authorities that "the *Bhārata* is the fifth Veda.
"Śāstras" refers to the *Smṛtis*. "Purāṇas" refers to the *Skanda*, *Vāyu*, *Liṅga*, and so forth. "Āgamas" refers to...

The *Kāmika* and other [Tantras]. In that regard, within the Taittirīya branch of the Yajurveda, the internal wearing of the *liṅga*, consisting of the contemplation of the Jyotir-liṅga, is prescribed. In the Taittirīyaka, it says:
"The small, free from evil" (*Tai. Ā. 10.10.3*).

In this regard, since the wearing of the *liṅga* is twofold— consisting of both internal and external wearing— and since both types are established by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, they must now be examined; first, however,
in order to demonstrate that the wearing of the internal *liṅga* is established by the *Śruti*, [the text proceeds] with the *Dahara-vidyā*.

He establishes that [the Self] has as its object the light-linga (jyotir-liṅga) situated within the interior of the heart-lotus, beginning with the words "In the Taittirīyaka," etc. "The small, stainless [abode]"—this is the nature of the mantra in the Upaniṣad:
"That lotus which is the abode of the excellent, situated in the middle of the city, small and stainless; even there, in that small [space]..."
"The sky is free from sorrow; that which is within it is to be meditated upon" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.3).

Beginning with this and ending with "that which is within it is to be meditated upon," the injunction for meditation is prescribed. When the inquiry arises as to what that [which is to be meditated upon] is—
Regarding this, the commentary states: This lotus of the heart which exists has eight petals.

Of what nature is it? It is *dahara*, small, because it is measured at the size of a thumb. It is free from evil (*vipāpma*), because as the locus for one-pointedness of mind, it is devoid of sin. It is the "excellent abode" (*varaveśmabhūta*), meaning the abode of the excellent (*vara*).
It is like a house, serving as the locus for the perception of the Supreme Self and as the locus for its meditation.

It is called a "city" (*pura*) because it is filled with all the limbs, such as the hands and feet; it is situated in the middle of that city, located between the belly and the chest. Furthermore, even within that, it resides in the small space of the lotus-like heart.

The sky is the form of Brahman, which is formless like space. Although Brahman is omnipresent, its smallness is figuratively attributed to it in relation to its location within the lotus, just as the space within a jar is considered small. Thus, another Śruti passage states:
"Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace..."
"In this [city], there is the small inner space" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1).

And that the small space (*daharākāśa*) is Brahman has been determined in the *Daharādhikaraṇa* (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.5). Therefore, "free from sorrow" (*viśoka*)—the masculine gender being a Vedic usage—refers to Brahman, which is denoted by the word "space" (*gagana*) and is devoid of grief. This being so, in that [space]...

"That which is the reality of Brahman within—in the middle of—the lotus, that should be worshipped; it should be meditated upon through a continuous flow of homogeneous mental impressions, free from heterogeneous impressions" (Sāṅkhyabhāṣya 10.10.3).
In this scripture, even there, [it says]: "In that small space is the sky, which is free from sorrow."
"That which is within should be worshipped;

that sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda and established at the end of the Veda—He who is beyond that which is dissolved in primordial nature is Maheśvara. By this [scriptural passage], Śiva is the wielder of the trident.

By the statement "Maheśvara" (Amarakośa 9.9.20), there arises the possibility of the misconception that even within the midst of the sky, some entity distinct from the reality of Brahman— which is denoted by the word 'gagana'— is to be worshipped; [therefore] let that not be so.
The commentator, having explained everything up to the end of the section on *viśoka*, has inserted the phrase "this being so" (*evaṃ sati*) in the middle.

Consequently, in the passage "that which is within that," the word "that" (*tat*) should not refer to the sky (*gagana*), but rather must refer to the lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), even though it is separated by intervening words. From this, the following meaning results:
Since the lotus of the heart is the dwelling place of the reality of Brahman, therefore the reality of Brahman residing therein is to be meditated upon.

Regarding the phrase "at the beginning of the Veda": at the beginning—that is, at the commencement—of the Veda which is to be studied, there is the *svara* (vowel), consisting of the musical tone (*svara*).

Sound is said to be of the nature of the *praṇava*. As stated in the words of Manu: "One should always place the *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end of the Veda; that which is not preceded by the *oṃ* slips away, and that which is not followed by it falls apart. Thus, as prescribed for recitation, it is established in the Vedānta, such as in the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad* and other texts.

It has been explained by means of the division of its measures (*mātrā*): that *praṇava*, which is dissolved into its cause, the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consisting of the measures— that is, having attained non-distinction through their conjunction (*saṃhitā*) after being in a divided state as *a*,
*u*, and *m*— has attained the state of non-distinction as *oṃ*.

By the word *maheśvara*, which—through its conventional usage established in the *Kośa* (lexicon)—is restricted to the exclusive Śiva who is the object of worship, the meaning is as follows: that which is to be propounded as the supreme and primary [deity] is *maheśvara*.
Through each individual *mātrā* of the *praṇava*, the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as the Vedas—the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman*—are [respectively] signified.

The words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ* denote these three worlds as distinct entities; however, by the word *om* taken as a whole, the intention is that the reality of Maheśvara, which is the basis of the entire collective totality, is expressed. This is stated in the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad* and in the *Kārikās* of the teacher Gauḍapāda.
And this is clear. In the Vedabhāṣya, however, taking the phrase "He who is at the beginning of the Veda is Maheśvara" as the subject, it is explained:

"The 'beginning' (*ādi*) of the Vedas—such as *agnim īḷe purohitam* (Ṛgveda 1.1.1) and *iṣe tvorje tvā* (Śukla Yajurveda 1.1)—is the commencement; in that commencement, whatever vowel (*svara*) and whatever phoneme (*varṇa*) [occur]..."
He exists in the form of the *praṇava*, and that sound, the *praṇava*, is established and expounded in the Vedānta and the Upaniṣads,
such as in the passage beginning, "This syllable Om is all this. And that sound, the *praṇava*, becomes dissolved at the time of meditation into *prakṛti*, the unmanifest cause of the world.

Having meditated upon Virāj, Hiraṇyagarbha, and the Unmanifest within the syllables A, U, and M, one should dissolve the form of Virāj into the syllable U, which is Hiraṇyagarbha; and one should dissolve that syllable U, which is Hiraṇyagarbha, into the syllable M, which is the form of the Root Nature (Mūlaprakṛti). Then, that which is beyond the Praṇava which has thus merged into Prakṛti— [is the Supreme.]

The supreme Nāda is to be meditated upon in the form of the fourth *mātrā*; this is to be known as Maheśvara. By means of this mantra, the reality previously designated by the term "gagana" has been explained; that is, it is explained by the statement restricted to the exclusive state of Śiva-Maheśvara. "Exclusive to Śiva" (*śivaikāntika*) means that, by necessity, it is Śiva alone.

The term "Maheśvara," when being employed, is connected with such statements as "the sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda," and so forth; because this constitutes a prescription of a real entity, [it follows that] meditation has qualities as its object.
In response to the inquiry as to what qualities it possesses, [the text] states:

"The supreme Brahman is Truth and Reality" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.12.1), because this prescribes the object to be meditated upon. Having thus referred back to the meditation enjoined by the injunction "That is to be meditated upon," [the question arises]: what is that [meditation]?

The meaning is that, when there arises a desire to know whether [the deity] has Viṣṇu as its object or Śiva as its object, the determination that it has Maheśvara as its object is made by means of the scriptural passage, "The sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.3), aided by the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti-nyāya*). By that—
There is no deficiency even in the absence of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), which convey the sense of being enjoined.

Regarding the phrase "by way of having a quality as its object": according to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa scripture, "In whatever manner one meditates upon it, that very thing one becomes," meditation is the cause of various fruits precisely by conforming to the qualities that serve as its own modes.
The point is that since knowledge distinct from non-conceptual [knowledge] is necessarily possessed of a mode (saprakāraka), meditation must have qualities as its object.
"Ṛtam, satyam, param brahma"— Ṛtam, satyam, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa...

"In the very same context, by the mantra recited as 'To the dark-brown one, whose vital seed is drawn up, who has diverse eyes; salutation indeed to the one whose form is the universe' (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.12.1),
there are three attributes— namely, being dark-brown, having the vital seed drawn up, and having diverse eyes— "

Based on the lexicon stating "Virūpākṣa is the three-eyed one" (*Amarakośa* 1.1.32), since these [epithets] are determined to refer exclusively to Śiva and are prescribed as qualifiers of the object of worship, it is understood that the *dahara-vidyā* has Paramaśiva as its sole subject. Furthermore, the meaning of the mantra beginning with "Ṛta" is presented in the Bhāṣya as follows: "That which is this supreme..."

Brahman is that truth which is non-sublatable. Truth is of two kinds: the empirical (vyāvahārika) and the ultimate (pāramārthika). Forms such as Hiraṇyagarbha and the like constitute empirical truth. By means of setting those aside, the ultimate truth is demonstrated; thus it is qualified as "the Truth that is Reality" (*ṛtaṃ satyam*).

The meaning is that it is absolutely true. Such Brahman, for the sake of bestowing grace upon its devotees, assumes a human form consisting of Umā and Maheśvara. Therein, on the right side, which is the portion of Maheśvara, he is black in color; on the portion of Umā, he is tawny in color. And by means of yoga, he...

Furthermore, because the mantra "one's own semen [is placed] in the aperture of Brahmā" (svakīyaṃ reto brahmarandhre) prescribes qualities unique to Paramaśiva, it is understood that its essential nature is the Śiva-tattva.
By holding [the breath], one becomes one whose semen is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*). Because he has three eyes, he is Virūpākṣa.

The ellipsis is "by following such a Supreme Lord. May there be salutation to that very Puruṣa, the Virūpākṣa, who is the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*) because, as the cause of the world, his nature is the entire universe.

But is it not the case that in this very Upaniṣad, by means of the section beginning with "The thousand-headed God" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.11.1), Nārāyaṇa—possessing attributes such as having a thousand heads—is declared? Indeed, there exists this section: "The thousand-headed God, the thousand-eyed, the great Puruṣa, whose limbs are all this, who has extended beyond this world by ten fingers' breadth. From Him is born the vital breath, from Him the mind, from Him the senses, from Him the ether, the fire, the water, and the earth supporting all. And so forth. Thus, since Nārāyaṇa is already established here as possessing these qualities, why is he mentioned again? [This is the objection. This is the section: "The thousand-headed God, the thousand-eyed, the great Puruṣa, whose limbs are all this, who has extended beyond this world by ten fingers' breadth. From Him is born the vital breath, from Him the mind, from Him the senses, from Him the ether, the fire, the water, and the earth supporting all. And so on. Therefore, because Nārāyaṇa is already described in this very Upaniṣad through the section beginning "The thousand-headed God," [why is he mentioned again? This is that section.
The thousand-headed God, whose eyes are everywhere, who is the source of bliss for all,
the universal Nārāyaṇa, the imperishable, supreme Lord.
Nārāyaṇa, Hari, is the eternal supreme beyond all, the universe itself;
this entire world is indeed the Puruṣa, and upon him the universe depends for its life.
To Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Self of the universe, the eternal, auspicious, and infallible;
the great object of knowledge, the soul of all, and the supreme refuge.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light, the supreme Self;
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman, the supreme reality.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditator; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditation; and he who is higher than even the supreme is Nārāyaṇa, the one who is beyond the highest.
Whatever exists in this entire world, whether it is seen or even heard,
Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all of that, both within and without.
The infinite, immutable, and wise one, the ocean-born source of all auspiciousness;
and the heart, resembling the interior of a lotus bud, facing downwards.
Situated one span below the lower lip and above the navel,
it shines, filled with garlands of flames, as the great abode of the universe.
It hangs down, covered with veins, resembling a sheath;
at its end is a subtle cavity, and in that everything is established.
In its center is a great fire, with universal radiance and faces on all sides;
it stands consuming the food, distributing it, ageless and wise.
Lying horizontally, upwards, and downwards, his rays are continuous; they heat his own body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
In its center, a flame of fire is situated, extremely subtle and pointing upwards;
it is radiant like a streak of lightning standing in the midst of dark rain clouds.
Thin like the awn of wild rice, yellow, radiant, and resembling a minute atom—
within the center of that crest resides the Supreme Self.
"He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Hari, he is Indra, he is the Imperishable, the Supreme Self-ruler" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.11.1–2).
Although the preceding section concludes precisely at "He who is beyond is Maheśvara" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.3), the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka is indeed distinct from that.

By this much alone, it is established that the previously mentioned meditation on the "small" (*dahara*) has Maheśvara as its object, and that He alone is the one to be meditated upon in that *dahara*-meditation;
nevertheless, there is a discussion regarding the lotus-cavity of the heart and so forth even in this section.
This doubt should be understood as having been raised by the Sattva-nature.
Here, in order to resolve this, the author of the *Candrikā*,
relying upon passages from the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*, the *Atharvaśiras*, and the *Kaṭhavallī* that address the same subject matter, states:

Having established that the Dahara-vidyā has Paramaśiva as its object, [the author] describes the mention of Nārāyaṇa as the counter-correlative of the heart— which serves as the locus for the meditation— in order to prevent the aforementioned meditation from having an indefinite object, and for the sake of satisfying the aspirant's expectation; [this is done] by [the mention of] Nārāyaṇa.
By means of meditating upon the *liṅga* of light that is unique to his own heart-lotus,

he attains the state of Brahman; thus, he also applies such scriptural passages as "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman, the Reality" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 10.11.1), [concluding] that there is nothing higher than Nārāyaṇa.
Even in the case of a compound ending in the fifth case (pañcamī-samāsa), he shows the intention of a certain Śaiva; however,

since it is impossible to construe all the statements found in the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad in such a manner according to their own inherent force (svārasya), this interpretation will not be pleasing to those with impartial minds.

By relying on the etymological derivation that *nārāyaṇa* refers to "that whose abode (*ayana*) is the multitude of men (*nara*"), and by considering the beginning and conclusion of the three *anuvākas*, one should understand that the term *nārāyaṇa* refers exclusively to Paramaśiva; thus, the contingency of the present meditation having an indefinite object must be avoided.

Since worship consists of mental activity, and since multiple forms of worship toward a single symbol are observed in the scriptures, one may argue that there is no harm even if the worship of the *dahara* (the small space) has an indefinite object. However, one should not fall into the error of thinking that, if this were the case, the wearing of internal symbols (*abhyantaraliṅga*) would fail to be established.

It should be understood that because the internal wearing of the *liṅga* by worshippers is established without obstacle according to the first and third sections (*anuvāka*), the attempt to reconcile [the two views] through the identity of the two deities has been disregarded as it contradicts the Vīraśaiva Āgamas.
If not, then having meditated upon the stainless and pure lotus of the heart, in its center [one should meditate upon] that which is luminous and free from sorrow,
inconceivable, unmanifest, infinite in form, auspicious, tranquil, immortal, and the source of Brahman.

From here onwards, we shall follow the original text as written. Regarding the phrase "of Nārāyaṇa": thus, in accordance with the statement, "He who is supreme is Maheśvara" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.3), the term *Maheśvara* itself—by relying on its etymological derivation (*yoga*) as "He who is both Great (*mahān*) and Lord (*īśvara*)"—refers specifically to Nārāyaṇa.

The intention of one who suspects that this [interpretation] might be somehow untenable is as follows. He refutes this, saying "no. One should construe the passage by supplying the words "in the middle of that lotus of the heart which exists," based on such texts as, "The lotus of the heart is stainless and pure" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 6). "Stainless" (*viraja*) means free from the transformations of the dust of passion, hatred, and so forth.

Pure—meaning devoid of the six material modifications (*vikāra*) shown by the great seer Yāska, the author of the *Nirukta*, in the aphorism: "It is born, it exists, it grows, it transforms, it declines, it perishes" (*Nirukta* 1.2). Having reflected upon and meditated [on this] in the center—that is, within the lotus.

It is luminous, having the nature of stainless light. It is free from sorrow, being devoid of anxiety due to the absence of fear regarding destruction and the like, and because it delights in its own self, there is no separation from what is desired. It is inconceivable, not becoming an object of such thought as "how great is the measure of this reality? Why?

Thus, it is called the "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) because it is not manifest due to the minds of living beings being shrouded by ignorance. Regarding this, the Śruti states: "The Brāhmaṇas seek to know it through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Therefore, it is that which becomes the object of knowledge for others once their impurities have been destroyed by the performance of desireless sacrifices and other such practices.
It is that which does not pervade all things. Its form is such that it is devoid of both these types of limitations.
It is *śiva*, meaning its nature is auspicious (*kalyāṇasvarūpa*), or, by the etymology "that in which everything lies," it is the substratum of all.
It is *praśānta*, being of a single uniform aspect like the flame of a lamp in a windless place. It is *amṛta*, eternal. It is the source of Brahman (*brahmayoni*).
To Brahmā, the Veda, and Viriñci; that which is devoid of beginning, middle, and end; the one, all-pervading, wonderful Lord who is consciousness and bliss, formless;
accompanied by Umā, the Supreme Lord, the Master, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful.

(6–7) Thus, by the statement of the *Kaivalyopaniṣad*: "In the center of the heart, [is] the one who is the measure of a hair's tip, the Viśvedeva, the Jātavedas, the most excellent" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1), that which is well-known as the *yoni*, the cause—[which is] devoid of beginning, middle, and end; "beginning" being origination, and "middle" being...

It is devoid of the three states beginning with old age, as well as internal destruction; it is one, being devoid of a second of its own kind; it is all-pervading and omnipresent; it is consciousness-bliss. Here, by the use of the neuter gender, the sense is that it is the substratum of eternal knowledge and bliss, through the suffix *ac* (added after the class of words beginning with *arśas*). It is formless, without parts, and wondrous.
He is wondrous through his lordly powers, such as *aṇimā* and others, which remain unseen in the world; he has Umā as his companion.

Here, by means of the very letters *u*, *m*, and *ā* that constitute the *praṇava* (OM)—which denote Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra respectively—the feminine gender is intended to express the predominance of Śakti.

This is to be established by adding the suffix *ṭāp*. By means of those three forms, the Power (*śakti*)—which is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe—is designated by the term *Umā* as being situated on the left limb of Paramaśiva in the form of Pārvatī. She is his companion (*sahāyā*), meaning she moves together with him through the exclusion of non-conjunction (*ayogavyavacchedena*).

By whom [He is served], that Supreme Lord, the Lord of lords—the meaning is that He is one who does not have His lordship defined by being resident in any person other than Himself; the Master, the capable one; the Three-eyed One, whose eyes are the sun, the moon, and fire; the Blue-throated One, [so called] due to His being subject to the grace of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).

With a throat possessing a dark hue produced by having swallowed the *hālāhala* poison, or rather, bearing the luster of Viṣṇu fastened around His neck out of affection for His devotees; He is tranquil and devoid of mental distraction (*vikṣepa*).
According to the statement of the *Kaivalyopaniṣad*, Śiva alone is the sole subject throughout the introduction, conclusion, middle, and intermediate references.

The connection is with the verb "vidhāna" (enjoining) in the phrase "by enjoining," meaning by means of the *irovacana*, the *kaṇṭhavallī-mantra*, and the *chāndogya-vākya*, which enjoin these four things ending in the third case as the objects of worship in the meditation on the *dahara* (the small ether).

The phrase "attaining syntactic unity with that" connects by way of non-difference with the *Chāndogya* passage. The instrumental case in "by means of the injunction" (*vidhānena*) connects with the sense of causality (*hetutva*), which would otherwise result in having an indefinite scope. In the expression "the size of a hair-tip" (*bālāgramātram*), the suffixes *-dvayasaC*, *-dhaN*, and *-mātraC* are applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.37 to denote measurement.
Thus, by the statement of the *Atharvaśiras*—which is consistent throughout its introduction, conclusion, and intermediate references—namely:

"The person (puruṣa) is only a thumb's breadth in size, like a smokeless light; he is the Lord of the past and the future," and by the rule regarding the suffix *mātrac*, [it means] having a measurement like the tip of a hair, that is, like the tip of a child's hair.

The meaning is "subtle. *Viśvedevam* means having the nature of all the gods. *Jātavedas* refers to him from whom the Vedas have arisen or been produced; or, he who knows (*vetti*) or finds (*vindate*) every born (*jātam*) object. *Vareṇyam* means worthy of being chosen, that is to say, the most excellent.

By means of the *Atharvaśiras* statement which is exclusively devoted to Śiva through an examination of its beginning, conclusion, and middle—that is, by reflecting upon and investigating these three parts in their mutual consistency as a single unified whole.

"Beginning" (*upakrama*) refers to the commencement; "conclusion" (*upasaṃhāra*) refers to the closing passage; and "middle" (*madhya*) refers to the intermediate portion of the text. Through the reflection (*parāmarśa*)—that is, the investigation—of these three, they are understood as forming a single coherent discourse.

The sense is that by examining the purport [of the text], the statement from the *Atharvaśiras* is determined to have as its sole purport Śiva alone; thus, it is established that Śiva alone is the object of meditation in the "small" (*dahara*) meditation. "A thumb-sized" (*aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ*) means measured by a thumb. By using the word "thumb," subtlety is indicated.
By that form, it is Maheśvara himself, residing within the heart-lotus, who is denoted. "Puruṣa" means one possessing masculinity;

by this, the states of being neuter or female are excluded. Alternatively, according to the *pṛṣodarādi* rule, the word *puruṣa* is derived from the etymology "he who sleeps in the city" (*puri śete*), thus referring to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*). "Like a smokeless light"—by the word "light" (*jyotis*)...

It is said that [the fire] is blazing; for this very reason, the qualification "smokeless" (*adhūmaka*) is appropriate. This is because, according to the *Kāvyaprakāśa* (2.19), beginning with the verse "Union and separation...

(*saṃyogo viprayogaś ca*), it is stated that just like conjunction (*saṃsarga*), separation (*viprayoga*) also serves as a cause for the cognition of a specific distinction, as in the example "Hari is without conch and discus" (*aśaṅkhacakro hariḥ*).

And thus, the meaning is that he is of the nature of pure light, like a blazing fire devoid of smoke. Regarding the phrase "the Lord of what has been and what is to be" (*īśāno bhūtabhavyasya*): here, by the word *bhavya*, both the present and the future are expressed. Consequently, the meaning is that he is the master of all things existing in the past, future, and present times.

And by the mantra from the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (Kaṭha 4.13), [the term "sacrificial animal"] is applied according to the logic of the goat-sacrifice (*chāgapaśunyāya*). This is the intended meaning: in the injunction for the immolation of the sacrificial animal, "One should immolate the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.11.6), the word "animal" (*paśu*) denotes the class of animals in general.

Having introduced the attainment of the animal in general through the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) sūtra, "In the injunction regarding the animal, there is no restriction because there is no specific distinction" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 6.8.30), [the author] establishes the goat as the victim through the final (siddhānta) sūtra, "Or rather, it is the goat, because of the wording of the mantra" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 6.8.31), citing: "Of the goat, the sacrificial oblation, the omentum, the fat... (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.6.8.1).

Thus, since a specific animal in the form of a goat is mentioned in the mantra, it has been established that even though the injunction for the immolation of an animal prescribes an animal in a general sense, the goat alone is to be understood as the animal, in accordance with the requirement that the mantra and the injunction form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*). By that same principle— now, as for this which is in this city of Brahman...
In the Chāndogya passage beginning with "The small lotus-abode" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1),

although the specific nature of the object of meditation is not perceived through the words *yat* and *tat*, in the Taittirīya passage which teaches meditation on that which resides within the lotus of the heart— namely, "He who is supreme is Maheśvara" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad)— [the nature is specified].

Thus, by means of the term "Maheśvara" occurring in syntactic agreement with that [passage], [it refers to the one described in] Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11: "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace, and within it the small ether (ākāśa)..."

In the passage from the Kaivalyopaniṣad, "That which is within is to be sought; it is the lotus of the heart, stainless and pure," [the Lord is described] by means of five words: Śiva, accompanied by Umā, the Supreme Lord, the three-eyed, and the blue-throated.
In the Atharvaśiras statement, "the size of a hair-tip," by the term *jātavedas* situated upon the fire whose nature is Rudra;
and in the Kaṭhavallī mantra, "the size of a thumb," by the term *Īśāna*— it is specifically Śiva, the Lord of Umā, who resides within the center of the heart.

It should be observed with an impartial perspective that, because the four Upaniṣads teach [Him] as the object of worship, the status of the Lord Umāpati alone as the object of the Dahara-upāsanā becomes firmly established.
As for the purpose of mentioning Nārāyaṇa in this context, it will become clear immediately hereafter.
Now, regarding the phrase "this which": the remainder of the sense is that after the instruction on the previously mentioned knowledge, the Dahara-vidyā (the knowledge of the small) is taught.
"This which" refers to this proximate city of Brahman (*brahmapura*), the abode of the Self, the body, the dwelling, the house;
within it is the "small" (*dahara*) ether—meaning subtle, or capable of burning away evil. Within this...

In the lotus of the heart (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*), there is the inner space (*antarākāśa*); that is to say, within—that is, in the middle—there exists Brahman, which is as unbounded as space. According to the statement of Sāyaṇa in his commentary on the *Taittirīyaka*, the phrase "this being so" (*evaṃ sati*) should also be supplied here. Consequently, in the expression "that which is within it" (*tasmin yadantaḥ*), the word "it" (*tat*) refers once again to the lotus of the heart itself.
It is grasped.

By the Chāndogya passage, "That indeed is what one should desire to understand" (Chā. Up. 8.1.1), and by the word *yat*, that which is denoted by the term *ākāśa* must be understood as Brahman alone. Consequently, in that [lotus]—the Puṇḍarīka...

The meaning is that that which is internal, contained within, the Sadāśiva-tattva which is the nature of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), is what must be sought. He explains this very seeking: "That indeed is what ought to be desired to be known" (tadvāva jijñāsitavyam); it is that which one should desire to know.

The intention is that [the matter] must be determined through deliberation (*vicāra*). Since meditation (*upāsanā*) is preceded by the determination of its essential nature, the purport is that one should meditate after having ascertained the supreme reality of the Lord within the lotus of the heart.
And regarding the statement from the *Chāndogya*: although there is no word unique to Śiva in the *Chāndogya* passage...

Nevertheless, even in the absence of a term specifically denoting another deity, since the *Kaivalyopaniṣad* and other texts determine that Śiva alone is the object of worship within the heart-lotus by means of terms such as "the one with three eyes" (*trilocana*) and "the blue-throated one" (*nīlakaṇṭha*), which are common to Śiva and refer to the subject of meditation located within the heart-lotus.

In accordance with that syntactic unity, it should be recalled from what was stated immediately prior that, by virtue of the words *yat* and *tat* occurring in the Chāndogya passage "That which is within it is to be sought," it is appropriate to understand Śiva alone as being referred to.
And because, by enjoining Śiva as the object of worship through the *dahara-upāsanā*, if another deity were enjoined here, it would result in the contingency of having an indefinite subject matter.
Regarding the phrase "because of the contingency of having an indefinite subject matter": [one might object] that in a single instance, such as in a *śālagrāma* stone or in water, etc.,...

If it is argued that there is no fault in the meditation having indeterminate objects because, despite the identity of the symbols, we observe worship and so forth of many different deities in various places due to differences in the meditations, this is not so;
for the difference in meditation is established by the distinct and specific terms dedicated to each respective deity.
Even if having an indefinite object were not a defect because it has already been determined, since it is possible to establish a single meditation with a definite object,
the position of having an indefinite object must necessarily be rejected; for in the case of symbols such as water and so forth,
various distinct sentences serve to teach those respective meditations.
Since there is no ambiguity regarding the meaning, it is possible for [the text] to function as a prompt for unimpeded practice;
even if one accepts that, in the present case, a single Taittirīyaka passage is being drawn toward two distinct aspects of the object of meditation.
Because its meaning would be doubtful, its capacity to incite action (*pravartakatva*) would be destroyed; therefore, it is not possible to accept that [the texts] have an indefinite subject matter.
This defect should be understood as being raised with the intention that the three *anuvākas* share a single object of meditation (*upāsanā*).

Furthermore, in the context of injunctions for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*), there are three factors: the object of meditation (*upāsya*), the act of meditation (*upāsanā*), and the meditator (*upāsaka*).
When there arises an expectation for the nature of the object of meditation as something to be realized, [the text] states "Nārāyaṇa, the great object of knowledge" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.11.1),

and so forth; then, by demonstrating the small lotus with the words "resembling the interior of a lotus bud" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.11.2), it shows that what remains [to be known] is immeasurable (Mokṣadharma 6.7.21).

Thus, by means of the principle of the "unlimited locus" (*aparimitādhikaraṇanyāya*) and through this extensive argument, having established that Śiva alone is the object of the meditation on the small space (*daharopāsanā*),
he explains the consistency of the term "Nārāyaṇa" occurring within that context, beginning with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).

Regarding the phrase "in the seeker's desire": since worship necessarily involves a relationship between both the object of worship and the worshipper, once the nature of the object of worship has been determined through its syntactic unity with other Upaniṣadic passages, the term *Nārāyaṇa*— by the method of elimination— serves solely to provide the nature of the worshipper.
The author’s intention is that [the word *anta*] is appropriate here. In this very context, he also incorporates another reason:
because it is impossible to look toward anything else by abandoning Nārāyaṇa, who is heard in close proximity [to the term].

This is shown by the passage beginning with "of what remains when there is no measure" (*aparimāṇe śiṣṭasya*). It is heard in the section on the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*): "One cow should be given; six should be given; twelve [should be given]."
"Twenty-four should be given; a hundred should be given; a thousand should be given; an unlimited number should be given.

Regarding this, there is a doubt concerning the term "unlimited": does the word "unlimited" serve as a prohibition of the numbers already mentioned in proximity, such as oneness and so forth? Or rather...

Regarding "of the commonality of measure": in this context, the following is the sūtra of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "In the case of the 'unmeasured' (*aparimita*), there is a prohibition of number for what remains, because that is what is heard [in the scripture]" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 6.7.21). This is the meaning:
in the word *aparimita*, there is a prohibition of the measure consisting of numbers—such as oneness and so forth—which is prescribed for what remains by means of oneness and so forth.

A refutation is stated. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of its being heard as such" (*tacchrutitvāt*). This means because that number—oneness and so forth—is heard [in scripture] through the suffix *ktin* denoting an action; that is to say, because of its proximity.
In the same way, in the present context, regarding the locus of meditation, namely the heart, in the passage "resembling the interior of a lotus bud" (*padmakośapratīkāśam*).

When it is asked, "Whose heart [is meant] when this is being described?", since there is an expectancy for a correlative, the sense is that because Nārāyaṇa is the "great object of knowledge" (*mahājñeya*), that which is related to him must be understood as the referent due to his proximity. Even though this is a sūtra of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), namely, "There is no restriction" (*aniyamaḥ*, Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 6.7.23).

Since this very point— that [the number] is not restricted— is established by the two subsequent sūtras beginning with "ityādi," nevertheless, in a case where there is an absence of any such powerful contradictory authority— even though the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is set aside by the force of the natural understanding (*svārasika-pratyaya*) generated by the word *aparimita* (unlimited) and by the greatness of the scope of the statement "one [portion] should be given" and so forth— [the unlimited applies].

Since it would follow that He [Nārāyaṇa] would be the counterpart to that very small lotus, and because it is impossible for Him to be the object of His own worship within His own heart, it is established that Śiva alone is the one to be worshipped in the heart of Nārāyaṇa.
Nor does this contradict the scriptural passage: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.3).

It should not be argued that, upon hearing this sentence, the connection [of the qualities] with the lotus-hearts of the ascetics (*yatins*) alone should occur as the counter-correlates; for, by the logic of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) indicated by the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the subject at hand, which is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), [the qualities belong] to Nārāyaṇa.
The sense is that there is no obstacle whatsoever to determining the heart-lotus as the counter-correlative [of the "not-this"].

In reality, however, this is merely a supplementary argument, since it is more appropriate to understand the "worshipper" alone as the counter-correlative of the heart. As for the resolution of the doubt arising from the word "Nārāyaṇa," it has already been stated previously regarding "man" (nara).

According to the etymology "this is the goal (*ayana*) of *nārāḥ*," or by the derivation that *nārāḥ* refers to the waters—as stated in the *Manusmṛti*: "The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara; since they were his primordial abode (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa" (1.10)—it means "he whose abode is the *nārāḥ*."

Alternatively, by relying on its etymological derivation (*yaugikatva*), it is more appropriate to state that in this context the word *Nārāyaṇa* refers specifically to Lord Śiva; conversely, it is impossible to argue otherwise,
given the presence of many such epithets as "blue-throated," "three-eyed," and "accompanied by Umā."

Rather than abandoning the conventional meaning and resorting to the strained assumption of another meaning for [the word] as a whole, it is more appropriate to make such an assumption regarding the single word *nārāyaṇa* itself.

Nor is there any contradiction with the phrase "those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta" (*vedāntavijñānasuniścitārthāḥ*). [The reading is: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta."

"Those striving through the yoga of renunciation, whose being is purified, are all liberated at the time of their final end in the world of Brahman by means of the supreme immortality" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.3).
Regarding the *prayāja* offerings enjoined by the sentence "He offers the *samidhs*":

For, just as [the *hṛdaya* mantra] is necessarily connected to the New and Full Moon sacrifices because it is recited within their context (*prakaraṇa*), so too the *hṛdaya* mentioned in the section on Nārāyaṇa must necessarily be connected to Nārāyaṇa.
Moreover, from that [state], Hari— the Imperishable Self— revealed Himself to him as reclining upon the lotus of his own heart.

By the statement in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*, "The Murāri of the gods [worships] the Īśvara-liṅga" (62.23), which demonstrates the worship of the *prāṇa-liṅga* residing within the heart of Nārāyaṇa, [it is shown that this is consistent with] the *Bhagavad Gītā*:
"Into that very same Primeval Person I take refuge, from whom the ancient process of emanation has issued forth" (Bhagavad Gītā 14.4).
Having thus shown the Person who is to be taken as refuge by Kṛṣṇa, when it was asked "Who is He?", [he replied]:
"But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self (Paramātman), who..."

The statement "the Imperishable, having entered the three worlds, sustains them" is recited immediately prior to the passage concerning the small space (dahara). Regarding the word "of the ascetics" (yatīnām):
since they possess knowledge and are thus fit to be worshippers, it is their heart alone that should be understood as the object of reference.

The intention of the questioner is as follows: by the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*), just as the five *prayāja* offerings enjoined by the five sentences— "He offers the *samidhs*," "He offers the *iḍas*," "He offers the *barhis*," "He offers to *tanūnapāt*," and "He offers with the *svāhā*-utterance" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.6.1.1)— are subsidiary to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
The intention of the subsequent portion is that one who has recited the *Hṛdaya* mantra found in the *Nārāyaṇa-prakaraṇa* must accept its connection with Nārāyaṇa;
the meaning is that Sadāśiva, in the form of a *liṅga*, is worshipped by Nārāyaṇa within his own heart-lotus (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*).
He establishes this through the *Vāmana Purāṇa* and the words of the *Bhagavad Gītā*, beginning with the verse "Then the immutable Self" (*tato'vyayātmā*).

Although in the *Gītā*, after stating: "But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Supreme Self" (15.17), it continues: "Since I transcend the perishable and am even superior to the imperishable, therefore in this world... [the Lord declares His supremacy].

"Īśvara" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.17); "The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna" (Bhagavad Gītā 18.61). By thus determining that the Person who is one's own object of worship, residing within the heart, is the Lord who is the exclusive devotee of Śiva; and...
Because it must necessarily be admitted that Nārāyaṇa is connected with the heart, which is the locus for the meditation on the "small" (dahara);
now, even though in this manner, according to the aforementioned sequence, it is established that Paramaśiva is the object of meditation in the meditation on the "small,"...
If it is argued that there is no proof for its being in the form of a *liṅga* therein, and thus the wearing of an internal *liṅga* is not established,
this is not so; for in the *Haṃsa Upaniṣad* and other scriptures, as well as in the *Vāmana Purāṇa* cited [therein], it is determined to be of that very form.
By the statement, "And he is celebrated in the Vedas as Puruṣottama" (15.18),

his own status as the Supreme Person is declared; nevertheless, there is no contradiction whatsoever, because that declaration refers specifically to the Supreme Lord who dwells within the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

"Because there is no evidence for its being in the form of a *liṅga*. The word "in the Gītā" is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. This is because evidence for that [form] has been shown in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*. Regarding the phrase "the *Haṃsa Upaniṣad*": even if there were no evidence for its being in the form of a *liṅga* in the Gītā, nevertheless, since other evidence exists, nothing is lost by its being supported by such proof.
Such is the intention.
For instance: this is that supreme *haṃsa*, resembling ten million suns, by whom all this is pervaded.
Its activity is eightfold: on the eastern petal is the activity of merit (*puṇya*); in the southeast...
Sleep, laziness, and so forth occur in the south (Yāmya); cruelty of mind in the southwest (Nairṛta); sinful intent in the west (Vāruṇī);

the inclination for play in the northwest (Vāyavya); the thought of traveling and such in the north (Saumya); pleasure and affection in the northeast (Aiśānya); the acquisition of wealth in the center;
detachment in the pericarp; and the waking state in the filaments.

Having cited the *Vāmana Purāṇa* as authoritative evidence for the fact that the reality of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratattva*), which resides within the heart-lotus, exists in the form of a *liṅga*, he also cites a passage from the *Haṃsopaniṣad*: "This is He...
[and] "The supreme *haṃsa*... [which refers to it] by way of its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

Because of the common property of purity in discrimination— just as a swan is the agent that discriminates between clear water and milk— the authors of the scriptures employ the designations "swan" (*haṃsa*) and "supreme swan" (*paramahaṃsa*) for the knower of the Self. Regarding its eightfold activity,
twelve divisions are conceived for the lotus of the heart, corresponding to the eight directions.

There are eight petals. Four portions, in the form of the central filaments and the pericarp (*karṇikā*) as well as the *liṅga*, are conceived within the middle of the petals. It is stated here that through the sense of identifying with each respective part of the self, there arises a corresponding activity and a corresponding state for the self in those [portions], beginning with the words "on the eastern petal, Puṇyamati," and so forth.
On the eastern petal, in the relationship characterized by egoity (*abhimāna*), there arises the desire to perform meritorious deeds; in this manner, the subsequent [petals] are also to be explained.

In the pericarp (*karṇikā*) is dreaming; in the *liṅga* is deep sleep (*suṣupti*); upon the abandonment of the lotus is the fourth state (*turīya*). When the *haṃsa* [rests] in the resonance (*nāda*)...
Then it becomes dissolved, even that which is beyond the fourth (*turīyātīta*) (Haṃsa Upaniṣad 2). Here, in this *liṅga*, there is deep sleep (*suṣupti*);
thus, the nature of Śiva, who resides within the heart, as a *liṅga* is clear.
Although thirteen parts pertaining to the self are shown here, the mention of its being eightfold—stating "it becomes eightfold"—is [as follows]:

The states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (turiya), and that which transcends the fourth (turiyatita) are to be understood merely by the absence of the conventional usage of "mental modification" (vrtti). Regarding the nature of Śiva as the *liṅga*: otherwise, since there is no fourth element beyond the pericarp and filaments in the center of a lotus, [the state of] deep sleep would reside in the *liṅga*.
The sense is that it would be without an object.
As for the scriptural statements:
"In the *ādhāra* [cakra] it resembles gold; in the heart, it has the luster of coral."
"A yogi should contemplate the linga, which has the luster of crystal, between the eyebrows"—
such statements from the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* and other texts are to be considered here.
Now, regarding the meditation on the "small [space]" (*dahara-upāsanā*) in this Upaniṣad, [it is argued that] Nārāyaṇa is the worshiper.

Do not fear that by determining that Śiva is the object of worship, the statements such as "The Supreme Brahman is Nārāyaṇa" and "Nārāyaṇa is the highest" found in the *Sahasraśīrṣa* section of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (10.11.1) would be contradicted.

Because it is impossible for anyone other than Nārāyaṇa— who has attained the state of being that very essence— to be joined with [the supreme state], which is not shared by others. "In the receptacle, resembling gold" means in the receptacle, which is the site of external worship, or in the navel-cakra.
"Having the luster of coral" means having the hue of a young sprout (*pravāla*). Regarding the phrase "not shared by others":

the intention is that, compared to other worshippers, Nārāyaṇa’s contemplation of the Śiva-liṅga possesses an extreme excellence; thus, through the attainment of the state of Śiva, he too is declared to be the Supreme Brahman.
Some, however, maintain that the phrase "Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman" means "the Supreme Brahman who is beyond Nārāyaṇa.

For this very reason, instead of saying "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman," it is stated precisely as "Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman. Thus, according to the aforementioned reasoning, it is Śiva alone who possesses that supremacy; there is no contradiction whatsoever.
They say there is a contradiction; enough of this excessive detail.

Thus, having prescribed the internal wearing of the *liṅga* in the form of meditation upon the *jyotir-liṅga* in this Upaniṣad, the external wearing of the *liṅga* in the form of the chosen *iṣṭa-liṅga* is also enjoined:
"He establishes all forms" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.16.1).

Regarding the phrase "some, however": in this view, in the expression "having Nārāyaṇa as the supreme," a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*) is to be understood. [The mantras are: "Homage to the Lord of the Nidhana; homage to the one near the Lord of the Nidhana."

Salutation to the Upward One; salutation to the upward-facing Liṅga; salutation to the Golden One; salutation to the golden Liṅga; salutation to the Refulgent One; salutation to the refulgent Liṅga; salutation to the Divine One;
salutation to the divine Liṅga; salutation to Bhava; salutation to the Liṅga of Bhava; salutation to Śarva.

Salutation to Śarvaliṅga; salutation to Śiva; salutation to Śivaliṅga; salutation to Jvala; salutation to Jvalaliṅga; salutation to Ātman; salutation to Ātmaliṅga; salutation to Parama; salutation to Paramaliṅga. This establishes the universal emblem (sarvaliṅga) of Soma and Sūrya.
The mantra "pāṇmantraṃ pavitram" is recited in the sixteenth anuvāka of the Taittirīyaka Āraṇyaka.

Since the commentary composed by Sāyaṇācārya on these mantras is not available, it cannot be stated with certainty where their application lies; nevertheless, by examining the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the mantras—
Regarding the attainment of the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) in the prostration to Īśvara for those [mantras] ending in *namaḥ*:

[it occurs] by virtue of being an auxiliary to the worship of Gārhapatya, as prescribed by direct Vedic revelation in the passage, "He worships Gārhapatya with the verse addressed to Indra" (*MaiS* 1.5.11).

Just as there is a sublation of the status of [the mantra] "liṅgaprāptendropasthāna" being a subordinate element, so too, upon hearing the supplementary portion of the text "etatsomasya sūryasya," the word *etat*—
which refers back to the preceding collection of mantras and ends in a lost instrumental case— [denotes] Soma residing within the solar orb together with Umā, and [refers to] everything.

Since it is understood that the application [of the act] pertains to the installation of every kind of linga—such as those made of gold, jewels, or narmada stone—the status of prostration as an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the linga (as established by the context) is set aside.

Now, one might object: "In this case, because the verb 'sthāpayati' ends in the present indicative (*laṭ*) and lacks the optative (*liṅ*) or other such suffixes, the possibility of an injunction (*vidhi*) is not present."

It should not be argued that, just as in the case of "He sprinkles the rice-grains" and "He threshes the rice-grains" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 1.19.1), an injunction is possible because the form that serves as the motivator for an injunction exists—even in the absence of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth—so too should it be here; for in this case, the form that serves as the motivator for an injunction is absent. To explain:

"An injunction (*vidhi*) applies where [a thing] is not at all established by other means; a restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies when it is optionally established; and an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) is said to apply when it is established both there and elsewhere. (Tattvavārttika 1.2.4). From this verse, it is understood that where an act not established by any other means of knowledge is enjoined by this [injunction] alone, that is an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), such as "one [should thresh] rice-grains" (*vrīhīn*).
Regarding the statement "he sprinkles" (*prokṣati*):

"because of the absence of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. The meaning is that only the optative (*liṅ*), the imperative (*loṭ*), and others possess the capacity to convey what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*).
"Because of the presence of the form that functions as the motivator of an injunction": the very state of being unestablished (*aprāptatva*) is that form.

"Entirely unobtained" (*atyantamaprāpta*) refers, for example, to the injunction "one sprinkles the rice grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*). "When there is an option" (*pākṣike sati*) refers, for example, to the injunction "one threshes the rice grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*). In this case, since both [methods]—such as scratching with the nails and threshing—are equally applicable as means for removing the husks toward the primary purpose at hand, it is established by this very rule that the action must be performed by this [threshing] alone and not by the other.

In that case, it is an *niyamavidhi* (restrictive injunction), as in "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*). When there is the possibility of a combination— both in that specific instance and elsewhere— that which is enjoined therein is a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification), as in "five five-nailed animals are edible" (*pañca pañcanakhā bhakṣyāḥ*, Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa 17.39)— namely, the hare, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, [the iguana, and the rhinoceros].

By the statement, "The rhinoceros and the tortoise as the fifth," since the consumption of these and other five-toed animals would otherwise be permitted, this is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*) stating that only these five five-toed animals are to be eaten, and no others.

Because [the practice] is already established as an option; that is, both there and elsewhere. For example, in the case of "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten," the statement "among them, in this context, one establishes the wearing of all [five] marks" is not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) regarding the wearing of the marks.
Because this is established by the statement from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, "Having all faces, heads, and necks" (3.11), there is no lack of evidence from other sources; for it says:
"Having all faces, heads, and necks, dwelling in the secret cave of all beings, and all-pervading."
"The Blessed One is therefore all-pervading and auspicious. The meaning of this is as follows:
he establishes that among all the types of methods suitable for those who wear the *liṅga*, there is no application of any one [specific method] to the present case.
Regarding the phrase "sarvaliṅgam" (having all characteristics) in the present context,

it is because it is obtained from the statement of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad. Even though a single dharma such as the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*) and libations (*tarpaṇa*) appears in many Smṛtis, and a single dharma such as the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*) appears in many [Smṛtis]...

An injunction is observed in various recensions (śākhās); its status as an injunction is not contradicted by its function of making known a meaning that has been taught in another Smṛti or another recension.
For all such statements, [the injunction] applies individually to the students of those respective Smṛtis and those respective recensions.

Because it is accepted as being an injunction (*vidhi*) by virtue of its being a communicator of what has been promised; thus, it cannot be suspected that the statement from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, "He establishes all genders," contradicts its status as an injunction. Nevertheless, since they convey meanings that stand in a relationship of general and particular, they possess a mutual dependence of meaning.
It should be understood that this is intended to raise the doubt of a contradiction regarding its status as a ritual injunction (*vidhi*).

"He whose face, heads, and necks are everywhere" (*sarvānanaśirogrīvaḥ*) means Śiva, who, while being sustained, exists there in the form of the desired *liṅga*. Regarding the phrase "dwelling in the cave of all beings" (*sarvabhūtaguhāśaya*):

The meaning is that Śiva, who exists in the form of the *liṅga* as previously cited from the *Haṃsa Upaniṣad*—“He sleeps in the cave of all beings, in the small lotus, in the *liṅga*, [this is] deep sleep” (*Haṃsa U. 2*)—abides within in the form of the internal *liṅga*. He is "all-pervading" (*sarvavyāpī*).
It is devoid of the threefold distinctions; for this very reason, it is all-pervading (*sarvagata*).

Now, one might object that here, because the phrase "possessing all faces, heads, and necks" (*sarvānanaśirogrīva*) shares the same case-ending with its own substantive, Śiva, there is identity between them.
"Whose substratum (adhikaraṇa) consists of faces, heads, and necks. Due to its being a part of a living being (prāṇyaṅga), it is treated as a singular compound (ekavadbhāva).
This explanation should be understood as intending that the word ends in the possessive suffix *ac*, meaning "that which has [a substratum] consisting of all faces, heads, and necks."
However, one should not mistakenly assume this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because there is no word denoting a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) [to serve as the first member],

and because the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*) is prescribed only for *tatpuruṣa* compounds such as *śākapārthiva* or for words derived from verbal roots following prefixes (*prādi*). "Attained through the *Haṃsopaniṣad*" means "revealed by it."

"Devoid of the three kinds of delimitation" means that there are three modes of delimitation: delimitation by time, delimitation by space, and delimitation by substance. Delimitation by time is, for example: "A human being indeed lives for a hundred years. Delimitation by space is: "The abode of sea-monsters extends for a hundred *yojanas*."

Determination of objects (*vastupariccheda*) is as follows: "This is earth; this is water. [Reality] is devoid of these three kinds of determination. It cannot be described in such a manner—as existing for only this much time, existing in only this much space, or having only this specific material nature; that is to say, in reality...

The meaning is that Śiva consists of all things existing in all places and at all times. This is the essential point here: being the non-counterpositive of prior non-existence while being the non-counterpositive of destruction constitutes freedom from limitation by time; and being the non-counterpositive of absolute non-existence constitutes freedom from limitation by space.
The state of not being the counter-correlate of difference (*bhedāpratiyogitva*) is the absence of delimitation by any entity (*vastuparicchedarahitatva*).
Regarding the verse "He whose faces, heads, and necks are everywhere" (*sarvānanaśirogrīvaḥ*), for one who does not recognize [the suffix] *ac* as belonging to the *ārśa-ādi* group,
the intended meaning of the stated sense is obtained through the connection of the substratum and the superstratum (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) with the referent of the word "Śiva."
If you think that, because [the cognition] is determined by the act of awakening, one might doubt how there can be a perception of a substratum (adhikaraṇatā) that contains differentiation—
do not think so; for even in the case of two words with the same case-ending, there is the capacity to convey the status of being a substratum.

Because this was accepted by the venerable feet of Nīlakaṇṭhācārya in the section [of the Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya] beginning with "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition" (1.1.12), and because in that context the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sense of abundance (*prācurya*).
Regarding the phrase "nanvatrātra": how could there be the generation of a cognition of relation—distinct from identity—between two words ending in the nominative case?

This is because the locus-hood (*ādhāratā*) of a substratum is necessarily dependent upon the difference between the substratum and the located (*ādheya*), since the relation of being located (*ādheyatā*) as defined by itself is sublated [in this case].
Thus, it should be understood that locus-hood is inherently imbued with difference. [This applies] to one who is deluded.
He provides the answer in accordance with the knowledge of the questioner, saying "Do not think thus," and so forth.

In reality, however, because there is no connection between "possessor" and "possessed" (ādhārādheya-bhāva) for the term *sarvānanaśirogrīvaḥ*— which here functions as a matup-affix (*arśa-ādi*) derivative— there is indeed no [such] relation between these two.

This is the occasion for raising an objection and providing its resolution. Furthermore, the suffix *ac* should be applied in the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*), because the relation of "being located in" (*ādheyatā*) is not a factor that determines the occurrence of a grammatical operation (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*). Regarding the phrase "by the venerable feet of Nīlakaṇṭhācārya":
by accepting the presence of the letter *k*, when bliss (*ānanda*) and Brahman attain the status of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*), [it follows that] "Bliss is Brahman."

Having raised the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*)— based on the fact that the words "bliss" (*ānanda*) and "Brahman" (*brahma*) in such scriptural passages as "He understood" (*vyajānāt*, *Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.6) and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandaṃ brahma*) possess the same grammatical case-ending, which indicates their non-difference, [the opponent asks] how there can be a relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*)— [the author replies]: "Bliss is [an attribute] of Brahman..."

In accordance with the absence of contradiction from statements indicating distinctions such as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth, it is established as a settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) that Brahman is the substratum of bliss (*ānanda*).
This is the sense: in the Viśiṣṭādvaita system, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the bliss of Brahman.

Since the suffix *mayaṭ* is seen following the genitive case in passages such as "consisting of form" (*rūpamaya*), one must accept a distinction between bliss and Brahman; thus, in the statement "He understood that bliss is Brahman," [the bliss is distinct from Brahman].

It must be admitted that even in cases where words expressing a qualifier and a qualificand are used with identical case-endings, a distinction is sometimes perceived. Although in the present context, one might accept that the word *ānanda* ends in the suffix *ac* (as in *ānandavat*), thereby [denoting] its own substratum...

Alternatively, even if there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) through the relation of non-difference by accepting *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) itself, there is no contradiction; nevertheless,
since the grammatical rule "in Vedic usage, transposition is frequent" prescribes the nominative case even for the sense of the locative,
the relationship of locus and located is obtained without effort even in cases where the case endings are identical.
With the intention of asking why one must resort to the suffix *-ac* (as in *arśas-ādi*) or accept a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*),

Nīlakaṇṭhācārya stated this; however, in reality, since the matter is established by means common to worldly usage— as in "the blue pot" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*)— there is no need for such a resort to Vedic irregularity (*chāndasatva*) through the assumption of a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*).

Since such a reconciliation is improper, even those who maintain that the substratum [of Brahman] is distinct from its qualities— such as the followers of Ānandatīrtha (Madhvācārya)— must accept either the grammatical derivation stated in the *Mahābhāṣya*, "the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *matup* is desired after words expressing qualities," or the definition stated by the Naiyāyikas, regarding [Brahman] as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose... [and so forth].
Since this is accepted by all authors on the grounds that it would contradict the scriptural statement, "Austerity consists of knowledge" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9),
it is indeed proper here as well to accept the understanding of the substratum through the possessive suffix *matup*.
The statement of the teacher Nīlakaṇṭha, however, intends merely that one means does not invalidate another means [of knowledge],
so as not to contradict such scriptural passages as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" and "Whose austerity consists of knowledge";
thus, in the phrase "Brahman is consciousness," [consciousness] refers to the substratum of consciousness.
The explanation by Ānandatīrtha regarding the word "Brahman" is likewise the same;

in the passage "Vijñāna is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5), it is stated that Brahman is the substratum of consciousness (vijñāna). This is also observed in common worldly usage, such as in the expression "a pot with many parts" (bahukapālo ghaṭaḥ).

Nor should it be argued that if the phrase "without face, head, or neck" (ananaśirogrīva) were to mean a linga whose substratum is merely the absence of face, head, and neck, it would contradict the statement "therefore Śiva is omnipresent"; for [the Lord] assumes the form of a desired linga with limited adjuncts (*aupādhika-paricchinna*) for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees. Thus, [he appears as] one without face...

All this is entirely faultless. Regarding the example "the pot has many shards" and so forth: following common worldly perception, just as in the case of "the branch is on the tree," one superimposes upon the whole (avayavin) a substratum-hood (adhikaraṇatva) defined by its parts (avayava), and thus the cognition arises that "the pot has many shards as its substratum. Such is observed in experience.
The point is that even in cases where words stand in the same case-ending, their connection is observed to occur through the relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*).
Although such a cognition is accomplished here by the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself,

nevertheless, in the view of those who do not accept *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning), there must be a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*) in the final member of the compound.
This was stated with the intention that by accepting [this], there is also occasion for another kalpa occupying that same place.

Regarding "contradiction of the statement": the meaning is that since being limited and being unlimited cannot coexist in one and the same thing, the assertion of both in a single locus becomes sublated. Regarding "for the sake of favoring devotees": and thus...

This is because it is possible to construe the passage as follows: having first demonstrated, by means of the preceding statement, that the Lord resides in the lotus of the heart (*daharāmbhoja*)—which is of the nature of a cave—in the form of a subtle light-linga within the head and neck; the subsequent series of statements, beginning with "And the Blessed Lord is all-pervading," is intended to demonstrate His actual, unlimited form. Therefore...
Thus, the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "the Blessed One is all-pervading" is meaningful, as it serves to conjoin the previously understood limited form with [his] omnipresence.
Now, even so—

"A wise person should wear the *prāṇaliṅga* on the head, or on the neck, or on the belly, or on the chest, or likewise on the palm of the hand," according to the statement in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* (6.51).
Having fashioned it, always place the linga wrapped in cloth upon the head,
the neck, the belly, the chest, or in the palm of the hand.

Thus, by this statement from the Śaṅkara-saṃhitā of the Skanda Purāṇa, it is established that the Lord, who is in reality indeed unlimited (aparicchinna) in head and neck, assumes a limited form by His own will for the sake of favoring His devotees and presides over it; therefore, limitation belongs only to the assumed form, while His true nature is unlimited.
The sense is that there is no contradiction whatsoever in [the mantra] being located within the self (*ātmagata*).
Although the wearing of gendered marks (*liṅgadhāraṇa*) is well known, since it is absent in the mouth, one might wonder how this is so;
because it protects from such unexamined reflection, it is therefore called a *mantra*.
Mantra is proclaimed to be twofold, in the form of the signified and the signifier.
The signifier would be in the form of the phonemes, and the signified is Paramaśiva;
therefore, the great seers have declared the identity of the mantra and the deity.
Thus, according to the etymological explanation of Vyāsa, "namaḥ" is declared to be the seat (pīṭha); the letter *śi* is said to be the center,
the letter *vā* is the circular Gomukha, and the letter *ya* is remembered as the Golaka.
The syllable Oṃ is declared to be the liṅga; the six-syllabled mantra is called the liṅga.

Thus, according to the statement from the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*, "namas is the pedestal" (*namaḥ pīṭham*). That which serves as the support for the *liṅga*—consisting of parts such as the *yoni-maṇḍala* and so forth—is called the pedestal (*pīṭha*). The nature of that [pedestal] is superimposed upon the word *namas*, which is a constituent part of the mantra.

The nature of the middle [element] is superimposed upon the syllable *śi*, which is a constituent of the mantra. By the term "cow's mouth" (*gomukha*), the flow of water contained therein is expressed; the nature of that [flow] is superimposed upon the syllable *vā*. By the term "cow-ball" (*golaka*), the cavity serving as the support for the *liṅga* is denoted; the syllable *ya* is conceived as being of the nature of that [cavity].
