The syllable *oṃ* is also conceived in the form of the *liṅga*. Thus, since the identity of the *liṅga* and the mantra is established, and because [the mantra] does not exist apart from the form of the mantra, there is no contradiction in the statement from the verse "all faces, heads, and necks" (*sarvānanaśirogrīva*) that the face is the locus for the wearing of Śiva; this is the intended meaning.
Now, it may be asked:
"Should the wise man wear the *prāṇaliṅga* on the head, or on the throat, or on the belly, or on the chest, or likewise on the palm of the hand?"
By this statement, since many [texts] establish the wearing of the *liṅga* as the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*),

and because the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*) and the *liṅga* are one and the same, it can be said that [the Lord] is established in the mouth in the form of the mantra, and in the head and neck in the form of the *liṅga*.

And in this regard— just as there is an option between "one should sacrifice with rice" and "one should sacrifice with barley" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 6.31.13) because the purpose of producing the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is one and the same, so too it should be understood that [the sacred thread] is to be worn sometimes on the head and sometimes on the neck and other parts.

Anticipating the doubt as to whether that retention must be performed everywhere because of the mention of the locations, or only in certain cases, he provides the resolution: "And here, [the rule] 'with rice-grains'... [is given]. "Because the purpose is one" means that just as in the case of rice and barley for the production of the *puroḍāśa* cake, so it is with respect to the head and other limbs.
The sense is that there is a single purpose for those who wear the *liṅga*, namely liberation (*mokṣa*).
It should be understood that because they yield the same fruit, there is indeed an optional choice (*vaikalpika*) among these locations.
Furthermore, in this Upaniṣad it is said: "The perishable is *pradhāna*; the immortal and imperishable is Hara" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad).
Having thus introduced the Supreme Lord, [the scripture] states: "The wearing of the *liṅga* has been declared to be twofold, accomplishing all goals—
the external and the internal— by the sages who desire liberation."
Whether in the foundation (ādhāra), the heart, or the space between the eyebrows,
the continuous contemplation of the light-liṅga (jyotirliṅga) is called "internal" (antara).

"The perishable is Pradhāna. Pradhāna, which is denoted by the term *prakṛti*, is the three *guṇas* existing in a state of equilibrium; it is perishable (*kṣara*) and subject to transformation. "The immortal-imperishable is Hara. Hara is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), who is immortal (*amṛta*), unchanging (*akṣara*), and immutable (*avikārī*), or he is that which is signified by the *praṇava*. Having commenced—that is, having introduced—the [topic] in the support (*ādhāra*).
At the navel-cakra,
whether one is unable or indeed able to internalize the *liṅga*,
one should wear the external *liṅga* as well, because of the certainty that it is of that same nature. (6.29.38–47)

Thus, even the twofold dhāraṇā obtained from the statement in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*—by means of the [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad] passage, "From meditation upon Him, from union with Him, from becoming His essence" (Śve. U.
1.10)—is due to meditation upon Him, that is, internal contemplation in the form of the Jyotir-liṅga.

Having demonstrated that [the Self] is joined with the form of the desired *liṅga* such as the *yojana*, this passage beginning with "He whose faces, heads, and necks are everywhere" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 3.11) proceeds to show the locus for meditation (*dhāraṇā*) in response to the inquiry as to where it should be held.
In this context, having indicated the location for wearing the internal *liṅga* by the term "dwelling in the cave" (*guhāśaya*),
the failure to indicate the location for wearing the external *liṅga* results in a contradiction of the textual context that becomes as indelible as diamond-paste (*vajralepa*).
"Contemplation of the *jyotirliṅga*" (*jyotirliṅgānusandhāna*) means the contemplation of the *liṅga* composed of light.
The meaning is that remembrance itself is said to be the internal wearing of the *liṅga*.

"In that form" means in the nature of Śiva consisting of light; having firmly grasped such a conviction—this is a *pañcamī* case used with the elision of the suffix *-lyap*. This is obtained from the statement in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*.

The sense is this: since this very text is also extremely esteemed according to this [author's] view, the wearing of both kinds of *liṅga*—which is established as a duty by the force of its own words—is also taught by the *śruti* that serves as its source. "From meditation" (*anudhyānāt*) means from reflection. Thus, the wearing of the two-fold *liṅga* has been enjoined by *śruti*.
Having explained [the previous point], when there arises an expectation regarding the location where that [liṅga] should be worn, the passage beginning with "sarvānanaśirogrīvaḥ" proceeds;
by the phrase "guhāśayaḥ," it indicates the cave in the form of the intellect for the purpose of wearing the internal liṅga,
and by the phrase "sarvānanaśirogrīvaḥ," it indicates the location for wearing the external liṅga.

Thus, everything becomes consistent. Otherwise, by failing to state all the required parts, there would be a deficiency in the treatise and the phrase "having all faces" would be rendered meaningless; this is the intended sense.
If you do not accept this, then the expression "having all faces, heads, and necks" would be entirely purposeless.

For instance: does this sentence enjoin a distinction of face, head, and neck for Śiva, or rather their non-distinctness from him? Not the first; because of the maxim that "every sentence is restrictive," once only that much non-distinction is established, the universal identity (sārvātmya) enjoined by the scripture—"for all this is indeed Rudra"—would be contradicted.

It has already been stated that [the qualification] is purposeful; otherwise, it would be entirely meaningless. By means of the qualification "having all faces, heads, and necks," it is not possible to convey either non-difference from all faces and so forth, or the state of residing in all faces and so forth.

Because one of the two— being the self of all or being omnipresent— necessarily entails a contradiction, in such cases as the statement "he sees with the left eye," even without the particle *eva*, there is a cognition of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) to the effect that "he sees with the left eye alone."

The intention is that the attainment of the exclusion of others (*itaravyāvṛtti*) is the general rule. This very point has been stated: "Every sentence is restrictive" (*sarvaṃ vākyaṃ sāvadhāraṇam*). In the same way, when it is said, "In this village, the Kṣatriya is wealthy," one should also cite the resulting cognition: "Only the Kṣatriya here is wealthy," and so forth. Even though Devadatta has four sons...

In the phrase "they exist," it is not understood that "only Devadatta" [exists]; nevertheless, because the certainty of a sublation (*bādhaniścaya*) is present, even though there is no perception of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) regarding that specific part, there is indeed a perception of restriction regarding the other part, namely, "there are exactly four. And this is clear—now then:
In the sentence "Bring the black cow, Devadatta, with a stick," everything is specified— namely, that the object is indeed the cow,

the action is indeed bringing, and the agent is indeed Devadatta— as shown in the *Mahābhāṣya*, which demonstrates instances where the intended meaning is understood even without the use of the particle *eva*.

The meaning is that the word "tat" (that) is a term expressing the state of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatā*). The underlying intention is that it is impossible to posit a substratum (*āśraya*) and its characteristics without valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
[Objection: But surely, in the passage "having all faces, heads, and necks," there exists a word expressing the state of being a locus...

If it is argued that all this would be so, but that [the required condition] is not present here, we say: "Not so. Since the face, head, and neck exist as the substrata (adhikaraṇa) for this, by means of the possessive suffix *ac*, the futility of this sentence is avoided; for it is better to have the futility of a single word than the futility of an entire sentence.
For by the principle of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), that [meaning] must necessarily be understood through indication;

and this has been accepted in the *Pūrvatantra* regarding the sacrificial food (*havis*) pertaining to the animal sacrifice, in the passage: "There are eleven portions of the animal; he cuts off two of them" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 6.3.10.3).

The meaning is as follows: because the realization of that [deity] is inevitable, the very sentence "all these" (*sarvānana*)—since it would otherwise result in being purposeless unless it were intended to establish the wearing of the *liṅga* as its locus—serves as the authoritative evidence for the definition of the locus and so forth. In reality, however, [the deity is described as]: "The Puruṣa with a thousand heads" (*Ṛgveda* 10.90.1).

Just as in the verses, "Having hands and feet everywhere" (Bhagavad Gītā 13.13) and "Having eyes, heads, and faces everywhere," this [statement] also should be understood as indicating that [the Self] is the essence of all, by means of a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound signifying "that which has the face, head, and neck of all."

And it has been accepted in the *Pūrvatantra* (the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*). The meaning is that, in order to avoid the redundancy of a sentence, the figurative (secondary) sense of a single word has been admitted in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*. He demonstrates that very point:

"When the two-fold cutting [of the portion] is already established by the *codaka* (the rule of extension) according to the principle 'the modified sacrifice is to be performed like the archetype,' then those..."
Having raised the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) objection that the statement enjoining the duality of the cutting—"he cuts twice"—would be redundant, [the author replies:
although the sacrificer is one who takes four portions, the omentum (vapā) must nevertheless be prepared as five portions;
for in this sentence, the word *vapā* refers generally to all the animal-offerings (*pāśuka-havis*), including the heart and other parts.

Having accepted the secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*), since the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the over-pouring (*abhighāra*) exist even in the case of the heart and other organs for the sake of accomplishing the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvadāna*),
when three cuttings would otherwise result, the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) must be cut twice.

Regarding the oblation (*havis*), it is heard in the scripture: "There are eleven portions of the animal; he cuts off two from each. This means that in the animal sacrifice (*pāśukayāga*), there are eleven limbs of the animal, and from each one he cuts off twice—that is, he takes two portions of the sacrificial material (*haviravayava*) from them after the cutting-off (*avadāna*). And because this rite is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the Soma sacrifice...

In this very context, the prima facie (pūrvapak�sa) position is that because the rule of extension (*codaka*)— namely, "the modification is to be performed according to the archetype"— already establishes the requirement of two-fold cutting for the oblations of this [modified sacrifice], the statement "he cuts twice" would be redundant; however, [the sūtra states] that even though the sacrificer is one who offers four portions (*caturavattin*), the omentum (*vapā*) must be prepared as five portions (*pañcāvattā*).
Five cuttings (avadāna) of the omentum (vapā) are prescribed.

At the place of these five cuttings, the first cutting is made of clarified butter (ājya) for the purpose of under-spreading (upastaraṇa); the subsequent three cuttings are made of the sacrificial offering (havis); and the final cutting is again made of clarified butter for the purpose of over-pouring (abhighāraṇa). Thus...

The number five is completed. In this context, in order to avoid the redundancy of the statement "he cuts off those twice," the term *vapā* (omentum) is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to refer to animal-oblation materials in general; thus, the rule of "five-fold cutting" (*pañcāvatta*) applies even to the oblations such as the heart and so forth. Furthermore, in that case, by means of the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the over-pouring (*abhighāraṇa*), the number two [is established].

Since the number five must be completed by way of perfection, it follows that there should be three cuttings from the heart and the other organs. To set aside that [conclusion], it is stated: "He cuts those twice. Therefore, because the previously established number three in the cutting of the sacrificial portions (*havir-avadāna*) is sublated by the number two, the omentum (*vapā*) must be prepared with exactly five cuttings; thus, the previously obtained number five remains intact.

It has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the completion of the number [of portions] must be achieved either by making two cuttings (*avadāna*) for the purpose of spreading the underlayer (*upastaraṇa*), or by performing the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) twice. In this regard, just as the completion of the number five— expressed in the rule "he cuts those twice"— must be accomplished through the increase of the spreading and other acts, so too is its purposeful significance realized.
"Thus it is established; everything is well-founded"—this is our own path.

The ancient teachers, however, maintain that in the injunction "he establishes all the *liṅgas*," this is not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), because—as will be explained later—the qualification "the hand is the purifying mantra" establishes worship having the hand as its locus.
They said that this is because there is no possibility of obtaining [the result] across the three periods of time.

Just as the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *vapā* (omentum) toward the class of sacrificial offerings (*havis*) is accepted in order to avoid the meaninglessness of the sentence, so too,

in order to avoid the meaninglessness of the sentence beginning with "all faces, heads, and necks" (*sarvānanaśirogrīva*), [the figurative indication of the word *sarvānanaśirogrīva* toward the Supreme Self is accepted].
The intended meaning is that one must accept a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the substratum of all [the preceding terms] being beginningless.

As for the phrase "the former teachers, however": the two words *pāṇimantram* and *pavitram* are derived respectively through the analysis *pāṇau mantraḥ pūjanaṃ yasya* (that in which there is worship by means of a mantra in the hand) and *pūyate 'nena* (that by which one is purified).

This indicates that the *liṅga* is an object of worship held in the hand and remains pure even when worn during impure times. Furthermore, since such daily worship is not possible without wearing the *liṅga*, the wearing of the *liṅga* is established through the means of valid cognition known as *arthāpatti* (presumption based on the impossibility of otherwise). Thus, the wearing of the *liṅga* is already obtained [as a duty].
The meaning is that the former teachers stated that it is not possible for the word "sthāpayati" (he establishes) to be an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction).

The reason for their lack of approval here is that since the purpose can be accomplished even by worshipping with clay lingas and so forth, there is no *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility of explaining otherwise).
[Objection: Granted that it may not be an *apūrva-vidhi*, but [according to the rule]: "A Brāhmaṇa [should live] by officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts..."

If it is argued that this must be a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi), just as in the case of "one should acquire wealth" and so forth, that too merely imitates the wearing of a garland of sky-flowers; for regarding the subject of liberation, there is the statement: "One who recites the Rudrādhyāya, even if covered in ashes and lying on a bed of ashes, is liberated from all sins."

Just as the wearing of ashes, rudrākṣas, and so forth—prescribed in the *Śātātapa-smṛti* and other texts—is established as an optional practice, so too the wearing of the *liṅga* is established as an option; therefore, one must accept the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that "only the wearing of the *liṅga* should be performed, not the wearing of ashes and the like. Yet even that [rule] is undesirable.
Having refuted the status of this as an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction) through the preceding discussion— that "one should establish all [the lingas]"—
the author raises the objection that it is a *niyama-vidhi* (a restrictive injunction), beginning with the words "But surely" (*nanu*), etc. Regarding the statement,
"A Brāhmaṇa should acquire wealth by means of officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts," the acquisition of wealth...

The intention is as follows: just as the rule for acquiring wealth—stating that it is obtained through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts—is intended as a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) because those means alone are the causes for the absence of pleasure and pain [and thus lead to merit], so too this [rule] "one should wear the marks" may be intended as a restrictive injunction.
He refutes this with the words beginning "that too is like a flower in the sky," etc. Here:
In this context, the word *niyama* (restriction) refers to *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification). "In the case of the liberated object" means:

in the case of the object that is the nature of the liberated *puruṣa*. This is the intended meaning: under the interpretation of *niyama*, the syntactical construction of the statement "he establishes every *liṅga*" would be "he establishes only every *liṅga*. And thus...
This injunction would be intended to exclude the wearing of ashes, rudrākṣas, and so forth, in the case of the liberated person (muktapuruṣa),
because the act of "wearing" (dhāraṇa) ultimately results in the sense of "establishing" (sthāpana) with the body as its locus;
and that [exclusion] would result in an undesirable consequence.
The state of being a mass, the consciousness of a mass, the quality of saṃsāra as something to be abandoned,
the wearing of the marks of initiation, and likewise the wearing of sacred ash.
The wearing of rudrākṣa beads, as well as the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra,
the practice of the path of devotion, and the worship of the guru and the liṅga.
"And likewise for the yogin; for such is their clarity and acceptance [of grace]. These must be performed with effort by a devotee of Śiva. (5.26–29).
Thus it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* that these are necessary for all.

Because the wearing of vibhūti, rudrākṣas, and so forth is absolutely essential, that very point is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "piṇḍatā piṇḍavijñānam" (the state of being a body, the knowledge of the body, etc.). By the term *piṇḍatā*, the absence of sin (*pāpa*) is expressed; by the word *piṇḍa*, the pure self (*śuddhātman*) possessing that [absence of sin] is expressed. [This refers to] the fact that worldly objects such as sons, wife, and so on, are to be rejected and abandoned.
Knowledge; the wearing of the *liṅga*, sacred ash, and *rudrākṣa* beads as part of initiation;

the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣara-japa*); the performance of actions on the path of devotion such as hearing [the scriptures], chanting [the Lord's names], and sweeping the temple; and the worship and adoration of the Guru, the *liṅga*, and the *yogins*, as well as the acceptance of their grace—these are [the requirements].
The meaning is that these are the necessary duties for a devotee of Śiva. Here, the term "liberated one" (*mukta*) is an illustrative designation for the qualified person (*adhikārī*).

Now, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: since there can be no combination (*samuccaya*) of results—consisting of the prohibition of the non-performance of wearing the *liṅga* followed by the performance of it—and since a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) is thus impossible, [the text must be interpreted otherwise].

"Is it not so, then?"— in this context, the application of the terms *niyama* (restriction) and *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) has been made by mistake in reverse order; for when one adopts the form of excluding others (*itaravyāvartaka*), the term *niyama* applies to cases such as "only five five-nailed animals are to be eaten."

Furthermore, when one accepts the form [of the injunction] whose result is the duty to perform the wearing of the *liṅga* preceded by the prohibition of its non-performance, there is the application of the term "exclusive specification" (*parisaṃkhyā*) because of the similarity to the rule: "One must indeed approach one's wife during her season" (Gautama Smṛti 5.1). In reality, however, the application of the term "exclusive specification" occurs only in the preceding case.

"It is appropriate because, when a combination is impossible, there is an application of exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*). Even though in either exclusive specification or restriction there is no requirement for the possibility of a combination— since, for instance, by the injunction prescribing the eating of five-clawed animals as obtained through passion, it might at some time [occur]...

Even though this [prohibition] excludes other means such as tearing with the nails— which might occasionally be resorted to because the consumption of those other five-clawed animals has already been established, and because the grinding of husks is itself established as a cause for their removal by the injunction of threshing— it is nevertheless stated: "These [five] must be performed with effort by a devotee of Śiva."

The meaning is that since the necessity of performing [the rite] has been stated in [Si0 Śi0 5.29], the non-performance is prohibited by its very nature; therefore, there is no need for a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) or the like.
To this, it is replied: in the statement "he establishes all the *liṅgas*," this is indeed an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). Nor...

It should not be argued that there is no non-attainment [of the practice] at any of the three times because the wearing [of the *liṅga*] is already enjoined by the sentence "with all faces, heads, and necks" (*dhāraṇasya sarvānanaśirogrīva*); for this [sentence] is subordinate to the sentence "all *liṅgas*" (*sarvaliṅga*), which prescribes the wearing of the *liṅga* as the probans (*liṅga*) for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) to be established by itself.

"Not non-attainment throughout the three periods of time. The meaning is that, since the definition of an injunction (*vidhi*) is "that which brings about what is absolutely unestablished," the nature of being an injunction—consisting in the capacity to bring about what was not previously established throughout the three periods of time—is impossible [in this case]. Regarding the phrase "the locus to be expounded by itself": "itself" refers to the sentence *sarvānana*.
The subject-matters to be established therein take the form of faces, heads, and necks;
and that which prescribes the wearing of the *liṅga*— namely,

the statement "He establishes the universal *liṅga"* (*sarvaliṅgaṃ sthāpayati*)— which defines the substratum-ness residing in those [parts] as being related to their respective counter-correlatives, depends upon that [statement].
[It is so] by virtue of its conveying a meaning that possesses an expectancy to be resolved by a cognition residing within that which is to be known (*tadbodhya*). This is the intended sense:

a sentence that conveys mere substratumhood (*adhikaraṇatā*) without conveying the superstratum (*ādheya*) cannot, by virtue of being produced by itself, become the object of [the speaker's] intention (*tātparya*).

Furthermore, this [text] does not depend upon all the *liṅga* (indicative marks) and *vākya* (syntactical connections), because it functions as the determiner of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) prescribed by the passage, "Through the meditation on that which is co-substrate with itself, through its application, and through the manifestation of its true nature" (*na cāsya svasamānādhikaraṇa-tasyābhidhyānādyojanāttattvabhāvāt*).

This constitutes a difference [from other cases]. Here, because of the presence of *śruti* (direct scriptural statement) and *liṅga* (indicative marks) that are not shared by others, the term "he establishes" (*sthāpayati*) refers to the act of meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
Since it is not sufficient for the realization of the [true] nature of reality, it requires another sentence that makes known what is to be established.

In the present context, because the sentence "all [the lingas]" and the sentence "he installs all the lingas" possess a state of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) through their mutual requirement of each other's meaning, [they form a coherent whole].

The sense is that, because they have combined and thus constitute a sufficient means for the realization that is to be aimed at, it is impossible to suspect that one among them either attains what the other has already attained, or is redundant, or lacks necessity.
Regarding the phrase "na cāsya" (nor of this): it refers to the sentence beginning with "from the meditation upon [or the union with] that which is co-referential with itself."

That which is prescribed by that [text] is [the object] by virtue of being the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Here, "by virtue of being the determiner" means "by virtue of making it known," and "co-locus with itself" (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*) means "situated in its own context.
This very point is the seed of this doubt. By that which is proximate to itself...

The underlying sense is that since the fulfillment of a desire can be accomplished by one's own [proximate] means, it is utterly inappropriate for that fulfillment to be achieved through something remote. "Due to disparity" (*vaiṣamyāt*) means that there is a difference between the statement "By meditating upon Him" (*tasyābhidhyānāt*) and the statement containing the word "all" (*sarva*). He demonstrates this very disparity as follows:

— "Not shared by others": the word *liṅga* is not used for any deity other than Śiva; thus it establishes [this] in a manner that is not contradicted by the *Lokavedādhikaraṇa* or by grammar and the like.

Since it is determined that only those worldly words whose powers have been grasped possess Vedic status, the word "paśunā" (with an animal) and others are established [in the Veda] and are not employed elsewhere; for these two words are unique and not shared by anything else.

The sense is that when a word expressive of a specific meaning— which is capable of satisfying the expectancy for a substratum— is perceived, it is improper to satisfy that expectancy through a general statement that presents the meaning only with delay, by means of "meditating upon" (abhidhyāna) it.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the section on worldly and Vedic [words]": in the third quarter (pāda) of the first chapter of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*, it was established as a settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) that worldly and Vedic words have the same meaning. In this regard, compared to worldly usage—wherein *devāḥ* occurs for *devāsaḥ*, *bhavati* for *bhavāti*, and *karṇaiḥ* for *karṇebhiḥ*—in the Veda...

It should be argued that just as the injunctive character is accepted even for words such as *vilakṣaṇa* (heterogeneous) and *paśu* (animal), which depend on grammar and other sciences for the apprehension of their denotative power (*śakti*), so too should it be here.

Having raised the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position that, due to the observation of usage in accordance with worldly expectations, Vedic words might have other meanings, this Sūtra—"prayoga..."—is composed to set forth the established conclusion (siddhānta).
The meaning is as follows: [it concerns] the injunction (*codanā*) for the performance (*prayoga*) of ritual action (*karman*).

Because there is an absence of an injunctive statement, there would follow the consequence that the meaning is not understood; therefore, "unity of meaning" refers to the fact that worldly and Vedic words have the same meaning. Another reason is stated: "due to non-differentiation. This is because, according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, words with the same sequential order are non-distinct. From the non-difference of the word, there is also non-difference of the meaning.

The intended meaning is that [this] is appropriate. The underlying point is this: when words whose expressive power (*śakti*) has been grasped through worldly usage and the like are admitted to exist in the Veda as well, their capacity to convey meaning is established.

However, if one were to admit that Vedic words are distinct from worldly words and possess distinct meanings, then, due to the absence of any means to grasp their expressive power, there would be no comprehension of meaning.

Otherwise, those [Vedic] sentences would be purposeless, as they would not convey anything distinct from them; therefore, one must necessarily maintain that worldly and Vedic words possess the same meaning. This remains true even though [the Veda] depends on grammar and other sciences for the apprehension of word-potency (*śakti*). Thus, in the case of *paśunā*, there is the potency residing in the instrumental case-ending, and in *yajeta*, there is the potency residing in the verbal root *yaji*.

The potency residing in the verbal suffix (*liṅ*) and the third case-ending for the agent and the instrument are understood through scriptural rules such as "the third case is used for the agent and the instrument" and "in [cases of] invitation, addressing, and mantras. Therefore, it should be understood that there is a dependence on those [grammatical rules] here.
Why, then, should this not also apply in the present case? Just as, for example, even though the sentence "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*) depends upon grammar...

The meaning is this: just as the status of being an injunction (*vidhitva*) is not lost for the sentence "having all faces, heads, and necks" (*sarvānanaśirogrīvaḥ*), so too, even though it depends on the sentence "he establishes [the fire] with all the marks" (*sarvaliṅgaiḥ sthāpayati*), why should it not possess the status of an injunction? This is like the lack of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatvābhāva*) between the sentence "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*) and the grammatical rules (*vyākaraṇasūtra*).
Because there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) between the entire face [of the scripture] and the entire indicative mark (*liṅga*),

and because grammar and the like serve merely to establish the apprehension of word-potency (*śaktigraha*), even if that were the case here, since the wearing of the marks cannot be established without an investigation into the meaning of the sentence as a whole, it must occur at that very time.

Because it is not established that a sentence containing all [three] marks (*liṅga*) possesses injunctive force. Furthermore, the intended meaning here is that since it merely provides what is already obtained by a sentence that has not yet attained syntactic unity with its own, it cannot be an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), which is all-pervasive.
"By virtue of being useful merely for the apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*)," [meaning] "without an investigation into the meaning of the sentence. This is the intended sense:

in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), there exists a causal complex consisting of the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by words, which is dependent upon the knowledge of the *vṛtti* (the relation between word and meaning) that is useful for understanding the meaning of the specific sentence under discussion.

When the collection of phonemes (*varṇakalāpa*) is present, there is no requirement for any other sentence to produce the cognition that constitutes the intended meaning (*tātparyaviṣayībhūtabodha*) by virtue of being produced by itself. However, in the case of the phrase *sarvānanaśirogrīvaḥ*, even though the entire collection of causal factors— such as the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the words constituting it— is present, there is no cognition of the locus (*ādheya*).

Since there is indeed an expectancy for the entire sentence containing all the *liṅ* suffixes, there is no syntactic unity (*padaikavākyatā*) between the injunction regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśuvidhi*) and the grammatical rule (*vyākaraṇa*). However, in this case, because a syntactic unity between both is necessary for the cognition useful for performance (*anuṣṭhāna*),
and because it provides what has not been obtained by anything else that does not enter into syntactic unity with itself, it constitutes an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).
He states a certain objection: "because its status as an injunction is not established.
This means that the entire collection of masculine gendered words (*sarvaliṅgavākya*), which has not attained syntactic unity with the phrase "all-knowing" (*sarvajñānam*), [cannot be an injunction].

Since the status of the passage beginning with "The Blessed One" (*bhagavān*, Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.11) is determined to be an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) through the offering of praise for the masculine gender (*liṅgastuti*), [it cannot be taken as an injunction].
Furthermore, because it is impossible for that [meaning] to be established otherwise through this very truth.

As for what was stated— that because the meaning conveyed by the qualifying term "pāṇimantra" is already established by the impossibility of its being otherwise, an injunction is impossible— that is not so, for this [qualifier] also...
Since it is not established that each [part] separately possesses the power of injunction, it follows by implication that only the combined whole possesses the power of injunction.
Consequently, because both parts constitute a single sentence, one part cannot be rendered redundant by the other.
[Regarding the example] "the mantra for the hand": let there be no acquisition [of the mantra] through the rule "all [mantras]," but rather through the rule "the mantra for the hand."

The intention is that since the attainment [of the result] already exists, the impossibility of it being an injunction remains as before. In response to the doubt—how can "pāṇimantram" (the mantra on the hand) be an injunction when it lacks the injunctive suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth that serve as the basis for being enjoined—he says: "by way of inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapattyā*). Regarding the phrase "pāṇimantram":

The term *mantrapada* refers to the *liṅga*, because the possessive suffix *-ac* is accepted in the sense that "it possesses a mantra," and by the etymological derivation "the mantra is in the hand" (*pāṇau mantraḥ*), the *liṅga* held in the hand is expressed by the term *pāṇimantra*. Furthermore, the state of being held in the hand [of the *liṅga*] cannot exist without its wearing (*dhāraṇa*).

Because the statement containing all the gendered case-endings (*sarvaliṅgavākya*), by way of generally enjoining the act of wearing (*dhāraṇavidhi*), serves to provide a specific locus for that [act],

and because it is impossible for that [general injunction] to be established otherwise through dependence on this [specific one]; thus, in the phrase *pāṇimantra*, since it is to be worn, [the compound means] "that which has a mantra."

The word "mantra" is formed by adding the possessive suffix *ac*; thus, "pāṇimantra" means a "liṅga held in the hand. This is because of the statement in the Liṅga Purāṇa: "Therefore, the great liṅga should be worn; it is called 'pāṇimantra' according to the mantra."

The intention of the questioner is that the retention [of the mantra] is postulated by means of the *arthāpatti* (presumption) evidence, on the grounds that [otherwise] it would not be possible. Regarding the phrase "by way of providing a specific locus": thus, just like the word *sarvānna* (all food), the qualification *pāṇimantra* (hand-mantra) also serves to provide a specific locus in the form of the hand.

The sense is that since [the phrase "pāṇimantram"] has become merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the entire sentence containing all the gender-markers (*sarvaliṅgavākya*), the latter is not rendered redundant by it. Regarding the term "by that which depends upon it" (*tadupajīvakena*):

because the qualification "pāṇimantram" is an auxiliary that depends upon that entire sentence containing all the gender-markers, the latter is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*), and thus its redundancy is avoided.

The meaning is "due to non-connection" or "due to impossibility. Although it might seem inappropriate to state that the qualification "the mantra for the hand" (*pāṇimantra*) is dependent— since, in general, it is precisely the specific portion that is depended upon— nevertheless,
according to the maxim "that which is without fruit is a subsidiary when in proximity to that which possesses fruit," the qualification "the mantra for the hand" constitutes a subsidiary (*aṅga*).

Since the member [the hand] has its own purpose established through the support of the whole [the body], this statement regarding its being "dependent" (upajīvaka) should be understood as referring to that dependence.
This resolution should be understood as having been offered by accepting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) for the sake of satisfying the questioner;
however, in reality, the state of being located in the hand resides in the indicative mark (*liṅga*).

And here, because the statement "he offers the Agnihotra" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.9.1)— which enjoins the Agnihotra without specifying a locus— is otherwise inexplicable without the proximity of its characteristic marks, that proximity [is established].

It should be understood that this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) does not even arise; for although it might be possible to infer mere proximity common to [other objects] by means of a mark (liṅga) residing in the hands of household servants and others—since such possession is generally established—it is impossible to infer the specific act of wearing (dhāraṇa) itself. This is because of the suffix -ac.

From the statement "it has a mantra," only this much is obtained. As for how the specific element—that it is to be worn—is obtained, he cites the *Liṅgapurāṇa* as the authority: "Therefore, the great Liṅga is to be worn on the hand according to the mantra."

Having established that the sentence "he establishes all the marks" (*sarvaliṅgaṃ sthāpayati*) is an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), he establishes that the portion "the hand-mantra is the purifier" (*pāṇimantaṃ pavitram*) is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) with the words beginning "And here," etc.
Here, the meaning is the portion "the hand-mantra. [As for the example: "He offers the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*, Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.9.1).

Just as in the case of the sentence "he offers" (*juhoti*), where the locus such as the sacrificial altar (*pīṭha*)— though already established by all the gender-indicative sentences— is optionally available alongside the hand and so forth, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is enjoined that "the hand alone [is the locus]"; and it is not the case that,
because there is a locative case-ending (*saptamī-vibhakti*) denoting the status of being a locus in the sentence regarding the *āhavanīya* fire, the same logic applies here as well.

It should not be asked how this can be an injunction regarding a locus (*adhikaraṇavidhi*) in the absence of such [an explicit word], for even here the status of being a locus is understood through the recollection of an elided locative case-ending. By the word *pavitra*,
the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), which is the supreme purifier, is meant.
In this very context, purity is enjoined by means of removing impurity through the practice of wearing [the sacred thread] at the improper time;
here, since the word *agnihotra* functions as a name (*nāmadheya*), one attains heaven by means of the oblation that is non-different from the *agnihotra*.

Since the injunction for an offering (*homa*) without a specified locus implies a requirement for a particular locus in the sense that one "should perform [the offering]," and since the *āhavanīya* fire is also optionally available as a general possibility,
the sentence "He offers in the *āhavanīya*" restricts the *agnihotra* offering to having the *āhavanīya* alone as its locus; thus it is exactly so.

By the statement "he installs the *sarvaliṅga*," the installation without a specific substratum (*niradhikaraṇaka-sthāpanā*) is first enjoined. When there arises a requirement for a specific substratum, since both the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and other such bases— as well as the hand and so forth— are potentially available as options, the sentence "the mantra of the hand" (*pāṇimantra*) establishes that the worship of the *liṅga* must indeed have the hand as its substratum.
The intended meaning is that the rule "it must be performed" is what is enjoined.

Nor should it be argued that enjoining multiple things results in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), for as in the case of *āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālo 'māvāsyāyām* (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.3.3), even many [elements] may be enjoined with a single effort when they are not already established.
According to the principle stated in *Tattvavaiśāradī* (2.2.6), there is no fault in prescribing multiple [options].

Now, one might object: even so, by the phrase "he establishes the *liṅga* on all [surfaces]," the establishment of the *liṅga* is prescribed specifically on the ground (*bhūmi*), based on the inherent force (*svārasya*) of the word "establishes" (*sthāpayati*) and the practice of all people.

"And not [in the case of] multiple injunctions" means that it would involve the injunction of both— the state of having the hand as the locus and the state of being purified— with respect to the linga being worshipped.

This is like [the case of] "The cake on eight potsherds belongs to Agni," where both the state of having Agni as its deity and the state of being prepared on eight potsherds are enjoined with reference to the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).

In the case of such an injunction, there would necessarily be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). There is no such split in the injunction for the worship of the *liṅga* characterized by purity, which is further qualified by having the new moon day as its locus, and being characterized by the performance of the sacrifice with a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) prepared on eight potsherds (*aṣṭakapāla*) dedicated to Agni as its deity.

There is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). As it has been said: "When a ritual action is already established, more than one accessory (*guṇa*) cannot be enjoined; but when it is not yet established, even many may be enjoined with a single effort" (*Tantravārttika* 2.2.6).
[The phrase] "even so" means: even though the objection regarding the split in the sentence has been refuted. [The phrase] "only on the ground" means...

The meaning is "on a pedestal" (pīṭha) in the form of a copper vessel or the like situated on the ground; this is according to the natural sense of the word "places" (sthāpayati). Furthermore, because royal lineages possess a hundredfold qualities and because that [pedestal] alone is necessary as the object of focus, it is so; and thus, when that is the case, the mantra for the hand is "pavitram" (the purifier).

If it is argued that the qualifier "consecrated by the hand" (pāṇinā'bhimantritam)— meaning purified through the purification of the six paths (ṣaḍadhva-śodhana) and so forth, and therefore "pure" (pavitram)— is meaningful [only in this context], they reply here:
[the word] "he establishes" (sthāpayati) applies equally to both the ground and the body.

It is determined that the scripture prescribes the installation of the *liṅga*, because the scripture cannot tolerate restriction and because there is no decisive evidence [to the contrary]. Furthermore, according to the maxim "But when there is doubt, it is from the remainder of the sentence" (*Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 1.4.29),
the phrase "the mantra for the hand" (*pāṇimantram*) serves as the remainder of the sentence.
The sense is that this is because there is a corresponding understanding in such expressions as "Rāghava will place the jar" (*sthāpayiṣyati kalaśam*) and "he places [it]" (*sthāpayati*).

"Consecrated by the hand" (*pāṇinābhimantritam*) means rendered pure through the recitation of mantras preceded by the touch of the hand. "Purification of the six paths" (*ṣaḍadhvaśodhana*) refers to the paths consisting of the six types of ritual depositions (*nyāsa*).

The procedure for Vīraśaiva initiation, well-known from the Śaiva Āgamas, should be consulted in the relevant manual; it is not written here for fear of prolixity. By those [mantras], purification is performed, and by that [purification], the state of being a locus for the deity is established. The word "etc. (*ādi*) includes worship and other such acts. This is because [the consciousness] cannot endure limitation. Consequently, [the mantra does not reside] in the earth alone.

The sense is that [the injunction] is established. Anticipating the objection that even by that much, one does not obtain the fact that the object is solely worship performed with the hand as the locus, he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). Regarding the principle "but when there is doubt, [it is determined] from the remainder of the sentence" (*saṃdigdhe tu vākyaśeṣāt*), in the case of the text, "He places the pebbles smeared [with something]" (*aktāḥ śarkarā upadadhāti*, Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.5.12), there is a doubt as to whether they are smeared with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) or with oil (*taila*).

In the case of doubt, a determination is established by the observation of a praise of ghee in the supplementary passage: "Ghee is indeed splendor" (*Tai0 Brā0* 3.12.5.12), as in the phrase "smeared with ghee. Likewise, here too, in the injunction for installation—namely, "he installs the universal *liṅga*"—the term refers to any substratum suitable for installation in a manner common to all such bases.

When there is a desire to know the specific location— whether it be on the ground or elsewhere— the conclusion of the sentence, "The hand is the mantra-purifier," establishes that the installation of the *liṅga* must indeed be in the hand;
thus, by force of logic, its status as an injunction for the installation of the *liṅga* within the body itself is proven, as is respected in the Purāṇas and other texts.
In this context, since the word *mantra*— derived from a verbal root well-known to mean "to worship"—
possesses the sense of worship, it is established that a *mantra* is so called because it "protects" (*trāyate*) through "veneration" (*mananāt*, i.e., *pūjanāt*). Consequently,

while the term *pāṇimantra* (literally "the mantra in the hand") would be justified as meaning "worship performed with the hand as its locus," such worship is impossible in the case of an immobile object (*sthāvara*).
This is because [the term] is determined to mean "that which possesses a liṅga (organ) sustained by a body.

Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction even in the case of stationary beings (sthāvara) by resorting to a third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*)— namely, "that which protects through the mind by means of the hand"— for if that were the case, it would result in a dependent compound (*sāpekṣa-samāsa*).

The meaning of the word *pāṇimantra* as something consecrated by the purification of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvaśodhana*) and so forth cannot be established due to a lack of semantic power (*śakti*). He states [the following] because the meaning "the act of protecting through worship in the hand" is easily obtained, given that the root *mān* (or *man*) is well-known in the sense of "worship" in such expressions as "the guru is to be honored" (*gururmānyaḥ*). *##-* (This marker indicates the end of the preceding argument.)

The intention is as follows: just as one obtains the qualification of having the hand as the locus [of the action], since "having the hand as the locus" is sublated in the case of a stationary *liṅga* with respect to worship, it is determined that [the action] has as its object a *liṅga* held in the body. This is what should be understood here: regarding the qualifier "having the hand as the locus."
Although it is established from the context that [the rule] regarding the stationary liṅga refers only to the wearing of the liṅga on the body,

nevertheless, since the wearing of the permanent liṅga must be proven by other means of knowledge, this passage establishes merely worship performed with the hands as the locus; thus there is no fault.
Furthermore, he raises an objection regarding the instrumentality of the hand with the words "na ca pāṇinā" and so forth.

By resorting to a compound ending in the third case— meaning "it protects through the hand," that is, through the hand holding bilva leaves and other such items used for meditation and worship— that worship remains uncontradicted even in the case of a stationary linga.

The intention [of the opponent] is: "How is that obtained? [The answer is: because by resorting to this [interpretation], there would result the violation of the *samartha-paribhāṣā* (the rule concerning semantic competency). If it is argued that even when there is dependence on another word, such [an interpretation] is accepted because the meaning is understood (*gamakatvāt*), we say no; for in that case, the words *pāṇi* and *pada* would be redundant.

He refutes [the objection] with the words "If that were so," and so forth. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king’s prosperous man), the Vārttika rule *sāpekṣamasamarthavat* (that which is dependent [on another] is as if it lacks capacity) teaches that there is a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*) when there is dependence, in order to prevent the compounding of the two elements *rājan-ṅas* and *puruṣa-su*. This is established by the force of the governing maxim (*paribhāṣā*) *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* (a grammatical operation concerning words applies only when they are semantically and syntactically connected).
The intention is that because the rule prescribing a compound applies only when there is semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), the rule does not operate in such cases;

likewise, even in the analysis (*vigraha*) "pāṇinā mananāt trāyate" (he protects by means of the hand through reflection), since the word "manana" (reflection) is dependent upon the element "pāṇi" (hand), there is no semantic capacity, and thus the compound would not occur under the rule *sup-supā*. This is because [the compound] must be expressive (*gamakatvāt*).

In expressions such as *devadattasya gurukulam* ("Devadatta’s teacher’s family") and *caitrasaya dāsabhāryā* ("Caitra’s servant’s wife"), although the referent of the word "teacher" (*guru*) and so forth is dependent upon Devadatta and the like, the compound is nevertheless accepted because it is capable of conveying the meaning understood from its analytical expansion (*vigraha*). As Bhartṛhari has stated: "A relative term is always dependent [on another]."

"Everything is compounded; for that expectancy, like that of a sentence, is not lost even in the state of a compound" (Vākyapadīya 3.14.47). Alternatively, in cases where there is constant expectancy, it is intended that the referent of the word *devadatta* and so forth is first construed with the collective meaning of the compound through a relation involving the meaning of the prior member.
The understanding of the connection between the meanings of the parts, however, is established as a result. This method has also been stated by that very same [author]:
"Those which have a connection with a whole, such as a teacher or a family...
[and] having touched upon the parts by that very [whole], just as: "Those which have a connection with a whole..."
"Having touched their limbs by means of the teacher's house and so forth, they are joined with those who possess them" (Vākyapadīya 3.14.48).

Anticipating the objection that here too, since reflection (*manana*) is an action and thus necessarily requires a grammatical participant (*kāraka*), the compound will be free from impediment, he refutes it, saying "no."
Regarding the phrase "due to the futility of the word *pāṇi*":

one should not argue that, since it has been stated [the name] "trāyin" means "he who protects from mental [afflictions]," the word *pāṇi* is used to exclude the mind (*manas*) and other such instruments which would otherwise be implied as instruments; for [in this context], ritual actions such as the worship of Śiva must be performed.
Because of the statement by the learned, "by means of mental, vocal, and physical actions," these [actions] also attain the status of being instruments (*karaṇa*).

Furthermore, if one resorts to a compound with the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā-tatpuruṣa*), there arises the fault of partial co-referentiality (*ekadeśānvaya*). Nor should it be argued that this same fault applies even when resorting to a locative determinative compound (*saptamī-tatpuruṣa*), because of [the specific nature of] the term *pāṇipada*.
This is because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is accepted only with that which is qualified.

The point is that if [the word] ends in the locative case (*saptamī*), it serves its purpose by providing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Nor should it be argued that even if it ends in the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*), let it be for the sake of providing the instrument (*karaṇa*), as in the case of "one should sacrifice to the gods" (*devān yajeta*).

Since even when only the performance of worship is prescribed, the status of the hands and so forth as the instrument (*karaṇa*) is obtained by necessity alone, [the author] says "for the purpose of excluding that. This means for the purpose of excluding mental [worship] and the like. Since the presence of the mind is necessary for any action whatsoever, there is the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that it must be performed "with the hand alone."

He states that if that [qualification] were excluded, it would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (apasiddhānta): "The worship of Śiva and so forth must be performed through the actions of mind, speech, and body. [This implies they must be performed] by means of these specifically. Nor should it be argued that this same resolution is easily available even in the case of a *tṛtīyā-tatpuruṣa* compound.

Regarding the statement that "it is consecrated by Pāṇini" (pāṇinā'bhimantritam) as a third-case tatpuruṣa compound— where [Pāṇini] is the agent of the act of consecration performed upon the lay follower (upāsaka)— that is not correct, because it is contradicted by the fact that the act of protection has the Supreme Lord as its agent.

If the word *abhimantrya*, which signifies worship well-known in the Purāṇas, were taken to mean "having consecrated," it would entail accepting a secondary (metaphorical) meaning; nor is such an acceptance desirable, as it would contradict the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*.
In that [adhikaraṇa], it is stated: "That fire thought (*aikṣata*)."

Because the specific syntactic connection (*viśiṣṭānvaya*) [in the first interpretation] is contradicted; whereas in the case of a locative *tatpuruṣa* compound, the specific syntactic connection can indeed be maintained, since "having the worshipper’s hand as its locus" is possible even in the act of protection performed by the Lord being worshipped in the worshipper’s hand.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that—by accepting the figurative sense in passages such as "Those waters thought" (*tā āpa aikṣanta*) and following the majority of the textual readings—the term refers to the *pradhāna* by taking its figurative capacity for seeing, [the siddhāntin replies]:
because even when a word with a figurative meaning is observed in one instance, it is not possible for it to be so everywhere; therefore, [the term must be taken] in its primary sense.

Since accepting a secondary meaning is considered inferior, and since it is determined that the passage refers exclusively to Brahman by taking the primary sense of "the Seer," [the opponent argues] that this is because it conforms to the general reading: "That fire thought; those waters thought."
The meaning is: "because it is read in many contexts where the sense of 'seeing' (īkṣati) is superimposed [upon other objects].

Here, with the words beginning "they say" (*atra vadanti*), he establishes that it possesses all genders; by the phrase "the hand-mantra is pure" (*pāṇimantraṃ pavitram*), he addresses the doubt that its establishment might be prescribed as something common to earth and the other elements, according to another view.
Having composed [this work], he composes it himself, beginning with the words "To this we reply," and so forth. This alone is how it should be explained;

for since there is no previously unaddressed prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the immediately preceding text, the meaning manifesting itself naturally would otherwise be contradicted. "All of this is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*)"—this will be shown immediately below.
The meaning is: of the wearing of the *liṅga* which is enjoined by the scriptural statement, "By reciting [this], one establishes the *sarvaliṅga*";
[this occurs] through the *liṅga* being worn while it is made the object of praise in the form of a cognition of its excellence by means of the previously mentioned mantras ending in "namas."

Since all the indicative marks (liṅgas) lead to the determination of non-difference, it is established that all the previously mentioned mantras function as explanatory passages (arthavādas) for the injunction regarding wearing [the sacred thread]. Thus,
when the status of being an injunction and an explanatory passage is achieved, [regarding] the portion consisting of the explanatory passage...

The intention is as follows: once it is determined through a thorough examination of the Śaiva Āgamas related to that [Liṅga] that the subject matter concerns the Liṅga worn [on the body], if one does not accept that the injunctive portion (*vidhi*) is likewise [directed toward that same object], there would be a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the injunction and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
And that is undesirable, because of the established Mīmāṃsā principle that "only that which is enjoined is praised. Thus...
To this we reply: the entire passage beginning with "Obeisance to the Lord of the Nidhana" and ending with "This belongs to Soma and Sūrya" is purely explanatory (arthavāda).
In that regard—the unbroken, single Liṅga is indeed the supreme [form] taught by the Guru.
O Daughter of the Mountain, it has become threefold through the division into existence, vital breath, and the beloved.
Those made from consecrated liṅgas and those whose nature is that of the teacher’s conduct are declared by experts in the Śaiva Āgamas to be earthen and watery respectively.

O lady of excellent complexion, there are two types of lingas: those whose nature consists of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the subtle body (liṅga), composed of fire and air, and those known as the mobile Śiva-lingas.
The Linga known as the Prāsāda, which is of the nature of space, is the most extensive;
it is declared to be the Great Liṅga, the greatest, consisting of the principle of the Self (ātmatattva).
The intended meaning having been determined, only the literal word-by-word construction remains; that shall now be performed. Please pay attention:

"There may be one undivided *liṅga*; that very thing is called 'supreme' by the Guru," and so forth. Here, after the word "by the Guru" (*guruṇā*), the word "stated" (*ukta*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Alternatively, it should be construed as "by the Guru" in the sense of "by the great distinction."
In this regard, the ten kinds of *liṅgas* are to be enumerated as follows: 1. the unbroken *liṅga* (*akhaṇḍaliṅga*), 2. the *liṅga* of existence (*bhāvaliṅga*), 3.

the *liṅga* of vital breath (*prāṇaliṅga*), 4. the *liṅga* of the chosen deity (*iṣṭaliṅga*), 5. the *liṅga* of conduct in the form of earth (*pārthivarūpamācāraliṅga*), 6. the *liṅga* of the guru in the form of water (*āpyarūpaṃ guruliṅga*), 7. the *liṅga* of Śiva consisting of fire (*tejomayaṃ śivaliṅga*), and 8. the mobile *liṅga* (*caraliṅga*) consisting of air. (The remaining two are the *liṅga* of space and the *liṅga* of consciousness.)
The *liṅga* called the temple has space (*vyoman*) as its material cause (9); the Great *Liṅga* is the very principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*) (10).
Herein, the indivisible *liṅga* is the nature of Brahman. The natures of the others will be clarified later.
The praise of all these *liṅgas* is performed with ten mantras ending in "namas."

Thus, the praise of the ten types of *liṅgas* mentioned in the words of the *Siddhāntaśekhara* is seen through [mantras] ending in "namas. Among these, "namo ūrdhvaliṅgāya" refers to the *akhaṇḍaliṅga*, because it resides in the western wheel (*cakra*) of the single-petaled [lotus] situated above all the wheels. "Hiraṇyaliṅgāya namaḥ... [and so forth].
By this, the *prāṇaliṅga* is praised:
"Resembling molten gold, residing in the location of the *kanda*,
the wise know the *prāṇaliṅga* to be that which is always to be meditated upon by yogis."
Thus, because its nature as being made of gold is determined by the statement from the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*,

the mantra "Obeisance to the Golden Liṅga" (*suvarṇaliṅgāya namaḥ*) is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the chosen liṅga: "Obeisance to the pedestal" (*namaḥ pīṭham*) is declared, and the syllable *śi* is said to be the middle one.
The letter *vā* is known as Gomukha (Cow-face) and is circular; the letter *ya* is remembered as Golaka (Ball).
The syllable *oṃ* is declared to be the *liṅga*; the six-syllabled mantra is called the *liṅga*.
[The mantra] "Salutation to the Upper Liṅga" (*ūrdhvaliṅgāya namaḥ*) and so forth refers to the indivisible *liṅga* (*akhaṇḍaliṅga*).
To address the doubt as to how that [indivisible *liṅga*] can be understood through the term "Upper Liṅga," he says: "Of that, all... (*tasya sarva...*).

The meaning is that because it resides in the western wheel—which is situated above all wheels—and because it is situated above all wheels, the unbroken *liṅga* possesses the quality of being an upward-pointing *liṅga*. This wheel stands above all other wheels and consists of a single petal. Homage to the Golden *Liṅga*.

By this [verse] beginning with "resembling molten gold," the *prāṇaliṅga*— which is worthy of being designated by the term *hiraṇyaliṅga* because it is qualified by its similarity to molten gold— is praised. And by the phrase "Salutation to Suvarṇa," [the meaning of] "Salutation to Śiva" is expressed.

The "desired *liṅga*" is said to consist of the six syllables beginning with the word *namaḥ* that form the mantra-base; for by the word "of that" (*tasya*), there is the ascertainment that its nature consists of phonemes qualified by excellence precisely through its being a constituent of the *liṅga*-body. [Thus: *divyaliṅgāya namaḥ*.

Thus concludes the praise of the temple-liṅga presided over by the principle of space (*ākāśatattva*). Because of the etymological derivation that "divine" (*divya*) means "that which exists in heaven" (*divi bhavam*), there is no difference between the two. By the phrase "salutation to the *bhava*-liṅga," the praise of the guru-liṅga is performed.
There, Jyeṣṭhā consists of water and has the nature of the material cause for persistence;
Bhava is her Lord as the eldest (jyeṣṭha), and Jyeṣṭhā is declared to be his power (śakti).

Thus, because of the non-difference between the *bhava-liṅga* and the *liṅga* of the Guru presiding over the water-tattva, [one should offer salutation] with the words "Salutation to the *śarva-liṅga*," which refers to the *ācāra-liṅga*.
It is that which consists of Vāmā, the self, and the earth-tattva, and whose nature is Vāmā herself.
O you whose form is the abode of Śarva, emanation proceeds from Vāmā.

Thus, by the statement from the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*, because [the object] consists of phonemes characterized by "excellence" (suṣṭhutva)— which is the state of being a constituent of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) whose essence is mantra—
the praise of the *prasādaliṅga* is performed by the words "Salutation to the Divine Liṅga" (*divyaliṅgāya namaḥ*).
Because it is presided over by the principle of space (*ākāśatattva*), it is worthy of being understood through the etymological derivation "that which exists in heaven" (*divi bhavam*).
By the phrase "Salutation to Bhavaliṅga," [it is meant that] "In the beginning, he created the waters alone; upon them he cast the seed.
That became a golden egg, radiant like the thousand-rayed sun" (Manu Smṛti 1.8).

A hymn is composed for the Guru-liṅga presided over by the water-tattva, which is characterized by the power of sustenance (*sthiti*) and appropriation (*upādāna*). It should be understood that the term *bhava-pada* contains an implied causative sense, meaning "it causes [the world] to come into being" (*bhāvayati*). Thus it is said: "There, Jyeṣṭhā consists of water and has the nature of sustenance and appropriation; Bhava is her Lord, and Jyeṣṭha is Jyeṣṭhā."

"Her power is thus described. Here, the preeminence (*jyeṣṭhatva*) of the water-principle (*jalatattva*) is to be understood in accordance with the previously mentioned cosmogony: "In the beginning, he created the waters alone" (Manu Smṛti 1.8). By the phrase "Salutation to the Śarva-liṅga," the Ācāra-liṅga presided over by the earth-principle (*pṛthivītattva*) is praised.
Because the *ācāraliṅga*, which identifies with the earth-element (*pṛthivītattva*), is established as non-different from the *śarvaliṅga*;
and because the *śivaliṅga*— to whom "salutation to the *śivaliṅga*" is addressed—
and fire are both of the nature of Rudra, its Lord is Raudrāgneyī.
He is indeed Rudra, the Lord of Beings; Raudrī is held to be his power.

By this [verse], there is the cognition of non-difference between the Śiva-liṅga— which conceives itself as possessing the nature of fire (tejastva)— and that which is denoted by the term Rudra, who occupies the station of the Śiva-pada; thus, "Salutation to the blazing liṅga" refers to the mobile liṅga (caraliṅga).
Because the vital breath (prāṇa) has the nature of time, the power of time is indeed the wind;
he who is fierce and whose form is the wind is renowned as Kāla.
By this [mantra], there is non-difference between the mobile *liṅga* presided over by the *vāyu-tattva* and the blazing *liṅga* denoted by the word "Ugra.

[The mantras are: "Obeisance to the *ātma-liṅga*"; "Obeisance to the *bhāva-śiva-liṅga* presided over by the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*); obeisance to the blazing *liṅga*; obeisance to the supreme *liṅga*; obeisance to the *ātma-liṅga*."

It should be observed that the fact that these mantras, beginning with "namaḥ," consist of praises to the Śivaliṅga, Caraliṅga, Mahāliṅga, and Bhāvaliṅga is demonstrated in the root text itself, supported by the statements of the Siddhāntaśekhara. At the time of initiation (dīkṣā)...

The wearing of the external *liṅga* is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). That the wearing of other *liṅgas* is performed by disciples in the form of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) according to the instructions of the Guru is clear from this manual (*paddhati*) and the Śaiva Āgamas. This is expressed by the statement: "By the wearing of all *liṅgas*, one establishes the *sarvaliṅga*."

It is thus understood; for this very reason, the natural sense of the word *sarva* [is established], as it is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the Śaiva Āgama which accepts that the root *sthā* has the meaning of "sustaining. And so it is with the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

If the statement "he establishes all liṅgas" were intended to enjoin the installation of stationary liṅgas (sthāvara-liṅga) by referring to the wearing of external marks (liṅga) on the body— which are distinguished by the conditions of conduct prescribed in the scriptures—
then there would arise a lack of syntactic coordination (vaiyadhikaraṇya) between the injunction and its explanatory passage (arthavāda).

"The path is to be understood. Thus, in this context, since it is understood that the injunction for installation (*sthāpanā-vidhi*) consists in enjoining the installation of the "all-encompassing form" (*sarvaliṅga*) after having restated the internal characteristics of conduct (*caraliṅga*),
one must comply with the requirement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the injunction and its explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
It is indeed logical that [the subject matter] concerns the *liṅga* (sign) being maintained by the body.
Furthermore:
"The beginning and the conclusion, repetition, novelty, and the fruit..."
Exegetical statements and logical consistency are the marks for determining the intended meaning.
Thus, among the six types of indicators of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*), the opening statement (*upakrama*)— which is free from contradiction—

is more powerful according to the principle of the section on the opening of the Veda (*vedopakramādhikaraṇa*), namely *Vedo vā prāyadarśanāt* (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 3.3.2); therefore, the opening "Salutation to the upward-pointing Liṅga" (*ūrdhvaliṅgāya namaḥ*) [is authoritative].

Furthermore, if it is determined that the *prāṇaliṅga* refers to the Supreme [Brahman], then the statement regarding "all *liṅgas*" would have to refer to something other than the *liṅga* worn on the body, which would contradict the context.

This is according to the Mīmāṃsā rule: "Or the Veda [is primary] because of the observation of the majority" (*Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 3.2.2). This is as in the case of the injunction: "One should employ a Niṣāda-sthapati."

Just as, by following the brevity obtained through the introductory statement consisting of not relying on specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the Veda is postulated even for one who lacks qualification by resorting solely to a *karmadhāraya* compound, so too here, in the introduction,
[the text] says: "Salutation to the one whose mark is upward," "Salutation to the one whose mark is golden," and so forth.

Since the *prāṇa*, *liṅga*, and so forth existing within the body are being introduced [in this context], if the sentence concerning "all *liṅgas*" were to refer to stationary *liṅgas*, it would contradict the opening statement (*upakrama*), which is the most authoritative among the six types of indicators (*liṅgas*).
Nor can this be explained by the word *etad* ("this"), which refers back to the previously mentioned salutation, as in "of this Soma" or "of this Sun."

It should not be said that there is a division of the context because of the mention of salutations to Sūrya and Soma; for, since the opening and the conclusion are determined to have Śiva as their referent, the phrase "nor this [belongs] to Soma" [in the middle] applies. By the word "this," the previously mentioned salutations are understood. [The mantra continues: "Salutation to the Lord of the Nidhana."
Having understood through delusion that salutations made with such mantras as these exist for the sake of [worshiping] the sun and the moon,
he raises an objection regarding the contradiction with the context by saying "na ca" and so forth; [he does this] because, in reality,
[the word] "somasya" [in the mantra] refers to Umā.

Since a literal designation of Soma and Sūrya would result in a contradiction with the context, [the term] "Soma" here refers to the Sun—specifically the Soma residing within the solar orb—based on the etymological derivation *soma* as "he who is accompanied by Umā," as in the verse: "Soma purifies himself for some; others worship him as Ghṛta" (*Ṛgveda* 10.154.1).

This is because the meaning "of Śiva in the form of the *liṅga*" necessarily follows; according to the stated method, it means "of [Śiva] together with [the *liṅga*]. Furthermore, the phrase "of the Sun" means "of the Supreme Self whose nature is Śiva, residing within the solar orb. As it is said in the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa*: "He who is in the sun..."

The meaning is that there is no contradiction with the context [of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad], which states: "Abiding within the sun, he controls it; the sun does not know him; the sun is his body" (BṛU 3.7.9).
This is because the statement containing all the characteristic marks refers to the one who sustains the body—as in the case of the sacrificial post made of Udumbara wood.

In this regard, even the postulation of an injunction based on the fear that the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would otherwise be purposeless—as in the text, "The udumbara is indeed strength; cattle are strength; by means of strength he obtains for him strength and cattle, for the sake of attaining strength" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.1.6)—is appropriate.

"The sacrificial post (yūpa) is made of Udumbara wood. This is the meaning: as to why a post connected to the Udumbara tree is made, he says "ūrg vai" and so forth. Since the Udumbara is indeed *ūrk*—that is, its nature is nourishment (*ūrk*), its nature is strength (*bala*), which is to say, its inner essence (*antahsāra*)—and cattle also possess inner essence, [it is for the sake of] a substance that possesses essence.

By reason of the propriety of obtaining a substance possessing essence (*sāra*), one obtains animals that have internal essence by means of a substance possessing essence in the form of *udumbara* wood.

To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "For the attainment of vigor (*ūrja*)," meaning for the sake of obtaining strength through the medium of milk and other products. By the force of this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), [the injunction] "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is made of *udumbara* wood" [is established].

Even though the suffix *laṭ* (present tense) is present, there is an assumption of the sense of the optative (*liṅ*), namely "duty to be performed" (*kartavyatā*). Similarly, in the passage "he establishes all marks," even though the optative (*liṅ*) or imperative (*loṭ*) suffixes are absent, the injunction to wear the mark is inferred solely by the force of the restatement of what has already been stated.

If it is argued that even so, this [practice] cannot be considered a mandatory injunction (*nityavidhi*) because a fruit is heard [promised] in the previously cited statement from the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*: "Both external and internal [worship] should be performed by sages desiring liberation" (6.29), we say: not so.

Regarding the statement "it is not a mandatory injunction for what is eternal": because of the qualification of the eligible person as "by sages desiring liberation," the wearing of the *liṅga* is not established for one devoid of the desire for liberation; thus, it is proven that this is indeed an optional injunction (*kāmyavidhi*).
This is the state of being: those who constantly perform the twilight devotions (sandhyā), firm in their vows,
go to the stainless world of Brahmā, their sins shaken off.

Thus, because of the hearing of such scriptural results (*arthavāda*), the non-obligatory nature (*anityatā*) of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) does not follow; for if one were to eat food and so forth without worshipping at the three times of the twilight, [the scripture would state: "He becomes a consumer of sin."
Having passed through a hundred births as a dog, he becomes a caṇḍāla for ten million lifetimes.

The obligatory nature (*nityatva*) is asserted because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in failing to perform [the rite]; this is the same in the present case as well. For one who has taken devotion but does not bear the mark (*liṅga*), [it is said]: "One should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) for as long as life is sustained. And: "Those who perform these nights indeed become firmly established."

Just as the *rātrisatra* injunction is considered a *kāmya-vidhi* (optional rite for a specific desire) because the fruit of "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*), mentioned in its explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), serves as a qualification for the eligible performer (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), so too, since the one who desires to reach the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*)— as stated in the explanatory passage "those who perform the twilight worship have their sins shaken off"— is established as the eligible performer for the *sandhyā* injunction, the same applies to the *sandhyā* itself.

If it is argued that [the practice] must be considered obligatory (*nitya*) because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) regarding the sin incurred by non-performance— stated in such passages as "not worshipping at the three times"—

then [we reply that] this would also apply to the wearing of the sectarian mark (*liṅga*), since a sin is likewise declared for one who does not wear it, as stated in the passage beginning with "the devotee who does not bear the mark."
He states that permanence is established beyond dispute: "The same applies to the case at hand.
To begin with, the eating of dog-meat must be composed of food.
Thus, because the *Vātula* and other texts declare that a transgression occurs if one does not [study], it is said:
"The Veda fears the person of little learning, thinking, 'He might mislead me.
One should augment the meaning of the Veda by means of the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*" (*Mahābhārata* 1.1.267).

Even if one were to personally know the meaning of the Vedas, there might still be ignorance regarding it; but when that meaning has been determined by the sages, what doubt could there be for great-souled ones?
Since this has been stated, there is also corroboration for the aforementioned meaning in the Śruti;
for instance, in the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"In the Vedas, in the collections of Śāstras, in the Purāṇas, and in the Āgamas..."
The wearing of the marks has been declared as the supreme duty of a Brāhmaṇa.

Regarding the doubt as to whether the injunction "one should establish the *liṅga* everywhere" refers to the installation of stationary *liṅgas* or to the wearing of the *liṅga* on the body— [the resolution is found] everywhere through statements in the *Mahābhārata*, such as: "One should augment the meaning of the Veda by means of the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*" (1.1.267).
