Because it is appropriate to reach a definitive conclusion regarding doubts about the meaning of the Vedas by means of the assistance of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas,
[the author] shows the *Liṅga Purāṇa* as favorable to the position of wearing the marks (liṅgas) as accepted by oneself: "In the Vedas,
in the collections of scriptures, in the Purāṇas, and in the Āgamas, [this practice] has been declared for the Brāhmaṇa."
The wearing of the *liṅga* is supreme.
Having begun thus, the Yajurveda also declares: "The Liṅga indeed establishes everything.
Therefore, the Great Liṅga should be held in the hand according to the mantra;
having placed the Liṅga in the hand at the time of initiation, the Guru [worships] Śiva.
That mantra with which one praises is indeed called a *pāṇimantra*.
Because Maheśvara Śiva is pure, because he is the one who establishes [purity],
and because he purifies men, it is called "the Purifier" (pavitra).
Therefore, at all times— one whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, or even opening and closing one's eyes— one should wear the supreme liṅga.

"Whether pure or impure, one should wear the *liṅga* everywhere," and so forth. Here, after stating the necessity of wearing the *liṅga* through several verses, this very statement is shown in the *Liṅgapurāṇa* as authoritative evidence: "The Yajurveda also says everything..."

It is indeed stated that "one should install the *liṅga*. It should be understood that this record, having corroborated the statements from the *Liṅgapurāṇa* found herein as well as the Vedic injunction "one should install the *sarvaliṅga*," becomes established as the supreme authority regarding the relationship between the primary scripture (*śruti*) and its explanatory supplement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), free from dispute. This being the case:

In a Purāṇic passage serving as a supporting authority here, it is said: "Because the Guru, at the time of initiation, places the *liṅga* in the hand and praises Śiva with a particular mantra, they indeed call that mantra the 'pāṇimantra' (hand-mantra)."

"Because it is pure, because it propounds Maheśvara Śiva, and because it purifies men, it is called 'pavitra' (the purifier). Thus, since the term *pāṇimantra* is etymologically derived from its being the means for performing worship with the hands as the locus,
[this applies] at the time of performing worship with the hands as the instrument.
Always pure, the bearer of the *liṅga* [should carry] his own beautiful *liṅga*.
With a concentrated mind, he should worship the various daily rites as well as the occasional ones upon the palm of his hand with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
"One should perform [these acts] with the intention of offering them to Śiva for the sake of the full increase of right knowledge. Thus it is said. Also, in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā of the Skanda Purāṇa:
"He who, having placed his chosen personal liṅga upon the pedestal of his hand, directs the movement of his mind toward that [liṅga],"
O dear one, he whose soul is free from desire for the multitude of external activities is a true Vīraśaiva.
Having placed that very linga, the symbol of the Supreme Self, in the center of the lotus-seat of his hands,
a person should worship it with the offerings distinguished by the internal and external divisions, through the intellect of oneness.
Compared to the worship of external seats, this worship of the hand-seat is superior for all Vīraśaivas who desire liberation, and it should be performed continuously.
The dispute concerning [the scripture] being recited and so forth should be understood as refuted.

Thus, having established the necessity of wearing the *liṅga* through the *Liṅgapurāṇa* and the *Śruti*, he proves it further by a statement from the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā* of the *Skānda-purāṇa*: "He who with his hand... and so on. The word "nijam" (one's own) [is used].

The term "desired liṅga" (iṣṭaliṅga) refers specifically to that liṅga which is maintained according to the prescribed rule. "One whose mental activity is absorbed in that" means one for whom all activities of the mind—the movement of the mind—are absorbed in that desired liṅga.
By such statements, [the text refers to] the worship based on the hand, as ordained by the sentence "The mantra of the hand is pure."
O child, for one whose body is joined with the life-force liṅga,
there exists in the ultimate sense neither the impurity arising from birth nor that arising from death.
"Even at birth or death, the worship of Śiva must not be abandoned.
Thus it is stated that for one who has been initiated for life through the wearing of the *liṅga*, the worship of Śiva and other rites must be performed even during times of impurity.
Rites such as the worship of the gods must always be performed by those who have received initiation;
for those great-souled ones, there is no rule regarding ritual impurity, nor is there any birth-impurity (sūtaka).
For one who performs the worship of Śiva, for one who maintains the sacred fire,
and for those who are celibate students or ascetics, there is no impurity (sūtaka) in their bodies.
Thus it has been stated likewise even in the *Ādityapūraṇa*.
Now, one might ask: "If one performs the worship of Śiva even at an impure time, does that entail the performance of other ritual acts?
[The answer is: "It is a multitude of actions, a collection of rites. [This is done] with the intellect of unity—that is, with the cognition of the oneness of the Liṅga and the Supreme Self.

"Prāṇaliṅgāṅgasaṅginaḥ" is to be explained as "one whose body possesses attachment to the prāṇaliṅga. Regarding the phrase "karmāntarānuṣṭhāna": it refers to the absence of *sūtaka* (ritual impurity), which obstructs the performance of Smārta rites, among the Śaivas.

If it is argued that "all [mantras] indeed [are included]," it is not so; for there are mantras recited during the daily obligatory worship (nityopāsana) of the Vaiśvadeva and other rites, as well as those recited at times such as the daily twilight prayers (saṃdhyāvandana) which have been eternally prescribed, and those employed in the worship of the Sun and other deities.

And regarding the recitation of the Veda employed for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices: "There is no restriction regarding days unfit for study (*anadhyāya*) concerning the *mantras* used for the burnt offerings (*homa*);
for there is no such restriction in the daily rites (*nityaka*), since that is remembered as the 'Brahma-sacrifice' (*brahmasatra*). (2.105)

The intention of the question is that, according to the *Manusmṛti*, ritual acts (*karmāṇi*) must be performed even during times when study is prohibited. He provides the answer: "In the case of obligatory rites (*naityaka*), there is no prohibition against study; for that is remembered as the 'Brahma-sacrifice' (*brahmasatra*)," as stated in *Manusmṛti* 2.106.

Because of the authorization granted by the *Manusmṛti*, even during periods of suspension from study (*anadhyāya*), there is the recitation and practice of the mantras for the worship of the Sun and other deities obtained at the time of the *saṃdhyā-vandana*,

as well as the mantras for the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites, and the mantras for the *darśapūrṇamāsa-iṣṭi-homa* offerings; likewise, this applies to the lifelong vow of Śiva-worship, just like the study of the other Vedas.
For, just as there is no possibility of performing other ritual acts during a time of impurity,

so too, by that same principle, even when the worship of Śiva has been resolved upon for the duration of one's life, it is not to be performed during a time of impurity, as long as the study of the Veda remains a duty [to be fulfilled].
[Otherwise] there would be the consequence of having to perform other ritual acts.
And thus, even such statements as "O child, there is no *sūtaka* for him" must be understood as referring exclusively to the worship of Śiva;
for the necessity of maintaining the great resolve (*mahā-śaṅkalpa*) is precisely what is intended in the prohibition of impurity (*aśauca*).
It appears as "the seed.

Now, let us set aside for a moment the eternality of the worship of Śiva performed with the hand as the locus; nevertheless, one might object that since the left hand is extremely inferior, it is improper to perform that [worship] with it. To this, we say: no.

According to the Śruti, "One should drink with cupped hands or with a vessel that is not broken," since the right hand is prescribed as a constituent of the cupped hands used as the instrument for drinking,
[the prohibition applies] to the cupped hands employed at the mouth of the fire, which is necessary for all Vedic people.
"Bringing the full vessel" (pūrṇapātram ānayati), according to this Vedic injunction, refers to the joining of palms as a support for the full vessel.
"With chest, head, gaze, mind, and likewise speech"—the meaning is that the performance of the worship of Śiva takes place upon the seat in the form of the left hand. If [one objects]: "No."
By means of injunctions such as "one should drink with joined palms" and "he brings a full vessel into the joined palms," prostration performed with many parts—
namely the two feet, the two hands, and the two ears— is called the eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) prostration.
Thus, according to Baudhāyana, regarding the placement of Rudra (*rudranyāsa*), both hands possess the fitness for salutation to Paramaśiva;
this is because there is no fault in performing the worship of Śiva [with both].
Furthermore, since the left hand is employed as a constituent part of the *añjali* (the joined palms) in ritual acts, it is unfit for all other ritual functions.
The sense is that there is no evidence for the claim that the left hand is an unfit locus for the performance of worship because it cannot be used for speech.
Now, even if— according to the method you have stated— the phrase "he establishes all lingas" [is interpreted as follows]:...
If it is argued that, although the dedication to wearing the *liṅga* is established [by other means],
there remains doubt because Vidyāraṇya— the expounders of the meaning of the Vedas— did not explain it as being dedicated to that,
this merely mimics a whispering into the ears of the deaf; for even though they did not explain it, [the fact remains].

This is because [the text] has been explained as having that [meaning] as its primary intent by Kālahastidīkṣita, Mañcaṇa Paṇḍita, Ārādhya, and others. However, Vidyāraṇyasvāmin has disregarded it, because it is not applicable to the subject at hand and because explaining it otherwise would result in logical fallacies. Otherwise, [this would apply] even to the mantras of Durgā.

Since this was not explained by them, the application of this [text] to the worship of Durgā by Śaṅkarācārya— who did not know the truth of the Samaya-mata— would also be entirely inconsistent. Furthermore,
even by the venerable teacher Bādarāyaṇa, who was the foremost bearer of the meaning of all the Vedas, of this...
Since [this matter] has been corroborated by the *Liṅga Purāṇa* and other texts in accordance with the meaning stated in the Śruti,
and since it has also been corroborated by Paraśiva himself in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* and other works as a valid authority of both the Vedas and the Āgamas, there is no room for doubt.
"Everything is irreproachable.

By "Vidyāraṇyas," it is meant Sāyaṇācārya. "Like whispering into the ear of a deaf person" means that, similarly, it would be useless for one's own purpose. [This is established] by the Liṅga Purāṇa and other texts already shown.
The sense is that, since the intended meaning is established by those who support the present mantra, the alternative interpretation offered by other persons is irrelevant.
In this very Upaniṣad, its establishment is also achieved through another mantra: "Oṃ, salutations to Brahman."

"May there be for me retention without rejection; may I be a retainer; may it be heard by my ears; may it not fall away—[this] of mine and of such-and-such, Om" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.9.1). Now, one might object: "But the establishment of the wearing of [the sectarian] marks is not accomplished by this mantra."

"By another mantra" means by [the mantra] beginning with "Oṃ, salutation to Brahman; may there be retention for me," and so forth. Since the act of retention is transitive, it requires a specific object (*karman*); and because Brahman is present [in the mantra], it is appropriate to take that very [Brahman] as the object. Furthermore, since that [Brahman] is partless...

Since it is not fit to be worn [as a physical mark], this injunction results in the wearing of the insignia (liṅga) as taught in the scriptures, being non-different from that [Brahman]. He specifies the wearing itself by the term "non-rejection" (anirākaraṇam);
the meaning is "that which is free from disregard. He himself [explains] that the meaning of the word "non-rejection" is Brahman, which is to be eternally accepted.

It will be explained further on. Regarding the phrase "heard in the ears" (*karṇayoḥ śrutam*), the meaning is that it is "heard" because it is praised by the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇas*. "Do not let [it] fall away" (*mā cyoḍhvam*). The root *cyuṅ* means "to fall. In place of the singular of the second person in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, there is a substitution with the plural. [The sense is: "do not let it fall from the body."

The meaning is "bhūḥ. In the phrase "mama amuṣya," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of a general relationship. This is connected with the preceding [part of the mantra]: "Do not let [this] fall away from me, even though I have gone to the other world.
As for the question, "But by this mantra...": it refers to that which is understood in a general sense in the phrase "may there be support for me" (*dhāraṇaṃ me'stu*).
The intention of the objector is that, because the act of holding does not take a specific object as its complement, it is impossible for it to have only a generic sign (liṅga) as its object;
this applies to both of the two sentences: "May there be holding for me" and "May I become the holder."

Because there is an absence of words that convey a specific [object], only the act of wearing (*dhāraṇa*) is perceived. Nor should it be argued that the wearing of the *liṅga* is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), since there is no evidence for the wearing of other deities and because such a practice does not exist; for even though the wearing of other deities is unestablished, [the conclusion remains].

Since the wearing of the conch, discus, and so forth as a representation of Nārāyaṇa is established in the system of Rāmānuja and is thus authoritative, it is possible for that very practice to be construed as the counter-positive of the act of wearing.

And the term "non-rejection" (*anirākaraṇa*) means that Brahman is not subject to rejection—that is, it is not the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of things characterized by arising and perishing; rather, it is the acceptable reality. This is the meaning.

"By way of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*). The sense is that since the act of holding must necessarily have some object, and since the holding of another deity has been ruled out due to lack of scriptural authority and other reasons, it follows by process of elimination that the object is indeed the *liṅga*. "As a representative of Nārāyaṇa" means, that is to say, as occupying the position of Nārāyaṇa.
The view of the teacher Rāmānuja is that one should wear the conch, the discus, and other marks with the understanding that they are the very form of Nārāyaṇa.

The phrase "as authoritative" means that it has been accepted as authoritative by the followers of Rāmānuja. For this very reason, it is said: "One should not dwell for even a single day where a person whose body is not marked with the discus resides."
Thus, there is no contradiction with the text of the *Uttarakhaṇḍana*.
It must be stated that, through the connection with the word "dhāraṇā" (bearing), the bearing of the *liṅga* (mark) is established by implication (*arthāt*),
because the state of being presented by the word "nirākaraṇa" (rejection) occurs through such a power of the constituent parts (*avayava-śakti*) according to the view of other schools (*matāntara*).
Since it is possible to speak of Nārāyaṇa’s armor and its constituent parts, the aforementioned defects would not be avoided even if the connection with wearing them were established.
Furthermore—
One should shun like an outcaste that person on whose forehead there is no sacred ash, on whose neck there is no rosary of rudrākṣa beads, and in whose mouth there is no six-syllabled mantra.
One should not transgress, even in thought, the practice of smearing ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
since this is ordained by the Śruti, one who abandons it becomes fallen.
"From this meaning, the accomplishment of wearing the *liṅga* follows.

The sense is that since the state of being a category [of existence] (*padārtha*)—defined as the negation of the absence of possessing origination and destruction—is possible only in Brahman, it follows that one must wear the *liṅga* which is non-different from that [Brahman]. "According to the system of another school" means...

The sense is that this reasoning is common [to all systems], because in the Rāmānuja school and others, Nārāyaṇa as well as the conch, discus, and so forth, are accepted as being Brahman. Furthermore, [it applies] to the wearing of the *vibhūti* (sacred ash), rudrākṣa beads, rosaries, and the six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣaramantra*).

In the Śaivasiddhānta as well, since these [substances] are prescribed as eternal, they too possess the status of being the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) to the wearing mentioned in the cited mantra;
for it is heard that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in failing to wear *bhūti* and *rudrākṣa*, and thus it is precisely those two that are intended here.

The connection is accepted as being with the status of the object of the act of holding (*dhāraṇa-pratiyogitva*). Furthermore, in the case of "may I become a holder" (*dhārayitā bhūyāsam*), an injunction is impossible because, being in the optative mood of benediction (*āśīr-liṅga*), it lacks the capacity to enjoin.

Nor is there the presence of the characteristics that necessitate an injunction, since [the meaning] is established otherwise by the entire sentence containing the optative suffix. Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

The position: To this it is replied—the meaning accepted is simply: "May I become the bearer of that Brahman which is the nature of the *liṅga* and is to be accepted because it is not to be rejected. As for that which...

The claim that even Nārāyaṇa and his armor cannot be set aside due to the power of their respective parts is incorrect, because of scriptural statements such as the *Atharvaśikhā*: "All these—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—are produced from Him. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2).
These three, whose nature is that of the causal agents, were born directly from Maheśvara;
previously, they were all assigned by their father to the three types of duties.
"Brahmā [is the agent] in creation, Hari in protection, and Rudra again in dissolution" (7.1.13.13, 15).
Even by that much, the wearing of the *liṅga* is certainly not established.
Furthermore, because the optative (*liṅ*) is shown here in the sense of a benediction (*āśīḥ*) in the phrase "may I become," it cannot possibly be a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*); thus he says:

And [there is] the impossibility of an injunction (*vidhi*). Nor is it prompted by an injunction (*vidhiprayojaka*). It should be understood that the nature of being prompted by an injunction consists in the state of not being already established (*aprāptatva*). He states this very point: "because it is otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddhatvāt*). To this, it is said: because of the scriptural hearing (*śravaṇa*) of the birth of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others from Sadāśiva.

Furthermore, because [the worship] of the conch, the discus, and so forth is censured by such statements from the *Śivapurāṇa* as "one should not dwell for even a day where there is a body marked with the discus," and because the birth of Nārāyaṇa is heard [in those texts].
And regarding his conch, discus, and other marks:
"One whose body is marked with the discus should not dwell for even a single day in such a place;
if he were to remain, he would become a great sinner, equal to a thousand killers of Brahmins."
If one wears the Sudarśana [mark] on a family-destroyer (an outcaste) due to ignorance, greed, or passion,
one should perform a bath with the sacred water (sacala-snāna) upon seeing him.
And because [this view] has been refuted by such passages, it lacks the status of being presented by the term "non-refutation.

We shall examine this further below. However, there is no refutation of this [view], because of the absence of its production [as stated in the scripture]: "The Creator is the cause of causes; the Meditator is the cause, but He is the object of meditation."
The intention of the subsequent text is that there is no possibility for these [entities] to be objects that cannot be refuted.

However, he will provide the resolution for the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) based on *ibhūti* and so forth later on; but for this [entity], namely Sadāśiva, there is no refutation. As for this Sadāśiva:

The previously mentioned [attributes] such as being the progenitor of Nārāyaṇa and being the object of meditation are to be construed with what follows. By demonstrating that [other] causes possess the aforementioned qualities of being the progenitor of Nārāyaṇa and so forth, and being the object of meditation, they are not refuted; rather, they are connected as the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) to the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).

In reality, having prescribed the general act of wearing with the thought "May I become a wearer," when the inquiry arises as to "what is to be worn," the injunction of the *oṃ* syllable— expressed by the word *oṃ*— as the absolute *liṅga* (emblem) of "mine" and "that person" establishes that only that [emblem] is to be connected with the act of wearing. Thus, non-rejection is what is to be accepted.

The literal meaning is: "May I become a wearer of that *liṅga* which is the very nature of Śiva, denoted by the word *oṃ*, and which has been heard by my ears as being expounded in the Vedas and the scriptures.
Now, one might object:

The syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*—these two emerged from the throat of Brahmā in ancient times; therefore, both are auspicious. (Nārada Purāṇa 1.51) He is the cause even of Brahmā and the others; he is the Ordainer (*dhātā*), the Brahman, the meditator, the performer of meditation, and the Cause.
The meaning is that the Supreme Cause, the Supreme Lord, is to be meditated upon.

Not only does the status of the *liṅga* as the object of wearing follow from the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word "non-rejection" (*anirākaraṇa*), but it is also clearly stated in the remainder of that very same scriptural passage: "Of me, of such-and-such [a deity], Om."
He establishes that this has been stated by means of the passage beginning with "vastutastu" and so forth.

Thus, because the letter *a* signifies auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), and since it is established—based on the statement "The letter *a* is indeed all speech" (*Ai. Ār. 2.3.6*)—that *a* is included within all speech and serves as the source (*prakṛti*) of the *praṇava* (*oṃkara*), and furthermore, because the letter *a* denotes Viṣṇu...

If it be argued that the status of the *oṃ* syllable as having the meaning of a gender (*liṅga*) is not established, it is not so; for the *Tāpanīya Upaniṣad* states: "One should meditate on the letter *a* as Brahmā at the navel, the letter *u* as Viṣṇu in the heart, the letter *m* as Śiva between the eyebrows, and the *oṃ* syllable as the Lord of All at the end of the twelve. (*Nṛsiṃha Upaniṣad* 3.4).
Thus, having expressed the entire Śiva-nature in these three ways by means of these very three measures (mātrās), one awakens it through the half-measure (ardhamātrā).

Thus, by this statement from the *Śivapurāṇa*, it is established that in the hymn to Śiva composed by Viṣṇu in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*, the word does not have the meaning of "liṅga. This is the intention of the objector, who argues that because the syllable *oṃ* signifies auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) and is derived from the stem *akāra* which denotes Viṣṇu, [it cannot mean a phallic emblem]. [The text continues: *akāram*...
By the Tāpanīya Upaniṣad passage beginning with "Brahmāṇam," by the statement from the Śiva Purāṇa,
and by the Liṅga Purāṇa, the Viṣṇu-stotra, and other such texts,
[it is established that] the half-mora (ardhamātrā) portion of the syllable Om is the support for the three moras (mātrās).
The intention of the subsequent passage is that the status of [the syllable] as having the meaning of a *liṅga* is established by the fact that it is understood to denote Paramaśiva.

This is because, by the verse "Salutation to you, the Omniscient; salutation again and again to Oṃkāra," the Oṃkāra, whose nature consists of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), is declared to be the denoter of Paramaśiva.
Nor should it be argued that the syllable *oṃ*, having *a* as its constituent part, denotes Viṣṇu—who is denoted by *a*—because all words have *a* as their constituent part;

for if the denotatum were established solely through that which is denoted by *a*, it would follow that the expressive power (*śakti*) of words is entirely destroyed. This is because of the scriptural statement: "The letter *a* is indeed all speech" (*AiĀ* 2.3.6).
This is because it serves as a glorification, as in the passage, "All speech is woven together by the syllable Oṃ" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.3);
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting each preceding [statement].

"Because it would result in the total abolition of all [linguistic] capacity"—this is the sense that the denotative power (*śakti*) of no word whatsoever could be established for any object other than Viṣṇu.
To the question, "What then is the interpretation of the passage 'The letter *a* is indeed all speech'? he says: "Because it is laudatory.

The meaning of the word *saṃtṛṇṇā* (pierced through) is "pervaded. [This refers to the three vowels] by virtue of being the material cause (*prakṛti*) and the substratum of dissolution (*layādhiṣṭhāna*).

He states that because they are dissolved into the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) of the preceding measures, it is established that even those [measures] denote only the supreme reality (*paramātmatattva*) which is expressed by the half-measure; for he says: "because the opposite would result.
For this very reason, their status as signifiers of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is also established.

Because he constantly bestows peace at the commencement of all undertakings for those humans who desire his auspiciousness, he is therefore remembered as the god Śiva. (Mahābhārata 7) "All these Dānavas and Suras are equal to me."
"I am auspicious (*śiva*) to all beings; therefore, O gods, my state is *śivatva*. (Mahābhārata 8.2.3).
From this etymological explanation of the word "Śiva" in the Karṇaparvan, it is certain that Śiva is the bestower of all auspiciousness.
Nor should it be argued: "Even if the syllable *oṃ* denotes Śiva, what follows from its reference to the *liṅga*? [For] in the *liṅga*...

This is because, by the previously cited statement from the *Haṃsopaniṣad*, deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is determined to be the very nature of Śiva as the *liṅga*; furthermore, it is directly intended for that [Śiva] according to the scriptural declaration: "The syllable *oṃ* is declared to be the *liṅga*."
Regarding what was stated—that there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) only with the wearing of sacred ash (*bhūti*) and rudrākṣa beads—we propose this alternative:
is the concomitance due to their being primary, or because they are inseparable from the wearing of the *liṅga*?
As for the *oṃkāra*, it has been stated [in the *Nārāyaṇīya Purāṇa* 1.51.10]: "The *oṃkāra* and the word 'atha'..."
With the intention that the quality of signifying auspiciousness is entirely conducive to its denoting Śiva, he says:

"It promotes tranquility," and so forth. Because Śiva increases auspiciousness, bestows auspiciousness, and is himself of the nature of auspiciousness, it is most appropriate for the syllable *oṃ*—which signifies him—to possess the character of being auspicious (*māṅgalika*).
"What follows from this?"—the sense is that it is not established that the syllable *oṃ* refers to the subtle body (*liṅga*). Regarding "deep sleep [occurs] in the subtle body":

since deep sleep—which is synonymous with absorption into the Supreme Self—is demonstrated to occur when the individual soul (*jīva*), which moves within the petals of the lotus of the heart, reaches the subtle body, [it follows that] the subtle body...

The sense is that such a doubt should not be entertained because [the practice] culminates in the realization of the nature of the Supreme Self. Previously, it was questioned why the wearing of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads—being established by worldly custom and scripture—is not considered the counter-positive (pratiyogin) to the act of wearing; he refutes that with the words "As for what was said," and so forth.

Not the first, because there is no word present that could bring those [other objects] to mind; for it is nowhere well-known that the syllable *oṃ* brings to mind the earth (*bhūti*) and the rudrākṣa. Not the second, because that would result in an undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). However, some maintain that by the term "non-exclusion" (*anirākaraṇa*), both the earth and the rudrākṣa are included, while by "om," the linga is grasped. And thus:
They say that in all three cases, there is a primary connection with the injunctive sense (*vidhi*).

As for what was stated—that because the form *bhūyāsam* here is in the optative of benediction (*āśīr-liṅ*), an injunction is not possible—that is weak; for [we see] "May I become wise" (*medhāvī bhūyāsam*, Ṛgveda 10.151.6) and "I alone... (*ahamekaḥ*).
Because that [possibility] exists here just as in the case of *prathamamāsam* (*Aitareya Āraṇyaka* 1),

one should not argue that while such a possibility exists there due to the presence of a form that prompts an injunction (*vidhi-prayojaka-rūpa*), no injunction is possible here because of its absence;
for even here, the injunction "May I be one who wears [it]" (*dhārayitā bhūyāsam*, *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 10.9.1) has been established.

Having cited the passage, "The wearing of the *liṅga* establishes the universal *liṅga*" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 10.16.1), [the author] accepts that this is merely an injunction regarding the locus, namely the mantra on the hand; otherwise, he states:
"There is the word *oṃ*, which denotes the *liṅga*, but there is nothing whatsoever that denotes *bhasma* (ash) or *rudrākṣa*."
"Because of the absence of a word" means "because it would result in what is already accepted. The intended meaning is that there is no purpose in refuting a statement that is not contradictory.

"By the absence of being established otherwise" means that since the wearing of the *liṅga* prescribed by the text "it establishes all *liṅgas*" is already established, there is no characteristic of being an injunction (*vidhi*)—namely, the state of being previously unestablished (*aprāptatva*)—according to your own view. However...

One should reflect as follows: the opponent argues that by restating the wearing of the prescribed marks with the words "he establishes all marks," the subsequent injunction "the mantra in the hand" merely prescribes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) alone;
thus, the essential form required for it to function as an injunction is indeed present. [The mantra is:
"May I become wise" (Ṛgveda Khila 10.151.6).
Or, let this be considered merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); nevertheless, its status as referring to the wearing of the marks (*liṅgadhāraṇa*) is not lost,

because that very point is established by the Smṛti through such passages as "What was heard in the ears is not to be rejected" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 10.9.1), and according to the method already stated, [it refers to] "the small, free from evil" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 10.10.23).
Furthermore, because of the statement, "He establishes the universal *liṅga* of this [soul]" (*Tai. Ā.

10.16.1*), and because the mantra "Obeisance to Brahman" occurring in that same context cannot possibly refer to anything other than the practice of wearing the external and internal *liṅga*, as evidenced by its focus on such wearing; this has been explained in detail elsewhere.
And this very point is further corroborated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Salutations be unto You, O Brahman, the Teacher, the Great Soul;
for the universe, being a product, is not indeed subject to death, since it is merely the negation of that [Brahman]."

Thus, although wisdom (*medhā*) is being prayed for, just as one infers an injunction— "one should make oneself wise by means of this mantra"— on the basis of the indicative power (*liṅga*) consisting in the capacity of the words, so too in the passage "may I be a holder" (*ahaṃ dhārayitā bhūyāsam*,
Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.9.1), the act of holding is [inferred] solely on the strength of that indicative power.

The intended meaning is that there will be the postulation of an injunction (vidhi) in the form "one should do. The point is this: although there is not even a trace of suspicion regarding an injunction in the phrase "I was," nevertheless, just as an injunction is postulated in the sense that "the Lord alone is to be meditated upon as eternal," so it is here as well.

He says that even in the opposite case, there is no deficiency whatsoever: "Let it be for now," etc. "Even so," etc.: in this interpretation, by the communication of the state of not being refuted and the nature of being the syllable *praṇava*, one should understand that because the bearer of the *liṅga* obtains both praise of qualities (*guṇa*) and commendation (*stuti*), it possesses the character of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) and the character of an injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*). "Its having another purpose," etc.
By the force of the context, even the salutation "Obeisance to Brahman" has as its object Brahman in the form of the *liṅga* alone.

"Upabṛṃhitam" means explained in detail. Regarding "by death": because of the rule that "for one who is born, death is certain," the entire universe that is produced is overcome by death; but Brahman...
Brahman is non-repudiation because it is the primordial cause;
O best of teachers, may there be for me the retention of that non-repudiation.
Renowned in the Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas, and heard by my ears,
may I become the God who sustains all, the cause of everything.
The gods, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, who are well-known and likewise heard of in the scriptures—
all of them were destroyed by Mṛtyu, the enemy of all.
"Let these be rejected by me; they must never be worn. May I not become a wearer of the gods, O deities, as you are sinking."
"They are unable to cross over me as I sink in the ocean of death;
this *oṃ-liṅga* of mine is above, so take refuge in both me and it.
Because it is the cause—meaning, because it is the fundamental cause—it cannot be refuted by anyone. Therefore:
That alone is called non-rejection; everything else is called rejection. Therefore, the meaning is: "May I become the sustainer of Brahman alone, and not of other gods. He states the reason for this:
"the gods who are sinking"—meaning that the gods themselves are submerged in *saṃsāra* and are unable to effect their own deliverance.

The intended meaning is: "How will they be able [to do so]? Here, the repetition of the words *devān* and *surān* is avoided by relying on the etymological sense (*yaugikatva*) of the word *sura*, based on the statement in the *Vālmīki-Rāmāyaṇa*: "Because of their grasping at *vāruṇī* [liquor], they are called *surāḥ*" (1.45.38). [This is to be addressed] to the teacher with the words: "And take refuge in me and in him."
This is a prayer; its meaning is: "Make me take refuge in that [Lord] whose nature is the Oṃkāra-liṅga.
This is stated in the *Yātrākhaṇḍa* of the *Kumārasaṃhitā* within the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
And likewise for those of great asceticism, for the renunciants (yatis), for the yogis,
for the twice-born followers of Śambhu, for the devotees of Śiva (śaivas), and for those who bear the linga.
And of the great Pāśupatas who observe the vow bearing my name,
and of the high-souled Brāhmaṇas devoted to the Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra].
O Lord of Mountains, out of affection for me, this should be given constantly to all those who delight in the five-syllable mantra, who serve the twice-born, and who are perfected beings (siddhas).
Those who perform the observance known as the wearing of the *liṅga*, which is designated as belonging to Maheśvara,
go to the abode of Śiva.
The auspicious vow called Pāśupata consists of the worship of the Śiva-liṅga;
it may be performed six times a day, three times, or once a day for Maheśvara.
"O Brahmin-sage, those who worship [it] go to the abode of Śiva.
Passages such as these, which reinforce the stated meaning, are to be considered.
In the Taittirīya recension itself—
He who is the bull among the meters, possessing all forms, who was born from the meters out of the immortal—may that Indra inspire me with wisdom; may I become a bearer of the immortal, O God.

Regarding the mantra "He who is the bull among the Vedas" (*yaśchandasāmṛṣabhaḥ*): although both this preceding mantra and the present one are intended to pray for the power of retention so that one who has studied the Vedas may not forget them, nevertheless, because they were also explained by the Blessed One Vedavyāsa in the Purāṇas as being directed toward the wearing of the *liṅga*, their primary intent must certainly lie there as well.
It should be understood as follows: "He who is the bull among the *chandasa*s. He is the bull—the master—of the Vedas, both by virtue of being their author and their subject matter.
"My body is most wise; my tongue is most sweet."

"From my two ears, [let it be] heard extensively. This very point is also established by the mantra: "The treasury of Brahman, covered by wisdom—protect what has been heard" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 7.4.1). "May I become a bearer of the gods" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 7.4.1).

Viśvarūpa is the inner controller of all. Regarding the phrase "He was born from the Vedas (chandas) out of immortality (amṛta)": the ablative case in *amṛtāt* is used with the intended meaning of being the cause of the fruit for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*), just as the instrumental case is used in the expression "he dwells by means of study" (*adhyayanena vasati*). Thus, *chandobhyo'dhisambabhūva* means he was manifested preeminently; that is, he was made known with excellence. He was Indra.

May he cover me with wisdom. May that Indra, the possessor of sovereignty, the Supreme Lord, cover me—that is, may He envelop me—by means of *medhā*, the intellect known as the power of retention; in other words, may He unite me with it. "May I become the sustainer of the immortals (*amṛta*). The genitive case is used here to express the relationship of purpose.
O Bhavānī, may I become a bearer—that is, a performer of the bearing—of the Lord Śiva in the form of the *liṅga* for the sake of liberation.
May my body be firm and well-observed; this is the meaning. May my tongue be most sweet and pleasant-spoken. Through both my ears, may I hear much—that is, may I be widely renowned.

May it be heard in its specific form. "Thou art the sheath of Brahman; thou art the support of the Veda. [The prayer continues: "May the Veda be covered and protected by me through *medhā*—the power of retention"—in this context, the word *deva* refers to him who is the supreme deity among deities (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 6.7).

7) Thus, because of the usage [of the term] in reference to Paramaśiva in such passages as "Therefore, the Lord is remembered as Śiva" (*Mahābhārata*), and because there is an absence of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) prescribing the meditation on any other deity, as well as an absence of such practice (*ācāra*).

Since the word *dhāraṇa* ends in the suffix *lyuṭ* with the sense of the agent, it means "one who supports the deity. Thus, for the sake of attaining liberation through the truth of the immortal, [I pray] "may I become a supporter of the deity";
for this purpose, "protect my learning," which means "guard what I have studied. Alternatively, it may mean by virtue of the power of retention (*dhāraṇā*).

The meaning is that it is "covered" (*pihita*), i.e., placed within a casket; that is to say, having become such [an image] in the form of a *liṅga*. Having become thus, protect—that is, preserve—the *liṅga* which is non-different from that [Self], which has been taught as something to be upheld (*dharya*) by me in the *Śruti*, *Purāṇas*, and so forth, so that it may not fall away from my body for as long as I live.

The meaning is "one should act. He shows the authority for the fact that the word *deva* denotes Paramaśiva alone through its primary sense (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*) by stating: "Therefore, Śiva is remembered as the God" (*tasmād devaḥ śivaḥ smṛtaḥ*).
This is because the suffix *lyuṭ* [in *deva*] denotes the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113). For this very reason...

The justification for its masculine gender is as follows: if it were intended to express an abstract state (*bhāva*), then by the rule *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ lyuṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.114–115), the neuter gender would have resulted; therefore, Indra—who is capable of both restraint and favor—is Śiva in the form of that *liṅga*, [who] may [endow] me with wisdom.
"He shall spread [it], he shall unite it"—thus it was explained by the former teachers.
It may be so. He states the meaning of the word *indra*: "one who is capable of restraint and favor.
Such capability alone is supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*). "May he spread [it] through wisdom (*medhā*). Without wisdom...
In the retention of the Vedic texts, negligence is inevitable; let this not occur—for this purpose, this prayer for intelligence (*medhā*) should be understood.
Here, the following is considered: "He who is the bull of the meters, possessing all forms" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 7.4).

1) It must be admitted that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because of its connection with the word "yat" (which). And since such a statement requires a prior injunction (*purovāda*), the following passage from the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad is intended here: "In the middle of that crest-lock, the Supreme Self is established" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.11.12).

The introductory statement: Having described the heart with the words, "resembling the calyx of a lotus" (*taittirīya-āraṇyaka* 10.11.6), and having shown the cavity within it with the words, "in its center there is a hollow" (*taittirīya-āraṇyaka* 10.11.8), [it continues]: "in the middle of that is a great fire" (*taittirīya-āraṇyaka* 10.11.9).
Beginning with these words and ending with "the Supreme Self is established" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.11.12),
having thus demonstrated the cavity within that [heart] by way of demonstrating the Supreme Self, [it refers to] such a Self as "He who is the Bull among the Vedas" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 7.4.1).

Having restated this with the words "by this [means]," the injunction "may I be a sustainer" (*dhāraṇo bhūyāsam*) is established. And thus, when the meaning is "may I be a sustainer of the deity"— that is, a sustainer of the Supreme Self residing in the middle of the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), an internal sustainer—
the connection with the word *yat* occurs because of the employment of the relative pronoun.

The intention of the objector in stating that "being the first" (*prāthamya*) and so forth is the definition of the subject (*uddeśya*) is as follows: because of its connection with the word *yat*, which serves as the mark of being the subject, the phrase "the bull among the Vedas" (*chandām̐sam ṛṣabhaḥ*) must be understood as the indicator of subjecthood; and since subjecthood is dependent upon [the object] being already established (*siddhatva*).
The attainment [of this goal] here is required by a certain scriptural statement, and that statement is found in close proximity in the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*.

Nor is there any proof for the wearing of sectarian marks (*liṅga*). Furthermore, in this context, by the presentation of the characteristic mark of Brahman in the term "Viśvarūpa" (the Universal Form), and by the use of the word "Brahman" without any qualifying prefix in the phrase "you are the sheath of Brahman," [the text refers to] the Supreme Self.

If it is argued that this is because the act of internal retention (*antardhāraṇa*) is thus understood, do not say so; for according to that school’s view, in the phrase "may I become one who possesses the retention of God" (*devadhāraṇo bhūyāsam*), the "retention of God"—that is, the Supreme Self—is established as meaning internal reflection or meditation (*upāsana*). And thus, regarding that crest-lock (*śikhā*):

"The Supreme Self is situated in the middle" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.11.12)— this refers to that [Self] which was introduced by the preceding statement, [described] by such passages as "the small, stainless one, the abode of the highest" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.23).

If it were accepted that this very [mantra] is the object of the injunction "may I become a sustainer of the gods" by virtue of its being established as the object of worship through the preceding statement (*purovāda*), then the purpose not already obtained from the preceding statement would not be accomplished;
for a sentence that proceeds to enjoin something not obtained from the preceding statement does not do so merely by restating what has already been obtained from the preceding statement.
One attains success only by establishing the very meaning already present therein;

thus, this alone is what should be upheld. By that statement, Nārāyaṇa, who dwells in the space of the heart-lotus, is revealed. Consequently, this is the established meaning: that which is Nārāyaṇa...

The Lord of the Vedas resides in the space of the heart-lotus; one should maintain the thought, "May I become that very God," and "May I become the one who performs internal contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of Him," and so forth.
Nor is it the case that [the goal] is attained through the image of Śālagrāma and the like, which is determined to be non-different from Him.

It must be stated that external retention (*bahir-dhāraṇa*) is also obtained [as an option], because its retention would be contrary to established practice. Therefore, he resolves [the objection] by stating "not so," [meaning] that by this [text] only the contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of Nārāyaṇa is enjoined.
This is the intention: [of] the previously demonstrated Nārāyaṇa who is within the small [space], free from evil...
Since the meditation in the form of contemplation (*anusandhāna*), beginning with the words "becoming the dwelling of others" (*paraveśmabhūtaṃ*), has already been enjoined previously,

it cannot be said that [the passage] is intended to enjoin that very same thing again through the phrase "may I become a sustainer of the gods" (*devadhāraṇo bhūyāsam*); for if it were so, the entire sentence would now result in being redundant.

For this very reason, in the passage [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.18], "When there is darkness, that is neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being; Śiva alone is," as well as in the passages leading to the state of darkness, such as [Sūtra Upaniṣad 2.2], "He becomes one with the Supreme God who is beyond darkness," and [Sūtra Upaniṣad 6.1], "The divine God is one, Nārāyaṇa."

Having raised the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that because Nārāyaṇa is established as the presiding deity of *tamas*, the term "Śiva's state" (*śivapada*) must also refer to Nārāyaṇa, [the author] proceeds to establish [the correct conclusion] by means of the introductory phrase "When [there was] darkness" (*yadā tamaḥ*), following an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) of all other passages that establish *tamas*.

It has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that if the word "Śiva" in the passage beginning with "For him who has thus proceeded, there is neither day nor night" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 4.18) were intended to refer to Nārāyaṇa, it would lack the status of an original injunction (*aprāptavidhāyakatva*) because its antecedent statement (*purovāda*) would not support it;
therefore, it is the word "Nārāyaṇa" occurring in the antecedent statement itself that must be understood as referring to Śiva through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and other such means.
In the *Karṇāmṛta* and other works, Appayyadīkṣita states: "Nor [is there any contradiction],

because by the phrase 'of the immortal' (*amṛtasya*), the fruit in the form of liberation is enjoined with reference to the Supreme Self— which was already established as the object of meditation within that crest-lock (*śikhā*) by the preceding statement, 'And in the middle of that crest-lock' (*na cāsya tasyāḥ śikhāyā madhye*, Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.11.12)."
The same objection applies to that [text] as well:

"When there was darkness" (*yadā tamaḥ*). The meaning of the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*)—which is contained within the sentence linked by the relative pronoun *yat*—is that it is necessarily a prescriptive rule for what was not obtained from the preceding sentence. In this context, [it is said]: "The divine, singular god Nārāyaṇa..."

Thus, having raised the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that—on account of its proximity to the preceding sentence—"Śiva alone" might somehow mean Nārāyaṇa by the word "Śiva"—[the author replies]: if that were so, [it would contradict] the following: "When there was darkness, there was neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being; Śiva alone existed" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.18).
Otherwise, this statement would indeed be redundant;

for this sentence fulfills its purpose only by imparting knowledge of Śiva, which was not obtained from the preceding sentence. However, if the word "Śiva" were taken to refer exclusively to Nārāyaṇa, then since that knowledge was already established previously, it could not function as such an injunction.

This was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by Appayya Dīkṣita. Nor is that defect [of the argument] still present even within the conclusion of Appayya Dīkṣita— namely, that the word *Nārāyaṇa* itself refers to Śiva through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth— as shown previously.
Because [the attainment] has already been established by the preceding statement, "He attains union and residence in the same world" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 1.6), there is no lack of its attainment;
for even in your own view, regarding the passage "May I become a sustainer of the gods," [it is likewise established].

If it is argued that there would be a prescription of a meaning contrary to the preceding statement in the rule for wearing a large-sized *liṅga*, we say: not so; for [the rule] "He who is the bull of the Vedas, the omniform" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 7.4.1) refers to the middle of that tuft (*śikhā*) [in *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 10.11].

12) Thus, this alone is the *purovāda* (introductory statement); this is the restrictive rule (*niyama*). However, because it establishes all gender markers, this alone is the *purovāda*. The fruit, which is the gross mark of the fingers, is enjoined as being obtained precisely through that; otherwise, this very sentence would be purposeless.

It should not be argued that, just as Nārāyaṇa was previously mentioned, Śiva would now also appear to have been previously mentioned; for if Śiva were accepted by the word "Nārāyaṇa," there would be no clear cognition of Śiva because the mental state would be drawn toward the conventional (rūḍhi) aspect [of the term]. Therefore, for the sake of a certain cognition of him, it is said: "Śiva alone."

This is because [the latter interpretation] is necessary. If the term "Śiva" here were taken to refer to Nārāyaṇa, there would necessarily be a redundancy in conveying—by means of a secondary (gauṇī) function—a meaning that has already been determined as the object of cognition through the primary (rūḍhi) power of the word at the outset. As for the meaning of the scriptural passage beginning with "yadā": when, prior to creation...

Darkness, consisting solely of ignorance, existed; there was neither day nor night, neither the existent (sat)—the cause such as atoms and so forth—nor the non-existent (asat)—the effect such as the gross elements and so forth. Rather, the meaning is that at that time Śiva alone, the stainless one, existed. Since the existence of darkness has just been stated here, it follows that "only Śiva" [existed].
The mention of *kaivalya* (isolation) should be understood as intending the exclusion of any second entity of the same class, based on the state of possessing eternally manifest consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "contrary to the preceding statement": in that preceding statement, "of that crest," the meditation on Nārāyaṇa was [prescribed].
The sense is that there would be a contradiction with the context, as the wearing of an external *liṅga* has already been enjoined here. However,

in the phrase "he establishes the *sarvaliṅga*," the wearing of the *liṅga* consisting of Sadāśiva— which was enjoined there— is merely restated here by the term "bearing of the deity" (*devadhāraṇa*), and the fruit in the form of liberation (*mokṣa*) is enjoined by the words "of the immortal" (*amṛtasya*).

This is not an unintended consequence; for in the *Pūrvatantra*, in order to avoid the redundancy of the injunction prescribing duality, the avoidance of that redundancy was achieved by accepting a secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) in the passage, "The omentum must be prepared as five-fold" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 7.20.9). Here, however, [the goal] is achieved without resorting to figurative sense, through the maintenance of the deity.

In the passage "May I become [a mendicant]," what burden is there in establishing complete consistency by prescribing liberation as the fruit of wearing external marks? Nor can there be an alternative interpretation based on the "Sarvalinga" (All-Marks) passage, even in a general sense.
Because it is impossible for that which prescribes a specific result to be established otherwise.
[Objection: Even so, how can Janārdana be the means to liberation, given the traditional teaching (smṛti): "One should seek knowledge from Maheśvara; one should seek liberation from Janārdana"?

If it is argued that this is merely a prescription for liberation indicated by a mark (liṅga), we say no; for [the scriptures state]: "Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.14);
"Having known the Lord, they become immortal" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.7);
and "Śiva alone, the source of auspiciousness, is to be meditated upon, having abandoned everything else."

"Nor is this an accepted consequence (iṣṭāpatti). One must not say that the futility of the sentence is indeed what is intended; for the futility of the sentence "he cuts twice" has already been avoided by accepting even a slight figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of the word *vapā* in the rule "the omentum (*vapā*) is to be prepared with five cuttings. Thus, there is no acceptance of the sentence's futility.
Because it is impossible for anyone other than one whose heart is empty [of all else] to speak [thus],
and because scriptures such as *Śikhā* 3 establish that Śiva alone is the means to liberation by means of excluding all others, there is a contradiction between the Śruti and the Smṛti.
Because the Smṛti is weaker according to the principle of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "according to the principle of the section on contradiction": this means by what is stated in the Sūtra, *virodhe tvanapekṣaṃ syādasati hyanumānam* (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.3). As for the meaning of that Sūtra: in the case of contradiction—that is, when there is a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti—[the Smṛti] would be independent [of its source], for [only] when such [a source] does not exist is there an inference [of it].

The remainder of the sense is that scripture is an authority independent [of other means of knowledge]. The meaning is that when a Vedic statement is absent and not directly perceived, inference—namely, tradition (smṛti)—becomes an authority. Thus, there is a conflict between the scriptural text, "One should chant the udgītha while touching the *audumbarī* [post]," and the traditional rule, "The entire *audumbarī* must be wrapped."

In a case of mutual contradiction, the Smṛti rule regarding the "covering of all [the sacrificial post]" is abandoned due to its conflict with Śruti; likewise here too, because of the contradiction with such Śruti passages as, "Having known Śiva,

one attains ultimate peace" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.14) and "Having known the Lord, they become immortal" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.7), [the claim that] "one desiring liberation [should worship] Janārdana" must be rejected.

The sense is that memory is considered weak. Nor [is it an obstacle], because by the injunction "May Indra strengthen him with intelligence" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 7.4.1), the production of intelligence is prescribed, and since that [intelligence] is an internal quality, it pertains to internal meditation.
It must be said that the attainment of that very Dharma is what is truly auspicious, according to the Śruti: "May that God unite us with auspicious mindfulness" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.19).
O child, for one who possesses the connection between the subtle body and the physical limbs, there is no rebirth.
Through the perfect accomplishment of simultaneous knowledge, one shall thereafter attain liberation.
And because, according to this statement from the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*, the knowledge that produces liberation is dependent upon Śiva in the form of the *liṅga*, its wearing must necessarily follow;
otherwise—as it is said: "Indeed, Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone."

"And he is not the Lord" (na ca sa mendraḥ). Since *medhā* has the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its referent, the question arises that even the meditation on the Lord (*īśvara-dhāraṇa*), which is the cause of that [medhā], must be understood as being of the nature of meditation (*upāsanā*) itself, for the sake of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between cause and effect. [This concerns] the Supreme Lord.

He gives the answer— stating that "even though held in the body in the form of the *liṅga* by virtue of possessing all powers and being all-pervasive, it is capable of producing fruit everywhere"— beginning with "That God is auspicious for us" (*sa no devaḥ śubha*) and so forth,
and "the union of the *liṅga* and the body" (*liṅgāṅgasaṅga*) and so forth; [this applies] even to external actions through their connection with the mind.
By such statements as [Bhagavad Gītā 3.20], pilgrimage to sacred sites, bathing in the Gaṅgā, and so forth,
would not be generators of the means to liberation;
furthermore, because the wearing of the *liṅga* is an internal factor by way of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Furthermore, if this [mantra] were intended to enjoin the wearing of external emblems on the body, then the specific injunction regarding external objects—“May my body be most observant;
may my tongue be most sweet; may I hear much with my two ears” (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 7.4.1)—would also become meaningful.
It is stated that because it is being performed, its capacity to produce a mental excellence is sanctioned by the scriptures—
namely, the passage "By action alone, indeed, [he attained perfection]," as well as the passages concerning pilgrimage to sacred sites, bathing in the Ganges, and the wearing of the *liṅga*.

He states that for the sake of attaining the "far-seeing" quality of the body and the "sweetest" quality of the tongue—qualities sought here even while residing within the body—the wearing of external marks (*bāhyaliṅga*) alone is appropriate, beginning with the words "Furthermore," etc.:
"Having become Rudra, one should worship Rudra; one who is not Rudra should not worship Rudra."
He who possesses a connection with the limb of the vital-force-liṅga is Rudra; there is no doubt in this matter.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*, since the non-difference from Śiva is established through the very connection with the *liṅga*, the excellence of the body is also established; for the *guruliṅga*— which has the *iṣṭaliṅga* as its material cause and which presides over the water-element— is situated at the tip of the tongue, whereby one attains the state of being intoxicated with honey (*madhumattama*).

Because for one who possesses a *prasāda-liṅga* whose material cause (*prakṛti*) is the *bhāva-liṅga*, and who identifies with the principle of space (*ākāśatattva*), the accomplishment of extensive hearing is established through the function of the sense of hearing;
and because, in the worship of Rudra, it is required that the worshipper attain the state of Rudra, and of that...
He establishes that the wearing of the *liṅga* must necessarily be performed because it is dependent upon the wearing of the *liṅga*, stating:

"Having become Rudra, one should worship Rudra. The words of the scripture also cohere [with this view], as the firmness of the body and so forth are naturally established upon the attainment of the state of Rudra.

Regarding the phrase "having the nature of the chosen *liṅga*": because the qualities such as being the presiding deity (*abhimānitva*) of the water element (*jalatattva*) and the ether element (*ākāśatattva*) have been produced within the maintained *liṅga* through the power of the mantric consecration (*māntrika-saṃskāra*), there is a connection between the sense of taste and the sense of hearing [with their respective elements].
Thus, this [interpretation] becomes more reasonable; for this reason as well, that which was stated— that this [text], being intent on the wearing of external marks,
renders untenable the term *viśvarūpa* (the universal form) and the unqualified word *brahman* when they refer to the wearing of limited, physical marks— is also not acceptable.
For the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees, Śiva himself, whose essential nature is the limited *liṅga*, is described in the *Atharvaśiras* and other texts with such passages as:
"I am the one facing east; I am the one facing west" (*Atharvaśiras* 1.1).

Because the teaching of Śiva’s universal selfhood leads to the conclusion that he alone possesses the form of the universe— as stated by Śaṅkarācārya in his *Aparādha-stava* through the use of the unqualified term "Brahman" (*brahma*) for the *liṅga*— there is no logical inconsistency in this usage.

The intention is that [the truth] must be heard and reflected upon. "I am facing east," "I am ancient," "I am facing west," "I am modern"—this statement refers to the Supreme Lord who has assumed a limited form out of affection for His devotees. Therefore, regarding the Supreme Lord in His form as the *liṅga*, the two terms "Viśvarūpa" (the Universal Form) and "Brahman" apply.
The sense is that the application [of the suffix] is not untenable.

Others, however, [argue that] because of the resulting lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the word *gopāya* in the passage "Protect what has been heard by me" (*śrutaṃ me gopāya*, Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 7.4.1), [the suffix must be applied] in the passage "May I be one who upholds the gods" (*devadhāraṇo bhūyāsam*, Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 7.4.1).

The word "deva" is to be split [into *deva* and *iti*], and it is construed with the word "gopāya" (protect); thus, based on the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the wearing of the *liṅga* is not established by the attainment of the phrase "may I become a bearer of immortality," one should abandon the construction of the word "deva" with the word "dhāraṇa" (bearing) which is heard in proximity.

By the principle of the "infinite remainder" (*aparimitādhikaraṇanyāya*), since it is impossible for [the word *brahma*] to be construed with "protect" (*gopāya*) here, one must accept that the word *brahma*—

which is heard in proximity in the text "Thou art the sheath of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ kośo'si*, Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 7.4.1)— is to be construed by changing its case-ending; otherwise, [there would be a fault] regarding the word "support" (*dhāraṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "others, however" (*anye tu*): because the second-person singular form "gopāya" (protect) is observed there, it should be understood that "O God" (*deva*) is the vocative address. Furthermore, the word "of this" (*asya*) is to be construed with both "dhāraṇā" (retention) and "amṛtasya" (of the nectar). And thus, [the result is] liberation.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the wearing of the *liṅga* is not established merely by the acquisition of another object; rather, it must be maintained.
However, proximity (*pratyāsatti*) itself will serve as the regulator of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*), according to the principle of the "unlimited locus" (*aparamitādhikaraṇanyāya*).
The nature of this principle has already been explained above. [This applies] to the word "deity" (*deva*) by virtue of its proximity.

Even if one accepts the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇa*), the vocative address will still be obtained in the word *gopāya*. For, by transforming the genitive-ending term *brahmaṇaḥ* into a vocative case ending, the syntactic connection "O Brahman, protect! (*brahman gopāya*) becomes possible; thus, [there is] the destruction of suffering—
They also state the following resolution: "Because it is impossible for liberation through what is expressed [by words] to follow [from such a source]," regarding the meaning of this Śruti:
"O Brahmins, endowed with faith, you who are joined to the body by the Prāṇa-liṅga..."
Establish this path which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He who, with a body free from attachment, wears the auspicious Śiva-liṅga as his very self,
shall cross over the ocean of worldly existence— which is restless with the breaking of attachments— by means of the submarine fire that consumes the limbs of passion.
Always worship those Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva, devoted to virtuous conduct, bearing the *liṅga*, and wearing sacred ash and *rudrākṣa* beads.
Thus, certain previously cited passages from the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*, which bear the character of supplementary exegesis (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), should also be considered.
Among the various branches of knowledge, the Veda is supreme; and among the Vedas, the *Rudraikādaśinī* is supreme.
In that regard, there is the five-syllabled mantra; within it, the two syllables "śi-va" are present.
Thus, in the *Rudraikādaśinī*, which is the crest-jewel of all the Vedas,

the reply is that it cannot be stated in such a way because the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is sublated when the state of liberation (*rūpamokṣa*) is joined with the meaning of the word "retention" (*dhāraṇa*). [The texts] have acquired the character of supplements (*upabṛṃhaṇa*).

The sense is that by hearing the word "wearing" (*dhāraṇa*) in the phrase "the wearing of the auspicious Śiva-liṅga," the impression of a Vedic injunction regarding the wearing of the deity is conveyed.
Among sciences, the Śruti is the most excellent; therefore, the *Rudraikādaśinī* (the eleven Rudras), which is the crown of all sciences, is [supreme], and within that as well—

Regarding the mantra, "O Rudra, that form of yours which is auspicious, non-terrible, and not appearing as evil" (*apāpakāśinī*), there is also the Śruti: "O Rudra, that form of yours which is auspicious, non-terrible, and [not] appearing as evil among sinless devotees" (*Tai. Saṃ. 4.5.1.1*). He is called Rudra because he causes *rudam*—the weeping born of the suffering of saṃsāra—to *drāvayati*, i.e., melt away.

Or, Rudra is so called because he causes ignorance (*rudam ajñānam*) to melt away (*drāvayati*). O Rudra, that body of yours—which is non-terrible (*aghorā*), peaceful in form (*śāntākārā*), auspicious (*śivā*), and the bestower of all blessings (*sarvamaṅgalapradā*)—is the one that shines without sin (*apāpakāśinī*).
Śiva, as delimited by the body in the form of the *liṅga*, is endowed with tranquility and self-restraint within the vessel of the devotee.
The established meaning is "to be maintained. In that regard, one should reflect upon the term "vigilant. And this is corroborated in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*:
"O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is non-terrible (*aghorā*) and does not manifest evil..."

The meaning "that body of yours which shines and is beautiful in the form of the Śiva-liṅga" implies that the wearing of the liṅga (liṅgadhāraṇa) is a duty to be performed. He states that this is the meaning accepted in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* with the words beginning "And it is corroborated," and so forth.
Since he is praised with the Yajus, therefore the devotee of Śiva is freed from sin.

He who bears the *liṅga*, whose inner self is disciplined, and whose mind is constantly fixed on the worship of Śiva— having joyfully bowed to Vīreśvara, I shall likewise demonstrate the wearing of the *liṅga* according to the injunctions in the Yajurveda and also in the Ṛgveda. (6.61)
This treatise, which establishes the necessity of wearing the *liṅga* according to the *Yajurveda*, is completed.
Now, he declares that its necessity is also established by the *Ṛgveda*: "One should act likewise even in the *Ṛgveda*.
"O Brahmaṇaspati, your purifier is spread out; you, the Lord, encompass our limbs on every side."
"One whose body is not heated does not enjoy that; only those who have been cooked [by austerity] reach that state" (Ṛgveda 9).

Here, by the word *brahman*, the *liṅga* (the subtle body) is meant; based on the etymology "that which makes known the hidden meaning," it is designated as such because it is the substratum thereof. That *liṅga* is the eternal *brahman*. (6)
36) "The *liṅga* is the eternal Brahman" (*siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, 6.35), and [in the mantra] "O Lord of Brahmā, this pure *liṅga* is yours. Thus, by the word "Brahman," the Śiva-liṅga is designated.

Although demonstrating the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *liṅga* is unnecessary— since the word *brahman* possesses its own activity through its own etymology or through its inherent power of conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) and so forth— nevertheless, by the phrase "it makes known the hidden object" (*līnam arthaṃ gamayati*),
[the nature of] the Śiva-liṅga [is established].

"That which is designated as Brahman" is also evident from Śaṅkarācārya’s *Aparādhastava* and from his vision at Prayāga. The meaning is that its Lord— the presiding deity— abides there, existing with that [universe] as His body.

The word "tat" is to be supplied [as the subject]. Since there is an absence of lexicographical authority (*kośa*) and the like for the two words *pavitra* and *padavitata* having the sense of a *liṅga*, and because there is an absence of usage by the elders (*vṛddha*), a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) is impossible; therefore, they are taken as qualifiers of the [implied] object.
Thus: O Brahmaṇaspati, by way of delimitation through the body in the form of a *liṅga*...

O Supreme Śiva, presiding through the state of being embodied, that body of yours—which is the form of the *liṅga* denoted by the term "Brahman"—is pure; according to the manner described, it is fit to be worn even at times of purity or impurity.
It is pervasive and manifold, distinguished by various types such as the *iṣṭa* (the chosen) and so forth, or by the distinctions among the bodies of devotees and the like.
O Lord, you are capable of both restraint and grace; from every side (*viśvataḥ*),
by virtue of attaining the state of being the cause for the realization of the hidden reality, you [perceive] through the realization that the entirely hidden Brahman is your body (*sarvataḥ*).

The intention is that the etymology of the word *liṅga* is shown by the fact that it "sings" (*gayati*) a hidden meaning in order to make known that "it becomes" (*bhavati*) worthy of being designated by the term *brahman*.
Regarding the phrase "the word *tat* is supplied": the meaning is that it is supplied so as to provide a substantive for the two words *pavitra* and *padavitata*.
He states that the very impossibility of accounting for the meaning of these two words (*etatpadadvaya*) is the proof for the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the word *tat*:

"the impossibility of the [syntactic] members" (*avayānupapatti*). The particle *ca* in the phrase "and because of its indicative nature" (*sūcakatvācca*) restates the causal sense of the ablative case.
He states the collective meaning with the words beginning "O Lord of Brahmanaspati" (*he brahmaṇaspate*), etc., by way of [their] being embodied (*śarīribhāvena*).

The meaning is "in the form of the Self. Even with regard to the desired distinctions, the meaning is "in various forms such as the *iṣṭaliṅga* (the chosen form) and the *prāṇaliṅga* (the vital-force form). Regarding the phrase "by the distinction of the devotee's body," since distinct *liṅgas* are maintained for each individual body, there is also a multiplicity of the devotee's bodies.
"You pervade and occupy the limbs—that is, the bodies—of the devotees while being sustained;
the meaning is that you are joined with the limbs of the devotees by means of the body in the form of the *liṅga*.
Now, an objection is raised: "In the phrase *brahmaṇas pate*, the word *brahman* refers to the stationary *liṅga* (the stone phallus); therefore, O [Lord]..."
O Brahmaṇaspati, O Supreme Śiva residing within the stationary linga through the state of being embodied,

this linga denoted by the word "Brahman" is pure, sanctified by purification through the rites of the paths (*adhvaśodhana*) and other means; it is expansive, and diverse in its various forms— such as self-manifested (*svayambhu*), revealed by sages (*ārṣa*), or fashioned by men (*pauruṣa*).
It should be understood that the purpose is to establish the reality of the *liṅga*. Regarding the phrase "you are joined with the limbs of a devotee":

although there is no explicit injunctive suffix such as *liṅ* here to indicate a mandate, the intended meaning is that an injunction will be inferred through the practice of established conduct (*sadācāra*), such as the wearing of the *liṅga*, which is taught by the Śruti. [This occurs] through the distinction between what is self-manifested, what is composed by sages (*ārṣa*), and what is composed by ordinary persons.
Otherwise, since it would be impossible for [the Lord] himself to maintain a body, there would result the logical inconsistency of the previously cited statement: "Thou secketh limbs on every side."
Nor should it be said that even for Him there is a connection with the body of the devotee by way of His own undivided nature;
for, in that case, since He must be described as possessing the characteristic of Brahman— namely, all-pervasiveness due to His being undivided—
there would be no purpose in speaking of a connection with merely the body of the devotee.

Now, one might object: since this mantra beginning with "pavitram" is enjoined for the consecration of the *daśāpavitra* [woolen filter] during the Soma sacrifice, how can it have the purpose of supporting the wearing of a *liṅga*? For in that context, there are clearly manifest *liṅgas*, such as the *jyotirliṅgas* of Viśveśvara and others, as well as the *ārṣa-liṅgas* of Agastyeśvara and others.
The meaning is that there are innumerable man-made [liṅgas], such as Hariścandreśvara and others, due to their differentiation from that [original liṅga].

As for the phrase "nor of that": the point is that since even a stationary liṅga is non-different from the Supreme Lord and is all-pervading, the portion [of the verse] stating "he searches for his limbs even in that" is not contradicted. "Due to the absence of purpose" means:
Since it is stated that [the Lord], who pervades the entire universe, is connected with the body of the devotee, the statement regarding its lack of purpose is indeed appropriate.
Regarding the *some*, i.e., the *somayāga* sacrifice; and regarding the consecration of the *daśāpavitra*, which is a white [woolen] filter.
A specific type of cloth made from woolen threads spun into yarn, serving as a specialized support for the purification of the distinguished Soma juice;
its application is directed solely toward that purpose.

If it is argued that there would be a contradiction with the *prakaraṇa* (context) if this mantra, which is recited in the section on Soma, were intended for the wearing of the *liṅga*— since it belongs to the sequence of invocations to various deities at the time of the *sandhyā-vandana*— that too is without substance, because [the context] merely concerns the application (*viniyoga*).

The application of mantras elsewhere— such as those whose connection to the word "Brahman" was understood from the previously cited examples— is restricted to Agni and others alone in the *grahayajña* sacrifice, by virtue of the direct scriptural statement (*vācakaśruti*) such as "Agni is the head, the summit of heaven" (*Ṛgveda* 8.44.16).

Because the application (*viniyoga*) [of the *Puruṣasūkta*] is observed in the worship of Bhauma and others, it says: "One should worship the Giver of Wealth, who possesses universal forms, with the *Puruṣasūkta*.

Regarding the phrase "by virtue of being applied": the meaning is that it is taught in the *Kalpasūtra* as being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of the *daśāpavitra*.

The intent of the question is as follows: "How can there be a focus on the wearing of the *liṅga*? It is impossible to maintain that the passage concerning the wearing of the *liṅga*—which is read within the context of the Soma sacrifice—is focused on that very practice, because it has been taught by a scriptural statement (*ārṣavākya*) to have another purpose, and it is unworthy of trust to claim a different purpose for what has already been established as having another.

"That too is without substance" means that the sense is this: since the application (*viniyoga*), which functions to communicate the portions of utility necessary for the accomplishment of the specific nature of each sacrifice, does not sublate the relationship of subsidiary and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) as it is perceived through the power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*). He demonstrates that very point:
"Agni is the head," and so forth;
for it is observed that the *Puruṣasūkta*, even though it refers to another deity, is employed in the ritual of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
If, however, there were a restrictive rule that "whatever is employed here [must refer to this specific deity]," [it would be contradicted].
