[The application of a mantra] occurs only in a context where the mantra is composed of words expressive of the primary subject matter. Indeed, there is no restrictive factor for the word *pavitra* to denote a *daśāpavitra* (a fringe filter).
Therefore, in a context of application not containing a direct expressive scripture (*abhidhāyaka-śruti*), [the mantra serves] to illuminate the subject at hand.

If it be asked how this is so, [the answer is: even though there is an application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra dedicated to Indra— "O Indra, you are never ungracious to the donor" (*Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā* 1.5.4)— to the worship of the *gārhapatya* fire, as stated in "With an *aindrī* [verse], he worships the *gārhapatya*" (*Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā* 1.5.11).

The meaning is that, in the worship of the planets beginning with Maṅgala (Mars), the mantra—by virtue of the scriptural statement of its designation—is directed toward Indra; this refers to the worship of the planets starting with Mars. Regarding the phrase "to another deity":
even though [the mantra] such as "sahasraśīrṣā" has Viṣṇu as its referent due to its indicative marks (*liṅga*), it is used in the sacrifice to Kubera.

The sense is that, because their application (*viniyoga*) is observed [in various contexts], there is no fixed rule that mantras must be restricted to a single purpose. Regarding the phrase "not composed of a direct expressive scriptural statement" (*abhidhāyaka-śruti-aghāṭita*): the sense is that since mantras are useful merely for manifesting the deity and the ritual action, if the words denoting those [deities and actions] were absent, the recitation of the mantra would be useless.

In the case of the mantra "kadācanastarīrasi nendra" (O Indra, you are never a deceiver), although its status as an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the worship of the Gārhapatya fire is established by the injunctive sentence "he worships the Gārhapatya with the *aindrī* [mantra]," the fact that it has Indra as its subject matter— derived from the power (*śakti*) of the words contained within it—
is not lost. Its illumination of the subject at hand (*prakṛta*), however, occurs through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and other such means.
It should be understood that [the mantra] belongs to Indra according to the principle of the *aindrī-adhikaraṇa*.
As for what was said regarding the contradiction with the context (*prakaraṇa*), that too is not so; for it is said:
"Soma is the progenitor of the hymns, the progenitor of heaven, the progenitor of earth."
In the verse, "The progenitor of Agni, the progenitor of Sūrya, the progenitor of Indra, and the progenitor of Viṣṇu" (Ṛgveda 9.96.5),

since it is impossible for the inert *soma* creeper to be the progenitor of Nārāyaṇa and others, the word *soma*— by the power of its double meaning (*śleṣa*)— refers to Śiva as well, [who is] accompanied by Umā.

The meaning is that, just as the *gārhapatya* fire is also invoked by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) due to the force of an injunction and is not thereby contradicted, so too here, even though [the mantra] is a subordinate element of the consecration of the *daśāpavitra*, its own primary meaning is not lost.
He resolves the contradiction with the context (*prakaraṇa*) previously raised, beginning with the words "as for what was said," etc., regarding the Soma.

By the verse beginning with "pavateḥ janitā," the literal meaning perceived at first sight is that Soma— a specific creeper— is the progenitor of the purifying sacrifice (*pavateḥ pāvanasya yāgasya*),

of the thoughts (*matīnāṃ*)— that is, the sacrificial intentions which, through the medium of the transformation of their own essence, constitute the highest intellects— and of heaven (*divaḥ*), the fruit of the sacrifice,
as well as of the earth, the sun, Indra, and Viṣṇu. However, [the true meaning is otherwise].

Since the capacity to generate the Sun, Indra, and others is sublated in the case of a specific creeper, and since Śiva is understood through the etymological derivation "he who is accompanied by Umā," it has been established as a settled conclusion that the accomplishment [of the ritual] occurs by taking him [Śiva] as the referent;
therefore, there is no contradiction even if the section on wearing the *liṅga* belongs to the section on Soma. Furthermore, this...
By the Vedic revelation, "Soma to the one with matted hair" (Ṛgveda 9.67.11),

which conveys Śiva’s connection with the Soma sacrifice as characterized by its origin, and by the revelation that "Rudra is invoked," which— by substituting the word "Rudra" for the word "Soma"— conveys the identity of the Soma sacrifice with Rudra.
"For I am indeed the enjoyer of all oblations and the bestower of their fruits;
having become the body of all gods, I am the Self of all, abiding in all"—
thus [is stated] in the Kūrma Purāṇa by the words of Śiva, demonstrating Śiva's [nature].

Because the Soma sacrifice is determined to have Rudra as its presiding deity through the demonstration that he is the consumer of all oblations and the bestower of the fruits of ritual action, there is no contradiction with the context even for this mantra, which— though recited within that specific section— is devoted to the wearing of the *liṅga*.

Because it is proper to accept [the meaning] by the force of its inherent fitness (*yogyatā*), there is no contradiction with the context; for this is the true sense, as the Śruti text "This Soma is for Kapardin" (*Ṛgveda* 9.67.11) declares that the Soma sacrifice is connected to Kapardin,
and because it is stated that Rudra was invoked after the arrival of the Soma, thereby revealing the identity of Rudra and Soma.

Furthermore, because it is understood that the Soma sacrifice has Rudra as its presiding deity, there is no contradiction with the context (*prakaraṇa*) even if the passage read within the section on Soma is intended for Rudra; this is the underlying point.
Now, let us set aside for a moment the absence of contradiction regarding the context and so forth according to the stated method; nevertheless, [the text says] "pavitraṃ te... [etc.]...

If it is argued that, due to the absence of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth in this mantra, an injunction (*vidhi*) is not possible, nor is there a fulfillment of the form that necessitates an injunction— because the wearing of the *liṅga* and its sanctification prescribed by this mantra are established as otherwise accomplished (*anyathāsiddha*) by the injunction "he establishes all *liṅgas"— then this is not so.

Therefore, in accordance with the corroborative statement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) to be cited later— "That Śaiva, pure, and healthy *liṅga* should be worn"— and by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra "The Lord encompasses all limbs from every side" (*Ṛgveda* 9.83.1), it is determined that this *liṅga* should be worn.
Because it is possible [to establish the injunction].

Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of indicative marks (*liṅga*) and so forth," this has been resolved by the fact that such a mark is utilized for the postulation of an injunction based on conduct taught by the *śruti*. Therefore, that pure, auspicious, and healthy *liṅga* of Śiva should be worn.

He says "not so" because this Purāṇic statement, which supplements the mantra, and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the form of *prabhurgātrāṇi paryeṣi* (Ṛgveda 9.83.1), are favorable for the postulation of an injunction.
Furthermore, he addresses what was stated in the earlier work— that there is no form of the text that serves as a motivator for an injunction because it is established otherwise.

That too is incorrect, because of the difference between the Vedic branches (*śākhā*). For it is not possible for rites prescribed in one branch to be established otherwise through another branch; if that were the case, then certain rites prescribed in the Yajurveda branch would themselves have to be considered as prescribed in the Ṛgveda.
Because injunctions prescribing such [acts] would fail to function as motivators; enough, then, with this digression from the main topic.
Thus, by means of the passage beginning with "pavitram te" and ending with "paryeṣi viśvataḥ," the wearing of the sectarian mark (liṅgadhāraṇa) [is established].
And although that sanctity is prescribed by a single scriptural injunction, because it lacks an extremely desirable fruit,
the venerable Śruti, having spoken thus, [proceeds] to indicate the exclusion of other means.

"Due to the division of the branches" means due to the division of the Vedas. The statement "sarvaliṅgam" refers to a prose passage (*vākya*), whereas the mantra "pavitraṃ te vitataṃ brahmaṇaspate" (Ṛgveda 9.83.1) is a verse (*ṛk*). Consequently, since these two types of texts belong to different Vedic branches (*śākhā*), one cannot be established as redundant by means of the other.

The point is that even if one were to accept "establishment through other means" (anyathāsiddhi) despite the difference in Vedic branches (śākhā), then since rites such as the Agnihotra are prescribed in multiple branches,
all the sentences enjoining them would necessarily be established through other means by virtue of being composed by others [than themselves]. Consequently,
it would follow that no sentence whatsoever could be established as having injunctive force (vidhāyakatva).
It declares the causality of wearing the *liṅga* by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*):
"One whose body is not heated does not enjoy that which is uncooked" (*Ṛgveda* 9.83.1).

This means that he whose body is heated—that is, one whose cage of sins has been burnt away by the three initiations (*dīkṣā*) consisting of piercing (*vedha*), mantra-repetition (*japa*), and so forth—is not such a person.

"One whose body has not been heated" (*ataptatanuḥ*) means one who is devoid of the three initiations (*dīkṣā*); being "raw" (*āma*), that is, having an unripened internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), he does not perceive the nature of that Supreme Śiva. And thus, in accordance with the statement in the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*: "O child, for one whose limb is joined with the Liṅga, rebirth does not exist."

The implied meaning is that these three initiations alone are the uncommon cause for liberation. Regarding the phrase "by way of negative concomitance" (*vyatirekamukhena*): it means that in the absence of the cause of liberation, which consists of the wearing of the *liṅga*, there is an absence of the effect, which is liberation; thus, in the case of the absence of liberation...

This is by way of making known the pervasion of the absence of wearing the *liṅga*. Consequently, the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*)—defined as being the counter-positive of the absence that pervades the absence of wearing the *liṅga*—is established for wearing the *liṅga* with respect to liberation. And thus, there is no liberation for those who are devoid of wearing the *liṅga*.
By the statement "it comes to be," the fact that the wearing of the *liṅga* is the cause of liberation is obtained.
"By the three initiations" means by the piercing initiation (*vedhadīkṣā*), the subsequent initiation (*anudīkṣā*), and the ritual initiation (*kriyādīkṣā*). Regarding "in the cage of sins":
a cage (*pañjara*) is a place of confinement for birds; it is called a "cage" because it similarly acts as an obscuration.
It is also applied to evil.
However, the followers of Rāmānuja’s doctrine maintain that, based on the established usage in lexicons where "pavitra" and "caraṇa" signify the discus (*cakra*),
the word *pavitra* here has the meaning of the discus, as in the phrase *brahmaṇas pate*.

The term *brahmapada* denotes the four-faced Brahmā; his lord (*pati*) is Nārāyaṇa, for as the *Śruti* states, "Brahmā is born from Nārāyaṇa" (Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 1), he is the sovereign by virtue of being the progenitor. Thus, O Lord of Brahmā (*brahmaṇas-pate*), O creator of the four-faced one and others, your purifying discus (*cakra*) is spread abroad.
"O Lord, you are the regulator of all worlds; the limbs [of the body] are indeed the limbs of the devotee.

Having thus established that the *Ṛgvedic* mantra "te brahmaṇaspate" (RV 10.98.7)—which is sacred in its own context—refers to the wearing of sectarian marks (*liṅgadhāraṇa*), [the author] then establishes that the very same mantra, as intended by Rāmānujācārya, refers to the wearing of the heated seal (*taptamudrādhāraṇa*).
He begins the refutation with the words, "But those who follow the Rāmānuja school," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by the authority of a lexicon" (*kośaprasiddhyā*):
this lexicon appears to be a fabrication, as it is not found in contemporary manuscript collections of such works.
The meaning of *paryeṣi* is "you obtain. For this very reason, it is said: "One whose body is not heated [by austerity], being raw, does not enjoy that" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.24).

This [term] is also etymologically significant: *ataptatanuḥ* means one whose body (*tanu*) is not such as has undergone the manifestation of another form preceded by the transformation of its previous form by means of a wheel heated by fire; that is, one who is devoid of the practice of bearing the discus at the base of the arm.

They have explained that "one who is *āma*—meaning one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is unripened—does not attain" that which is the nature of the Supreme Brahman consisting of Nārāyaṇa; however, even that is not to be trusted. For although there is indeed a dispute over the status of the lexicon (*kośa*) composed by the deceitful Vaiṣṇavas, regarding [the verse] "The foot is the discus, the purifier," [it remains untenable].
Nevertheless, following the maxim "let the wicked man be satisfied," we accept [the opponent's position] only to refute it:

because there is no injunction for the wearing of the disc in the Vedic mantra. Nor is the passage "Thou searchest all limbs on every side" (Ṛgveda 9.83.1) an injunction for this, as it refers only to Viṣṇu.
Because it prescribes the connection of the sacred thread with the limbs of the devotee.

Now, one might object: since the mantra "pavitraṃ te" refers to the discus belonging to Viṣṇu, and because the act of wearing it is prescribed by the subsequent phrase "gātrāṇi paryeṣi viśvataḥ," this must refer to the wearing of Nārāyaṇa's [discus].
"He seeks the limbs of the devotee" means that [the mark] takes the form of a sprout produced by contact with a heated disc due to proximity.

In this view, their intention is that the use of the verbal root *tap* (in the compound *ataptatanu*) is understood in its well-known sense [of "heated"]. [The phrase] "of that imagined by rogue Vaiṣṇavas" [is used].
The point is that the very fact of not finding [the injunction] in the available manuscript collections is itself the mark of its being fabricated.

Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of an injunction for wearing the wheel": this means due to the absence of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. One might argue that, just as in the case of the theory of wearing the insignia (*liṅga*), an inference of an injunction will be established here as well, based on the descriptive restatement (*anuvāda*) in the form "he searches his limbs," which treats the matter as already established.
There is no room for doubt, because by addressing [the deity] as "O Lord of Brahman" (*brahmaṇas-pate*) and employing the second-person verb "you seek" (*paryeṣi*),

although Nārāyaṇa attains contact with the limbs of his devotees, the discus (*cakra*) does not attain that same status. In our own system, however, since the Śiva-liṅga is non-different from Śiva, when Śiva attains contact with the limbs of his devotees, the Śiva-liṅga [likewise attains it].

That [identity] is not obtained. The intention is that even in Vaiṣṇava texts, there is no established doctrine that being marked with a heated seal (taptamudrā) constitutes non-difference from Viṣṇu.
If it is argued that its establishment occurs through the well-known fact that [the mark] belongs to Him [Viṣṇu] alone, do not say so; for such an argument cannot withstand critical analysis.

To explain: is the discus to be worn as its emblem (*lāñchana*), or as its very nature (*svarūpa*), or rather as having Nārāyaṇa as its locus? Not the first, for it is said: "The Kaumodakī mace, the sword Nandaka, and the Kaustubha gem" (Amara-kosha 1.1.28).

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because there is no decisive reason (*vinigamaka*) for that very [discus] alone to be worn, given that its characteristic mark has been frequently perceived through the existence of the treasury (the *kośa*). Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for if it were of the same nature as that [discus], their non-difference would be established, and consequently, the relationship between the bearer of the mark and the mark itself—which presupposes a distinction between Cakra and Nārāyaṇa—would be impossible.

Because that would result in a contradiction with the *kośa* (theological treatise) that explains it. Even in the third case, does its being the substratum [of all] arise from its state as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of Śarva—as taught by the scripture: "Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 10.11.5)—or rather from its state as the embodied soul (*śarīrin*)?

For [if it were so], it would follow that everything must be worn because it subsists in all objects. Nor is the latter position tenable; for if one accepts that [the Lord] exists in the form of the embodied soul, then [the objection remains]: "Is it not well-known in that system that the Śālagrāma and other such objects are to be worn by Vaiṣṇavas? Therefore, by the word 'pavitram' (purifier), the discus [is intended]."

Anticipating the objection, "Is the all-pervasiveness of Nārāyaṇa intended here precisely through the medium of that [conch] because of its proximity?", he refutes it with the words "Not so. [He explains: "Containing a sense of difference. According to the lexicon, "The conch of the Lord of Lakṣmī is Pāñcajanya, and the discus is Sudarśana" (Amarakośa 1.1.28), [the term used] refers to the Lord of Lakṣmī.
The meaning is that it contains within it a distinction implied by the relationship of possession (*svasvāmibhāva*) indicated by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

This also applies to the third alternative, namely the view that the discus is to be held as having Nārāyaṇa as its substratum (*āśrayatva*). He examines this state of being a substratum with the words beginning "inside," etc. The underlying idea is: having pervaded all that [universe] both inside and outside...

Based on the Śruti passage, "Nārāyaṇa is present" (Tai. Ā. 10.11.5), does one accept that the discus has Nārāyaṇa as its substratum because it is established within the currently existing Nārāyaṇa, or rather, because the discus is the body of Nārāyaṇa—just as individual souls reside in bodies—in which case Nārāyaṇa exists in the discus as its very self?

The sense is that [the opponent] considers Nārāyaṇa to be the substratum because of his state of being stationary. He states that the first position is not tenable: "because it would follow that everything must be supported. This means that even jars, cloths, and so forth would have to be supported at that time. He states that the latter position is also not tenable: "by virtue of being the embodied one," and so on.
Regarding the term *śālagrāma*: those images of the Lord made of copper and other materials which are worshipped by Vaiṣṇavas just like a *śālagrāma* stone—
just as one would worship the respective icons installed within temples made of copper and other materials.
Furthermore, this would entail the necessity of performing worship, offerings, and so forth, even to the discus and other emblems held in the hand of Nārāyaṇa.
As for the claim that its establishment is achieved by the verse, "He whose body is not heated by austerity does not enjoy that, being raw" (Ṛgveda 9.83.1),
that too merely mimics the hope for rain-showers in a sky from which all clouds have departed.
The body of a Brāhmaṇa should be known as the abode of all the gods;
O King, if that [body] has been tormented, what can I say regarding his sin?
Whether one is devoted to bathing in the Gaṅgā or even devoted to the horse sacrifice,
upon seeing a person whose body is marked with the discus, that person should look at the sun and recite prayers.

And he should recite the Pauruṣa Sūkta; otherwise, he shall go to the Raurava hell. If a Brahmin has the mark of the heated disc on the tip of his arm, even if he possesses knowledge of the Vedas and the sacred fires, he too burns his lineage unto the seventh generation.

Since the wearing of the heated seal (*taptamudrā*) is prohibited by such statements from the *Dharmaśāstras*, and since an interpretation [of this mantra] as referring to that [seal] is impossible, it must be explained according to the method we have stated. Furthermore, if this mantra—read within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Soma sacrifice—were intended to refer to the wearing of the discus (*cakradhāraṇa*), there would be a contradiction with the context. It is not [the case].
Furthermore, in our view, that consequence has already been refuted.
If, even so, you accept that the phrase "ataptatanuḥ" (Ṛgveda 9.83.1) ultimately signifies one whose body is heated by the [solar] disc, then—

For it would follow that worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth must be performed upon those various images installed in their respective abodes and temples—just as it is performed on the discus and other marks held at the base of the arms [of the Lord]—rather than upon the person themselves.
As for the attainment of liberation by a Brahmin whose body has been heated, let that remain far off; even his present state [is not possible].

He states that Brahminhood departs [from the body], and because the body of a Brāhmaṇa consists of all the gods, a great sin indeed arises from its burning; this he says with the words "The body of the Brāhmaṇa is to be known," etc. Furthermore, in our view, such a consequence does not occur. This refers to the position that accepts the wearing of the *liṅga* as the primary goal.
The meaning is that there is no occurrence of a contradiction with the context (prakaraṇa) necessitated by the fact of being recited within the Soma-section.

He asks "How so? and says: "Because it has already been refuted"—this is the meaning. [He further explains: "By resorting to the etymological derivation (vyutpatti) of the word 'soma' as 'that which exists together with Umā'."

Regarding the phrase *avasānagatya*: this statement should be understood as being like the expression "having gone to the end" (*antato gatvā*). Although the commentary on *ataptatanuḥ*—namely, "one whose body (*tanuḥ*) has been heated (*taptā*) for Viṣṇu"—is extremely strained, nevertheless, even the Vaiṣṇava interpretation, such as "heated by the discus (*cakratāpitā*") and so forth, is equally strained.

Based on the traditional teaching that the syllable *a* denotes Viṣṇu, the word *āya* means "for Viṣṇu" or "for the sake of Viṣṇu. One whose body is not heated is *ataptatanuḥ*. Being such a person—namely, one whose inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is unrefined (*āma*)—one does not attain *sat*, which is the nature of the Supreme Brahman; rather, [the root] *śrī* signifies "cooking" (Dhātupāṭha 1476, kryādi).

The meaning would be that, being heated—that is, scorched—from the root *dhā* (to heat), they bear the callus (*kiṇa*) produced by that heat, and they "resort to" or "attain" that very callus; this is because it must conform to the prohibition stated previously.
Now, even so, the meaning "wheel" for the word *pavitra* is necessary due to its well-established usage in lexicons (*kośa*).

If it is argued that even so, there is no cognition of "purity" (*pāvitrya*) and so forth because conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) supersedes etymological derivation (*yoga*), we say no; for when an obstacle exists, a lexicon (*kośa*) is not admitted to be a means of grasping word-potency (*śakti*). For this very reason, in cases such as "the pot is blue" or "the cloth is white," [the word denotes] the quality (*guṇa*).

"All this has austerity as its root, austerity as its middle, and austerity as its end. The sages, self-restrained, subsisting on fruits, roots, and air, perceive the three worlds with all their moving and non-moving beings through austerity alone" (Manusmṛti 11.234–236). It is precisely of such austerity, as described in the Manusmṛti and other texts, that [the term] *ataptatanuḥ* ("one whose body has not been heated") refers here.

Furthermore, because it would contradict the straightforward interpretation that "one whose body is not heated" (*ataptatanuḥ*)—understood according to the propriety of being grasped by the root *tap* (to heat)—refers to one who has not distressed their body through such means as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances or the propitiation of the Supreme Lord, does not attain that state of Brahman; thus, it follows the maxim: "As is the Yakṣa, so is the offering."

It should be understood that it has been explained in this way precisely for the purpose of refuting that [objection]. Now, if it is argued that even when explaining [the text] as being intent upon the wearing of the *liṅga*, the contradiction with the interpretation that regards it as being intent upon austerity (*tapas*) remains exactly the same, do not say so; for [this explanation accounts for] the lifelong preservation of non-separation from the Śiva-liṅga, as well as the lifelong maintenance of its daily worship.

Because it is of the nature of supreme austerity (*paramatapas*). Likewise, even further on, he explains [the passage] beginning with "śrīñ pāke" solely with the intention of making known the fitness for the cultivation of meanings that are the opposites [of the preceding ones].
He asks: "But what is the authority for such a meaning? and says:

"Because of conformity with the previously mentioned prohibitions" means because of conformity with the prohibitions indicated by the statement of faults such as: "Having seen one whose body is marked with the [Vaiṣṇava] disc, a person should look at the sun and perform japa.
"Because conventional meaning (rūḍhi) supersedes etymological derivation (yoga)" means by the conventional power established in the lexicons composed by Vaiṣṇavas.

The sense is that there will be a sublation of the meaning "purification. Consequently, the intention of the objector is that this mantra should be explained solely as referring to the wearing of the *cakra*. Even assuming the existence of the lexicon (*kośa*), he provides a resolution by accepting its status as a lexicon, provided there is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).
When there is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) such as [the word's] being feminine (*gauḥ*), the *kośa* [states]:

"White and other [colors] are masculine when denoting the quality (*guṇa*), but they take the gender of the possessor (*guṇin*) when [denoting the substance]. Thus, although the *kośa* establishes that words like *nīla* denote color (*rūpa*), in instances where the words share the same case ending (*samānavibhaktika*), [the rule applies].

Since it is impossible to understand [the word] as denoting either a difference or a connection, and because accepting a primary power (*śakti*) for a word like *rūpavat* would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) alone is accepted. Furthermore, the principle that conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) overrides etymological derivation (*yoga*) applies only in cases where the conventional meaning is not contradicted; otherwise, in instances such as "bring the *paṅkaja*," even if the lotus is contradicted [by the context], [the word would still denote the mud-born].

Otherwise, there would be no awakening to the "lily" (kumuda) that is the meaning of yoga. However, in the present context, the status of being the meaning of the *cakra* is indeed sublated by the aforementioned direction. By this, the claim that the wearing of the *cakra* is established solely by the injunction "the heated *cakra* should be worn on the two arms" is also refuted, [given] the learned reciter (*anūcāna*) of the currently studied branch [of scripture].
Because that [text] is not seen in any recension, there is indeed dispute regarding its status as Śruti. Furthermore,

even if you were to accept its status as such by assuming it exists in scattered Vedic branches (*viprakīrṇa-śākhā*), its establishment would still not be achieved on that basis, because it is refuted by the aforementioned alternatives and because it contradicts the prohibitive scriptures (*niṣedha-śāstra*).

The sense is that, according to the maxim *sarvaṃ vākyam*, when the rule for holding the discus is prescribed with reference to both arms, the holding of the conch is established as a corollary (*grāhakatva*). Thus, it is the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) itself that is accepted. As for those [words] whose gender follows the qualities (*guṇiliṅga*):

Even in the case of the *Amarakośa*, which is an extremely authoritative source, the view that words such as "white" (*śukla*) denote the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted due to the fault of its being overly weighty;
for its status as an actual statement of the *kośa* is itself doubtful, as it is not found in the extant manuscript copies of the work.

The intended meaning is: how can the power [of the word] be accepted there in the face of contradictory statements prohibiting the wearing of the wheel (*cakradhāraṇa*), given the force of that [usage]? Regarding the phrase "non-sublation of the conventional meaning" (*rūḍhyarthābādha*): when that is sublated, however, there occurs the understanding even of the purely etymological (*yoga*) meaning. For this very reason—

The intention is that when the word *paṅkaja* (mud-born) denotes the lotus (*padma*), there is also the cognition of the night-lily (*kumuda*). This is stated merely out of an obsession with refuting the literal letters, on the grounds that conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) supersedes etymological derivation (*yoga*). In reality, however, this is irrelevant and even contradictory to the present context.

This is because it serves as the prompter for the doubt: "Why is there no cognition of both [the 'wheel' and 'purity']—which have attained the status of qualifiers—simultaneously, since they are not sublated in one and the same locus? An example is required here. "In the manner stated" means by way of reflecting upon the prohibition of wearing a wheel (*cakradhāraṇa*). "An *anūcāna*" refers to one who has studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (*sāṅga-veda*).

Because it is refuted by conceptual construction and because it conforms to the prohibitive scriptures, the possibility of the existence of such injunctive statements even in those branches that have been lost is discarded, due to contradiction with reasoning and contradiction with both perception and scriptural testimony. This applies even in the case of authoritative Smṛtis regarding branches that are no longer perceived.

The point is that there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka-tarka*)— namely, the impossibility of the prohibition [of such acts] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)— which arises when one infers the absence of the status of being a practice of unobjectionable experts (*avigīta-śiṣṭācāra*) due to its non-perception, specifically as qualified by the absence of the existence of such an injunction in a severed branch of the Veda. Every sentence...
On his right arm, the Brahmin should indeed bear the Sudarśana;
on his left, he should bear the conch—thus says the all-pervading Lord, the knower of Brahman.
Thus, there is a contradiction with the scriptures and a contradiction with established practice; enough of this improper obsession.

But the venerable teachers [hold that] by the phrase "of Brahmaṇaspati"—referring to Rudra, the Great Seer who is superior to the universe, who in the beginning gave birth to Hiraṇyagarbha (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.4)—it is [established].

By such scriptural passages as "He first creates Brahmā" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.18), Paramaśiva is designated as the one renowned for being the progenitor of Hiraṇyagarbha. The term *pavitrapada* signifies the *liṅga*; [the scripture] states that he establishes the universal *liṅga*.
In the passage, "The hand-mantra is purifying" (*Tai. Ā.

10.16.1*), [the mantra] is [understood as such] because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "liṅga. Regarding the commentary on the *Rāmāyaṇa* verse, "It was strewn with flies," which is coreferential with the word "liṅga": "Clarified butter is indeed a thunderbolt" (*vajra*).

By the maxim shown by the author of the Mahābhāṣya, "that which includes a restrictive particle," even in the injunction "the heated discus is to be worn on the two arms," one obtains the specific form: "only the discus" and "only on the two arms. Thus, the knowers of Brahman declare: "A Brahmin should indeed wear the Sudarśana on the right arm, and he should wear the conch on the left."
The meaning is that by this very statement established in your own doctrine, "the wise know," that injunctional sentence becomes contradictory.
As for the phrase "Paramaśiva is designated": it is because he is the progenitor and the protector of Brahmā, who is Hiraṇyagarbha.

The meaning is as follows: "Because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is because Maheśvaratīrtha and others have accepted that in the Vedic scripture stating "The ghee is indeed a thunderbolt" (*vajro vā ājyam*), the word *vajra* refers to consecrated ghee due to its coreferentiality with the word *ājya*. And this is not the case for the word *pavitra* in the present context.
It should not be argued that although there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "mantra," there is no such coreferentiality with the word "liṅga" (sign);
for by the etymological derivation "that which protects through meditation" (*mananāt trāyate*), the word "mantra" also possesses the meaning of "liṅga.
Mantra is proclaimed to be twofold, in the form of the signified and the signifier.
The denoter would be in the form of phonemes, and the denoted is the supreme Śiva.

Thus, according to the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) by Vyāsa: "O Brahmaṇaspati, O Supreme Śiva, your *pavitra* [purifying] *liṅga* is *vitata*, meaning it is expanded due to its manifold nature through distinctions such as the *iṣṭa* and other forms;
you, the Lord who governs the unbroken cosmic egg (*jagadaṇḍa*), [pervade] the *gātrāṇi*, that is, the bodies of your devotees, from all sides."
Search everywhere,
in all parts, at all times, and in every direction;
establish the sign (liṅga) firmly within yourself through the instruction of the Guru.
Beginning with (Aṣṭādhyāyī Sūtra 6.2), [it is said]:
"The one supreme *liṅga* alone is well-established in this limb;
it shines forth in every direction through the nature of name, form, and action."
The *iṣṭaliṅga* is in the external limb, and likewise the *prāṇaliṅga* is within;

because the word *vajra* in the Veda signifies clarified butter (*ājya*), and because of the grammatical coordination in the phrase "the *pāṇimantra* is the purifier," the *bhāvaliṅga* likewise exists, well-established in the limb of the Self.
The Great Liṅga is in the organ of the heart; the Prasādaka Liṅga is in the organ of the ears;
the Caraliṅga is in the organ of the skin; and the Śivaliṅga is in the organ of sight.
The Guru-liṅga is located on the limb of the tongue, and likewise on the limb of the nose;
the Ācāra-liṅga is indeed perpetually well-established.

Just as the subtle body (liṅga) is established in the limbs of the organs of cognition in their respective order, so too is the subtle body established in the limbs of the organs of action in their respective order.

The intention is that, according to the manner of expression found in the *Anubhavasūtra* within the latter portion of the *Vātulāgama*—specifically in [a0 sū0 6|4-8]—the word *pavitra* will have the meaning of *liṅga*. Thus it says: "in the latter portion of the *Vātulāgama*."
Regarding the phrase "they say":
they say that the meaning is that you alone pervade all the limbs of devotion, being expert in bringing about the union of things that were previously unjoined.

Others, however, maintain that in the verse "pavitraṃ te vitatam," the word *vitata*—being derived from the root *tan* (meaning "to extend" or "to spread") like the word *tanu*—has the sense of "body"; thus, the word *brahmaṇaspati* has the sense of a masculine noun (*liṅga*). And so: "O Brahmaṇaspati..."

In the previous interpretation, the meaning of *brahmaṇas pate* is "presided over by the subtle body" (*liṅgaśarīra*). And in this [present] explanation, the meaning is "the progenitor of the four-faced one.
Regarding the phrase "others, however": in this view, he establishes that the word *vitata* has the sense of "body"—[as in the root] *tanu*, meaning "to expand."
By such statements as these:

"O Supreme Śiva, whose substratum is the *liṅga*, your pervasive body in the form of the *liṅga* is pure (*pavitra*), fit to be worn even at times of impurity. The Lord, possessing such a *liṅga*-body..."

They say that the literal meaning is as follows: Śiva, who bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation, pervades and enters the bodies of his devotees; thus, Śiva, as delimited by the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), is to be worn upon the limbs of the devotee. However, in the system of the Guru (the Pratyabhijñā school), there is this distinction: the statement of the subject (*uddeśya*) comes first, and the predicate (*vidheya*) follows.

Regarding the word *param*, according to the *Miśrakārikā*, in the verse "The purifier is spread out for you" (*pavitraṃ te vitatam*), since the word *pavitra* denotes the gendered object (*liṅgārtha*), the quality of being "spread out"— which is the meaning expressed by the word *vitata*— is the predicate; thus,
the proper sequence between the word expressing the subject and the word expressing the predicate is established.
If the word *vitata* were to signify the gender (liṅga), whereas purity (*pāvitrya*) is the object to be enjoined, there would be a reversal [of the meaning].
In accordance with the aforementioned sense, there is also an expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of this mantra in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"By union with a bee, a worm certainly becomes a bee."
Through the yoga of Śiva, a human being certainly becomes Śiva; this is certain.
The gods, such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and sages such as Gautama and others,
always wear the [liṅga] on their heads in particular.
Having begun thus:
"Brahmā is declared to be the *liṅga*, and Brahmaṇaspati is the Lord;
for that is renowned as the purifier, and through contact with it, the body becomes pure."
He says "Ṛk": "O Brahmaṇaspati, your purifier is spread out.
Therefore, that purifying Śaiva symbol, which is free from ailment, should be worn.
Indeed, one whose body is not heated by austerity, who is unrefined and devoid of purificatory rites,
and who is lacking in initiation, does not directly attain the supreme *liṅga*.
He who first performs austerity is called one whose body has been refined;
once fully ripened for liberation, he attains the wearing of the Liṅga.

"The statement of the subject comes first" means that it is just as in the case of "the mountain possesses fire. "The verse of Miśra" means the verse of Maṇḍana Miśra. "Brahman is declared to be the mark" (liṅga) is consistent with the first interpretation.
He who does not first perform austerity is said to be one whose body has not been refined;
being unripened for liberation, he does not attain the wearing of the insignia.

Thus it is said. Here, it is clear that the words "Brahman," "the sign" (*liṅga*), "it is declared," "for that is well-known," "it should be held," and "it is Śaiva" serve to reinforce the meaning already stated.
Furthermore—
Thus instructed by his teacher, who is learned in the scriptures,
the disciple should bear the Śaṅkara-liṅga upon his body through the yoga of the vital breaths.
The wearing of the *liṅga* is meritorious and destroys all sins;
it is honored by all sages who are experts in the meaning of the scriptures.
This *iṣṭaliṅga* is the direct remover of misfortune.
The wise man should always wear [the linga] upon his body with focused attention.
(Si0 Śi0 6.50) He should wear with focused attention the linga bestowed by his guru;
if the linga should fall due to negligence, he should even sacrifice his life.
Statements from the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*, the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, and other such works serve to corroborate the meaning already stated.

Furthermore, in the *Ṛgveda*, the establishment of that [truth] is achieved not only by the mantra "na kevalaṃ pavitram te" (*Ṛgveda* 9.73.9), but also by another mantra, "ayaṃ me hastaḥ" (*Ṛgveda* 10.60.12).
"This hand of mine is the Blessed One; this [hand] of mine is the more blessed one.
This is my universal medicine; this is the auspicious touch. (Ṛgveda 10.60.12).
He cites another mantra from the Ṛgveda itself with the words "This hand of mine," etc. The meaning, however, is as follows:

"This Blessed One, Sadāśiva in the form of the *liṅga*, is my hand; he has come into my hand. He is my mother, he is my father, he is the source of my life. This is your crawling forth; move forward, O Subandhu, go forth! (Ṛgveda 10.60.7)
In this context, by the word "Bhagavān," Paramaśiva alone is meant; for in such scriptural passages as,
"Then Kumāra questioned this Bhagavān Rudra" and "Then Sanatkumāra questioned the Bhagavān Kālāgnirudra" (Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad 2), the Lord is thus being praised.
Because the term *vṛṣabhadhvaja* is applied to Śiva in the *Harivaṃśa* and other texts; thus,
this Lord Śiva in the form of the *liṅga* is "my hand"— meaning he has come into my hand, he is related to me, and this Śiva is most blessed.

This is the meaning. This very one is Sadāśiva, my most venerable lord (*bhagavattara*), possessing all supreme sovereignty for me. He is my universal medicine (*viśvabheṣaja*), the very nature of the remedy that removes all diseases. He is the touch of Śiva (*śivābhimarśana*), the bringer of all auspiciousness. He is the mother, like a mother.
He is affectionate; this father is a protector like a father. He is the life-sustainer, being the means for your livelihood.

According to scripture—that is, by the authority of the sacred texts—this approach of yours is for Subandhu. O Subandhu! O friend of the universe without qualification! Come, come here. This approach of yours is this...
"The *liṅga* has come into my hand; your wandering is the place of your residence.
The meaning is: "Being *nirīhaḥ*—that is, devoid of the impulse to go out—remain in this *śivaliṅga*.
Here, the author himself will later provide alternative meanings for several words. In this context, by the word "Bhagavat" (the Blessed One) [the following is implied].

Sadāśiva himself says: Kumāra questioned the Lord Rudra, "Now, regarding Kālāgnirudra, should it not be said that 'the Lord has come into my hand'? Why, then, is the word 'hand' used? If this is asked, [the answer is as follows]:—
The Lord Āditya, Sūrya, the blue-necked, three-eyed,
thousand-rayed one, is studied by the Sāmaga, Adhvaryu, and Hotṛ priests.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Ādityapurāṇa*, beginning with "This golden person who is seen within the sun" and ending with the *Taittirīya* passage, "Salutations again and again to the Lord of Ambikā, the Lord of Umā, the Lord of Paśus," [it refers to] the one accompanied by Ambā (Sāmba), the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra, situated in the midst of the solar orb.
In Vedic passages such as "Sanatkumāra questioned the Blessed One— who was situated within the mandala, golden-hued, of radiant form, and possessing a pure smile" (Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad 2)—
and in the Harivaṃśa and other texts, the word "Blessed One" (*bhagavat*) refers exclusively to Sadāśiva, who is the Bull-bannered Lord (*vṛṣabhadhvaja*).
Because of the application [of the term].

Having raised the objection—"Why is it stated that 'this is my hand' when it has already been said 'it is in the hand,' which implies a contradicted meaning?"—he provides the resolution with the words beginning: "The Lord Āditya, the Sun, the blue-throated, the three-eyed," and so forth.

"That golden person who is seen within the sun"—as well as the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa: "He who dwells in the sun, yet is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body is the sun" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.9)—this too should be considered here. Thus:

By the statement, "He who dwells in the center of the solar mandala, accompanied by Ambā, the medicine for the world," and by other such words, [it is shown that] the Supreme Śiva, established as residing in the sun, is distinct from the mandala and so forth.

Just as one says "the three-eyed [Śiva] is in the sun" rather than "the three-eyed one belonging to the sun" in order to indicate the inseparable relationship between Śiva and the sun, so too, in the statement "this hand of mine is the Blessed One," one says simply "the hand" rather than "the one residing in the hand" in order to suggest the inseparable relationship between the hand and the Śiva-liṅga.
Since it can be said that "the Blessed One" has been mentioned,

the inclusion of Sāmbaśiva within the mandala is perceived; nevertheless, the metaphorical identification (abhedopacāra) seen in the expression "the three-eyed one is the Sun" is likewise found here in the phrase "this hand of mine is the Blessed One."

He says that it is to be seen "in the manner of the statement 'the three-eyed one is the sun. The point is that just as there is a metaphorical identification (abhedopacāra) of the three-eyed Śiva with the solar orb even though he resides within it, so too there is a metaphorical identification of "this is my hand" even though the Śivaliṅga exists in the hand in the form of an object of worship.
The fruit of the ritual practice (*upacāra*), however, is precisely the realization of an inseparable relationship between the hand and the *śivaliṅga*.

And this inseparability within the relationship consists in being the non-counter-positive of the absence of occurrence in the body of the devotee as delimited by the state of being alive. And by that—
Thus, it is established that the wearing of the *liṅga* must be performed at all times.
And so, because an inseparable relationship between the two [the *liṅga* and the wearer] is logically necessary,
[the *liṅga*] has been consecrated by the Guru and bestowed following the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*).
One should worship the linga held in the left hand with careful attention.
Whoever always bears Śiva in the form of a *liṅga* upon his hand or other limb,
know that my state— the abode of all prosperity— is held in his hand.

Nor should it be argued that even when the *liṅga* (ascetic marks) is maintained, there is no sublation (*bādha*) because the state of being the counter-positive of an absence existing by delimiting another part [of the body] is present; for one must include "being non-co-referential with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇatva*) within the definition of absence. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, even upon renouncing [the marks] after having previously maintained them, there would still be no sublation of such non-counter-positiveness.

This is because one must introduce the condition of "non-coexistence" (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), which consists in being distinct from that which possesses the property of being located (*ādheyatā*) in its own counter-correlative (*svapratiyogin*).

Furthermore, the qualification of the property of being located (*ādheyatā*) is by way of both relations: (1) being delimited by the time delimited by its own delimiting factor (*svāvacchedakakālāvacchinnatva*), and (2) being determined by the body that constitutes its own relatum (*svanirūpakaśarīranirūpitatva*).

With this intention, he will say: "preceded by the deposition (*nyāsa*) on the six paths. The deposition on the six paths is to be observed in the ritual of initiation (*dīkṣā*). In this very context, the statement from the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad* serves as the authority;
furthermore, in accordance with the corroborating statements from the *Vātula-vīra-āgama* and other sources, [the deposition] is performed on the hands and so forth.
Retention [of the *liṅga*] is obtained. Precisely because the connection with the hand-Śiva-liṅga is indivisible: "One should wear with diligence the *liṅga* bestowed by the Guru;
if the *liṅga* should fall through negligence, one should even abandon one's life."
That lowest of men who maintains his life-breaths once the *prāṇaliṅga* has fallen is to be known as a *caṇḍāla*; he is a traitor to Śiva, without a doubt.
One should hold the *liṅga* with vigilance upon the lion-throne of the hand;
if the *liṅga* falls through negligence, one should abandon one's life along with it.
One should not even mentally recall one who has fallen from the *liṅga* or who reviles right conduct.
Just as a *liṅga* established upon the ground is never uprooted again,
so too the *liṅga* established within the body is not separated even at the end [of life].

Such statements, as well as passages from the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā* and other texts prescribing faults regarding the separation of the *liṅga* and the body, are also consistent [with this view]. For even according to those texts, if the *liṅga* separated from the body is later re-united, there is merely an internal penance (*vāṅtaraprāyaścitta*) performed according to the rules prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*; however, if it is not re-united, [the fault is greater].
It should be understood that the intended meaning here is that expiation must end in death. For this very reason, it is stated in the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad:
"One should not eat what has been abandoned by him; do not covet the wealth of anyone" (ĪU 1).

He does not offer [it back], for it has been abandoned by Him; thus, "you should not enjoy" means that once your body has been abandoned by that Supreme Lord in the form of the *liṅga* and a separation has occurred, you should not enjoy the wealth of another—that is, do not covet the form of the Śiva-liṅga. Do not desire it.

For that reason, when the insignia (*liṅga*) has been abandoned through negligence or the like, and it is no longer maintained, you should not consume [it]; rather, you should relinquish the body itself by means of fasting and so forth. Do not covet, and do not appropriate, the insignia belonging to another as if it were your own wealth; for the insignia is indeed wealth.
Regarding the statement "the Kauṣītaki Śruti":
But is it not the case that even the Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the son of Devakī— ?
Then that Blessed One was born as Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds.

If it is asked: "How can the word *bhagavat*, which is used in expressions such as 'Sanatkumāro bhagavān' as a term common to celestial sages (*devarṣi*), refer specifically to the Śiva-liṅga?"— the answer is no, just as in the case of the statement, "He cuts with his hand, he cuts with a ladle (*sruva*), he cuts with an axe (*svadhiti*)," where the word *avadyati* (he cuts), though common to all these instruments, does not necessarily denote one specific tool.

In the present context as well, since holding [the Lord] by the hand and so forth is well-known for other deities, the phrase "being held in the hand" applies commonly to both gods and sages. Therefore, the intention is that in passages such as "This hand of mine is the Blessed One," there is the possibility of Brahmā, Sanatkumāra, and others being referred to by the term "Blessed One" (bhagavat).
Regarding the phrase "that respective sacrificial cake" (*tattatpuroḍāśa*): even though only one sequence of words is heard— namely, "he cuts off" (*avadyati*)—
by the force of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the words "hand," "ladle" (*srūva*), and "axe" (*svadhiti*), which have distinct meanings, and by the force of semantic competency (*yogyatā*),
[it is understood that] the sacrificial cake is cut with the hand, the clarified butter with the ladle, and the meat with the axe, each separately.

A separate explanatory passage (*avadāna*) is understood; likewise here too, by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is certain that the word "Bhagavat" refers to the *śivaliṅga*. Furthermore, [this is confirmed] by the supplementary statement: "This one who touches Śiva" (*Ṛgveda* 10.60.12). This...

Furthermore, because the word *bhagavat* is determined to refer to the *śivaliṅga* by means of the *yavavrīhyadhikaraṇa* principle—given that the sense is: "The Blessed One has come into my hand; He is touched (*abhimṛśyate*), that is, grasped (*parāmṛśyate*), as Śiva," which amounts to saying that He is the one established in the state of Śiva.

The intention of the concluding passage (*samādhānagrantha*) is that although the word *bhagavat* is common [to many], it refers specifically to the *śivaliṅga* held in the hand due to its proximity to the words "hand" (*hasta*) and "foot" (*pada*).

This is according to the principle of the section on barley and rice (*yavavrīhyadhikaraṇanyāya*), as in the rule: "One should sacrifice with rice or with barley" (*vrīhibhir yavair vā yajeta*; Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 6.31.22).

13) In this context, since the word *yava* is seen to be used by the Mlecchas for *priyaṅgu* and by the Āryas for *dīrghaśūka*, there arises the desire to know which meaning should be adopted in the present case:
"When other plants wither, these remain rejoicing" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 3.6.1.1).
10) Thus, by means of this supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), it is determined that only the *dīrghaśūka* [variety] is to be taken.

Having thus prescribed the wearing of the *liṅga* on the hand and so forth, an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) is made regarding that *liṅga* as the agent of creation and so forth: "In this regard, this is the mother; this is the father."
The status of being the creator of the universe is expressed [by this]. By the phrase "this is the universal medicine" (*viśvabheṣajam*),
which means "the medicine for the existence of the universe," that is, the destroyer of the disease of *saṃsāra*, the status of being the agent of dissolution is established.
Likewise here too, by the force of the elliptical completion of the sentence—"This [is] my Śiva-abhimarśana"—the sense is that by the word "Bhagavat," Śiva alone is understood.
Regarding "the state of being the agent of withdrawal": at various intervals.

By the description of [the medicine] as a remedy, its role as a protector is also understood through its capacity to pacify various diseases consisting of suffering brought about by *prārabdha* (past karma).
Now, in the phrase "this touch of Śiva," the word "this" (*idam*) refers to the hand mentioned previously.

One who touches Śiva— meaning one who touches Him with the application of sandalwood paste and so forth— is called a *śivābhimarśana*. Thus, at the time of worshipping a wooden pedestal or a liṅga made of stone or emerald, there is the application of sandalwood paste to the right hand.

If it is argued that this mantra does not enjoin the wearing of a sectarian mark (*liṅga*) on the hand and so forth— since the passage beginning with "the Blessed One" (*bhagavān*) constitutes an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding his status as the Blessed One, Mother, Father, and so on— this is not so;
for since the hand is insentient, the status of being the Blessed One cannot reside therein.

Because when it is possible for [the word] to convey a connection with an inherent quality (*samaveta-guṇa*), it is inferior to accept that it conveys a connection with a non-inherent quality (*asamaveta-guṇa*).
For this very reason, in passages such as "Soma is the progenitor of thoughts" (*somaḥ pavate janitā matīnām*, Ṛgveda 9.96.5), etc.,...

Because the *soma* creeper lacks the connection with the qualities mentioned in the mantra, it is said to have "non-inherent qualities" (*asamavetaguna*). This means its qualities are superimposed (*āropitaguna*).
By the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), the phrase "Soma together with Umā" is used in order to convey a relationship of inherence (*samavetasambandha*).
The authors' own statement that [the Linga] is "the manifestation of Paramaśiva" is also consistent with this.

Furthermore, at the time of worshipping the Śivaliṅga— which is the bearer of the burden of the play of creating, preserving, and dissolving all worlds— even for one who has merely touched it, [there is a result].

Since the hand is the object of praise due to its being highly esteemed, it serves as the locus for the Śiva-liṅga— which, according to our stated method, is an inexhaustible ocean of the jewels of infinite auspicious qualities through an indivisible relationship.

"Because of the absence of a connection with the qualities mentioned in the mantra. Even if a connection were somehow established, it should be understood that there is futility in praising that which is insentient (*jaḍa*). For this very reason, although [it is said] "Soma is the progenitor of the *pavitra*," even for insentient things like *kuśa* grass, the term *pavitra* is used with the intention of referring to the grace of their respective presiding deities.
Although praise is seen in passages such as "The two [stones] belong to Viṣṇu" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 3.7.4.11),

nevertheless, because qualities such as motherhood and fatherhood are sublated therein, the term "accompanied by Umā" is used; for, through the etymological derivation (*utpatti*), it is possible for the Supreme Lord— who serves as the single substratum for all praises according to the analogy of the ocean and its waters— to be present there.
The sense is that such a defiled interpretation is improper. This has already been explained previously:

since his state of being praiseworthy is established by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutikanyāya*), even in that [other] view, there is no loss of the fact that the intent is the wearing of the *liṅga*. He touches upon Śiva through an inseparable relationship.
He is called "Śivābhimarśana" because he always touches [her]. Such being the case, it is possible to praise him as "my hand," "the Blessed One," "mother," "father," and so forth.
Furthermore, in this view, there is no contradiction with the practice of using the right hand—the most honored hand—for applying sandalwood paste and other such acts.

According to your view, however, since the left hand serves as the locus for holding [the object], this word "this" (*idam*) in the phrase "this is Śiva" refers to the hand. Regarding the argument *kaimutika* (by way of a fortiori):
if even the right hand of a person who has had some contact with it—such as through its scent or smear—is thus worthy of praise, [how much more so the left hand].

He states with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*) and so forth that, until the time of worship, praise is effectively accomplished for the left hand— which serves as the physical substrate for the Śiva-liṅga— and for the neck and other parts of the body that generally always bear it.

Regarding the phrase "in this view": by the word "this," the view that accepts the hand of the giver of ointment and so forth is intended; by "your view," the view of the one who introduces the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument is intended.
It should not be said that such [an objection] is possible, because the superiority of the left hand has already been established.
Having consecrated it, one should unweariedly and with careful attention worship daily the chosen *liṅga* given by the Guru, held at the tip of one's own left hand.
Thus, because the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā* states that the fitness for practices such as wearing [the liṅga] and worshipping it is necessary there;
and indeed, since there is no other way to account for the statement "he establishes the universal liṅga" according to the different Vedic branches (*śākhābheda*)...

If it is argued that since the wearing of the *liṅga* is already enjoined by the mantra "pavitraṃ te vitatam" (Ṛgveda 9.83.1), which is recited in the same *śākhā*, its injunction here would be superfluous (*anyathāsiddhi*), we say: not so; for while the mantra "pavitra" enjoins the wearing of the *liṅga* on the body in a general sense...

When there arises the expectation as to where [the sacred thread] should be worn even upon the body, [the answer is given] because there is no other way to establish the hand as the locus through the mantra "This hand of mine is the Blessed One" (*ayaṃ me hasto bhagavān*).

Regarding "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddhi*): [it refers to the fact that] the mantra "This hand of mine... [does not serve to establish the hand as the locus] for the mantra "The purifier is spread out for you" (*pavitraṃ te vitatam*).

The point is that because [the mantra] is recited in a single branch (*ekaśākhā*), its being established by another means (*anyathāsiddhi*) cannot be ruled out by the mention of a difference in branches.

The response is that there is no such establishment by another means, because the first mantra prescribes the general act of holding, while the second prescribes the specific locus, namely the hand. This applies to the term "touching Śivā" (*śivābhimarśana*).

Their intention is as follows: since the word *abhi* signifies pervasiveness, it conveys that touch is present at all times; and since such constant touch is logically untenable without the wearing [of the mark], the wearing of the sign (*liṅga-dhāraṇa*) is established by the means of valid cognition known as *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard).

The ancient teachers, however, maintain that this [hand] is called *śivābhimarśana* because it always touches Śiva on all sides (*abhitaḥ*). Furthermore, since such constant contact with Śiva would be impossible without its being maintained [in a specific form], its establishment as such occurs in the hand and other [limbs]. Nor does the word "on all sides" (*abhitaḥ*) mean...
In accordance with the explanation that the word *abhi-* means "on all sides" (*abhitaḥ sarvataḥ*), it is understood as referring specifically to spatial pervasion;

however, since such a tactile sensation can also occur in a *liṅga* (phallic image) established upon the earth or other materials, one might suspect that its [the *liṅga*'s] wearing is not established [as the intended meaning]. Thus, he raises the objection: "And not... (*na ca*).

It should not be argued that the wearing of the *liṅga* is not established because such a tactile sensation can also occur in the case of a *liṅga* installed on the ground or elsewhere— since the phrase "by way of a portion" implies this;
for if the word "abhitaḥ" (on all sides) were taken to mean both place and time, then [the definition] would apply only to a *liṅga* held in the hand or similar locations.

Through the possibility of such a touch, the perfection of bearing the *liṅga* is achieved. For this reason, my hand is the touch of Śiva and, therefore, the very life-giving medicine for me; O Subandhu, O Supreme Śiva, this following and approaching of You has come upon me. By that, for me—

"Come, take my hand; being held, remain forever. Thus, because the right hand is the instrument for performing the worship of Śiva and the other hand is its locus, a hand characterized by perpetual contact with Śiva is most worthy of honor.

The meaning is that [the status of] being the Blessed One, mother, father, and so forth, belongs only to one who bears the *liṅga* on his hands and other limbs; for, however, in the case of one established upon the earth and so forth, tactile contact is not possible across the delimitation of all his limbs.

And this impossibility (*asambhava*)—whether "on all sides" (*abhitaḥ*) is taken to mean temporal pervasion, spatial pervasion, or both types of pervasion—is to be understood in relation to the *liṅga* established upon the ground. [The verse] "O Subandhu," etc., is a hymn of praise; for if the body were always connected with the *śivaliṅga*, its identity with the nature of Śiva would be established.

And this is established by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutikanyāya*), because it is stated: "He who is connected with the limb of the *prāṇaliṅga* is Rudra; there is no doubt in this matter. Oh, how great is the majesty of wearing the *liṅga*, since both hands are employed as the locus for its worship!
They say that because the entire body serves as the locus for signs such as conduct (*ācāra*), the whole body is praiseworthy as being for the sake of Śiva.

In reality, however, it is Paramaśiva alone who possesses a relationship with all three times; thus, [the body] is his excellent kinsman. This is according to the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so").
The meaning is "by the logic of the staff and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpanyāya*). As for its nature: if an elephant has eaten a staff, would it not be possible for it to eat a cake as well?
The point is that one who eats a staff will eat a cake without effort. So too here, in the case of the hand...

The sense is that if it is stated that one attains the nature of the Lord merely by being the instrument in the worship of the Śivaliṅga, then it follows that one will certainly attain the state of Śiva in a body that is always connected to the Śivaliṅga.
Regarding this scriptural passage, in its stated meaning—
Worshipping this beloved *liṅga* which has been given for as long as life lasts,
he places it upon the seat of his lotus-hand, his mind intent on its meditation.
The sage named Sadānanda, who was connected to the lineage of Hastaliṅga,
was a knower of the meaning of all the Upaniṣads and was solely devoted to the meditation upon Śiva.

Thus, he who always practices this determination of the six stages— the sole cause for attaining the state of Śiva— while worshipping the venerable Liṅga of Śrīkaṇṭha placed upon the seat of his lotus-like hand,
is a man of knowledge, is ancient, is great, and is the most excellent among the devotees of Maheśvara.
By that [merit], there would be no mortal or even a god found equal to him in the three worlds.
The instruction in the *liṅga-mantra*, the worship of the hand-throne (*karapīṭha*), the recitation (*japa*),
the wearing of my *liṅga* here, and the promotion of worldly conduct;

Statements from the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā* and the *Kiraṇāgama*, such as these, should be considered as corroborative evidence. Furthermore, the statement from the *Bṛhajjābāla Upaniṣad* (5.15), "Those who revile the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) revile Śiva himself," has the aforementioned meaning. The phrase "corroborative evidence for this" connects with the distant [term]. [This was stated by] Sadānanda.

Regarding the term "muni": the sage named Sadānanda, having placed his chosen *liṅga* upon the seat of his lotus-hand for as long as he lived and worshipping it, became liberated; this is the implied sense.
The six *sthala*s (stations) are well-known in the Śaiva Āgamas.
Thus, the statement from the Jābālopaniṣad also pertains to that same subject; for therein it says:
"One should not look at a man who has been excluded [from the rite] at the time of the *pūjā*."
Those lowest of Brahmins who were cursed by Dadhīci and Gautama shall descend in the Kali age as revilers and outcasts.
In the Kali age, men who have committed the murder of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, or the theft of gold will become outcasts, as will those who revile the Lord.

Thus, by establishing that those of sinful nature who revile Śiva must be excluded, it is demonstrated that reviling him is indeed a cause of sin; this very similarity [to such revilers] is what has been established regarding the reviling of the *tripuṇḍra*.
Those who revile the *tripuṇḍra*—it is this similarity that has been established for the reviling of the *tripuṇḍra*.

By the statement, "They indeed revile Śiva," which indicates that the reviling of the *tripuṇḍra* is identical to the reviling of Śiva, the text teaches the identity of the *tripuṇḍra* and Śiva. Through this realization of their oneness, [it is said]: "The vow known as the wearing of the *liṅga*, called Māheśvara—those who perform its wearing attain the supreme goal."
Thus, the similarity of the wearing of the *liṅga*— which is described in the *Upabṛṃhaṇa* texts as the unique cause of liberation— to the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra* is understood. Furthermore,
since similarity is necessarily defined in relation to a well-known correlate (*prasiddhapratiyogika*), the wearing of the *liṅga* must also be understood in accordance with that [correlate].
He establishes that it is *siddham* (accomplished) with the passage beginning "Moreover" (*api ca*) and ending with "the accomplishment of wearing the *liṅga*" (*liṅgadhāraṇasiddhi*).
The vow known as the wearing of the *liṅga* is called *Māheśvara*.
Those who perform this wearing attain the supreme goal.

Thus, in accordance with these corroborative texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), having ascertained that the wearing of the sectarian mark (*liṅgadhāraṇa*) is the uncommon cause for liberation, the similarity of the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra* to it has been stated. In this context, "similarity" means being different from that [the *liṅga*] while...

It is the state of possessing many attributes belonging to that [object]. For example, in such cases as "by steadfastness, like the Himavat," there is, in the object of comparison (upameya), the state of being different from the Himavat while simultaneously possessing attributes such as steadfastness belonging to it;

likewise, in the present case, it is the state of being different from the wearing of gendered marks (liṅgadhāraṇa) while simultaneously possessing attributes belonging to it, such as being the cause of liberation.

Regarding the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra*, it must be stated as follows: since, according to the maxim that "an absence (*abhāva*) is indeed defined by its two correlates— the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)"— it is impossible for an absence to be established without the establishment of its counter-correlate, this applies even in the case of the poetic figure of simile (*upamā*) in the view of the Alaṅkārikas.
Furthermore, because the establishment of a comparison (*upamāna*) is necessary, the wearing of the marks is established.

Nor can it be argued that, although in cases such as "He is like the Himalaya in steadfastness" the word *iva*—which expresses similarity—is present, making such a status possible there, in the present case it is absent; therefore, [the marks] cannot be understood as the counter-correlate of the difference constituting the similarity.

Thus, when the identity between the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra* and the wearing of the *liṅga* has been indicated through their shared characteristics (*vyañjana*), the wearing of the *liṅga* is established even by way of the figure of speech known as simile (*upamā*), based on the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object compared. To this effect, he says: "according to the opinion of the Alaṅkārikas."

It should be stated that the accomplishment of wearing the *liṅga* [is implied]; for even in the absence of words such as "like" (*iva*), its establishment occurs through its being the counter-correlate of the difference that constitutes the similarity understood [in the context], just as in cases such as "Bṛhaspati [is] in eloquence of speech."

Alternatively, if the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (simile) is accepted here, nevertheless, if the establishment of the wearing of gendered marks (*liṅgadhāraṇa*) remains unavoidable, then that simile— consisting of the relationship between the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*)—
is the poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
He states that similarity is understood even without the word "iva" (like), saying: "In eloquence, [he is] Bṛhaspati.
He further states that this is established even when accepting the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration) in the verse "those who revile the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*"), saying:
"In this definition, two things which are in fact distinct appear as non-distinct due to their mutual similarity."

The separate mention of the relationship between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) is because that too contains a sense of duality; thus, it is necessary for the wearing of the *liṅga* to be established as a counter-correlative (*pratiyogi*).
Now, even if the wearing [of the *liṅga*] by Śiva is established by this much, since his purpose is fulfilled through internal wearing alone, [is external wearing not redundant?]

If it is argued that there is the accomplishment of wearing [the linga] externally, it is not so; for even that which is primarily heard is imbued with duality. This means that even the relationship between the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) is constituted by duality.
One cannot be satisfied merely by taking up the wearing of the internal *liṅga* (*antarliṅgadhāraṇa*) as a way to establish the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).

Thus he says: "that which is primary" (*yatprāyam*). The meaning of *yatprāyam* is established by the maxim: "That which possesses a similarity relative to something else, and that [other thing]—both are understood as such. By this principle, since ashes are worn on the exterior of the body, the Śiva-liṅga, which serves as the object of comparison (*upamāna*), is likewise established as being so worn.
This is established in the *Kālāgnirudropaniṣad* and other texts of similar meaning; therein,

after demonstrating that the three lines consist of Maheśvara, Rudra, and Sadāśiva through the passage beginning "And its first line," it is taught that they are to be worn as being of the very nature of Śiva by means of the prescribed method of wearing them (*dhāraṇa*).
This is because the direct meditation upon Śiva is established by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutikanyāya*).

Just as that [direct meditation] is heard of as possessing similarity with its counter-correlative, so too is that [counter-correlative] understood. By implication, just as the similarity of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) to the object of comparison (*upameya*) is perceived in the *upameya*, the similarity of the *upameya* to the *upamāna* is likewise cognized through the principle of simultaneous cognition (*tulyavittivedyatayā*).

The meaning is as follows: the great sentence-meanings that convey the realization of the essential nature of the relationship between the signifier and the signified are "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7) and "I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
The establishment of the wearing of the *liṅga* through both statements is indeed free from any obstacle. Now, one might object:

in the passage "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), it is understood from scripture that the individual soul (*jīva*) is none other than Brahman itself as conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, the transmigrating being is that which is delimited by the body, senses, and so forth, which have ignorance as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

"The individual soul (*jīva*) is that which is denoted by the term 'thou' (*tvaṃpada*)," so says the Śruti. It is inferred from this passage that this Śruti will be found when a thorough investigation of the sequence [of the Upaniṣads] is carried out. The intended meaning is that this is due to [the self's] insentience (*jaḍatva*). Furthermore, this manifestation of supreme bliss occurs only in a general form.

"Like the sound of a son studying in the midst of a group of students" (Pañcadaśī 1.11–12),

"The world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is that reality which is perfect and of the nature of consciousness."

Having abandoned the mutually contradictory literal meanings of the referents of the words *tat* and *tvam*, which consist of the body and its limbs and are produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), [one realizes] that which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss.

The sense is that [the Self] is the Self of all. Regarding the phrase "for it is of the nature of its limb": the meaning is that the world of moving and non-moving beings constitutes its body. The phrase "the *liṅga* is expressed by that word (*tatpada*)" and so forth refers to the relation; and this relation is expressed by the word "is" (*asipada*).

This statement is made because the term *asipada* (the word "is") serves to convey a qualified existence (*vaiśiṣṭya-bodha*), and thus it is useful even for the cognition of such qualification. When two nominative-termined words are used in co-referential construction, the existence of the predicate as non-different from the subject is understood;
thus, this statement is correctly made:
"He is the yogi, he is the omniscient one, and he is called liberated while living."

Having abandoned the literal meaning denoted by the words for the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*, and having again discerned the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) with right intellect, one should contemplate: "I am indeed that."

Merely by the arising of right knowledge produced from the connection between the *liṅga*, the *aṅga*, and the *pada*—having thus taught the threefold contemplation (*bhāvanā*) born from sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) as something to be practiced—he states its fruit: "He is called one who possesses the connection between the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*. Now, [an objection]:
To the objection that even upon attaining a specific designation, nothing desired is actually accomplished in reality, he says:

"He is a yogi, he is omniscient, and he is called liberated while living. This means that yoga, the sovereignty born thereof, omniscience, and liberation while living are all established; thus, the attainment of a great fruit is achieved for him.

The state of being: not only this much, but he also attains liberation, the supreme human goal; thus it is said—having abandoned, that is, having cast aside, the literal meanings of the *liṅga* and *aṅga* words, as well as the *tat* and *tvam* words, which are qualified by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the nature of *māyā* and the limiting adjunct of the nature of *avidyā*.

Having grasped pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*), which is brought forth by the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (the definition that both excludes and includes), and reflecting "I am that very one," through the power of the true knowledge (*yathārthabuddhi*) arising from such reflection, [one realizes]:
"Ignorance (*avidyā*), along with its effects, has not been, does not exist, and will not be. Thus [it is said].
In the *Anubhavasūtra*:
"The *liṅga* is declared to be the word *tat*; the *aṅga* is said to be the word *tvam*.
The conjunction of these two, the *aṅga* and the *liṅga*, is proclaimed to be the word *asi*. (5.27)
Thus, it has been stated that the wearing of the *liṅga* is to be accepted by Vedic people because it is ordained by the Vedas composed by the supreme authority, the Supreme Śiva.
