It is known as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the three absences— namely, that the *avidyā* along with its manifestations (*savilāsāvidyā*) did not exist, does not exist, and will not exist.
The sense is that by the total eradication of ignorance, he attains even supreme liberation (*paramamukti*).
He also cites the *Anubhavasūtra* as proof: "The *liṅga* is declared to be that state" (*tatpada*).
Although it should have been stated as "declared by the word 'that' (*tatpadena*)," [the text says] "declared to be that state."

This statement must be understood as being made in accordance with metrical requirements, intended to express the non-difference between the object of knowledge and the knower; it should be interpreted in some such manner.

Furthermore, one must bear this in mind here: since the entire methodological procedure (*prakriyā*) presented here appears to accord with the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*), the misconception may arise among many that this very doctrine is the one intended here. However, it is not so.

It must be understood as follows: for in the Advaita Siddhānta, all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are indeed false (*mithyātva*). Here, however, the adjuncts are not false; rather, they possess only impermanence (*anityatva*) by virtue of being subject to origination and destruction. Likewise, in the Advaita Siddhānta, there is absolute non-difference (*abheda*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman. But in this system, [there is such a distinction] regarding the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

Because [the Self] is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of living beings and because living beings are its body, just as there is a conventional usage of non-difference— such as "I am a human," "I am a god," or "I am thin," "I am fat"— so too is a superimposed non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman conventionally expressed.
If that is so, for what purpose is non-difference established by abandoning the primary denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*) and adopting the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*)?

If it is asked: "For what purpose is a pair of adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the form of *māyā* and *avidyā* accepted to establish the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, when their distinction is already established by their very nature?"—listen: [it is for the sake of establishing the distinction] between that which is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), which possesses all powers, and which is omniscient...

Since the entire universe, consisting of both the insentient and the sentient, has become the object of the Supreme Lord’s identification through its identity with Him, the Supreme Lord is said to be the Self of all. However, for individual souls (*jīvas*), who are indeed of the nature of consciousness,
it is merely their respective bodies that have become the objects of identification through identity.

Living beings are said to be distinct and possessed of individual differences, having their respective bodies as their self. Because the Supreme Lord possesses all presiding consciousness and all powers, He is able to act upon the entire world exactly as He desires. As it was said by the Blessed One: "That [Self] has hands and feet everywhere."

"Having eyes, heads, and faces everywhere; having ears everywhere in the world, He stands encompassing all. (Bhagavad Gītā 13.14); and also: "The Lord dwells, O Arjuna, in the heart-region of all beings, causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine" (Bhagavad Gītā 18.61). But as for the individual souls (*jīvas*):

Because they possess identification with their own bodies and limited power, they have the capacity— provided there is no obstruction— to move only their respective bodies directly through their own will and effort. This being the case, the Supreme Lord possesses sovereignty in which all equality and superiority are eliminated, as well as the state of being the controller of the entire universe and the possession of all powers.

This has been shown to demonstrate that [the Lord] possesses the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *māyā*; however, unlike in Advaita Vedānta, it is not the case here that the entire universe is designated by the term *māyā* for the purpose of accounting for difference despite actual non-duality (*abheda*).
This is because the sovereignty consisting of the status of being the universal controller and so forth is caused by the conceit of identity (*tādātmyābhimāna*) with respect to that [universe].
The intention is that the state of having *māyā* as an adjunct (*upādhi*) is being stated; or, *māyā* is simply a particular power (*śakti-viśeṣa*).

Alternatively, setting aside the primary denotative meaning (*vācyārtha*) which serves as the adjunct, the perception of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) is for the sake of attaining the fitness for the practice of the meditation "I am He" (*so 'ham*), by means of the realization of one's own nature through the recognition of the indicated portion itself as one's own self by virtue of its being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*).
And such practice of contemplation serves to secure the grace of the Supreme Lord by strengthening one's refuge in the Supreme Self; from that, through the cessation of ignorance,
liberation— characterized by the absolute cessation of all afflictions— is accomplished.
The pride of the Supreme Lord does not contradict His omniscience; thus, it is His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
Now, His status as such is demonstrated even by virtue of being prescribed in the *smṛtis* of Gautama, Manu, and others, which set forth the meaning of the Vedas. In the *Gautama-smṛti*:
"The mantra in the mouth, meditation in the heart, the wearing of the *liṅga* on the head,

the *rudrākṣa* on the crest-lock, and sacred ash— this is the characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa. Here, "meditation in the heart" refers to the internal contemplation of the *liṅga*, and "wearing the *liṅga* on the head" refers to [the external application].
The wearing of external insignia (*liṅga*) has also been mentioned.

*Māyā* is said to be that in which pure *sattva* predominates. For the sake of strengthening this very practice, there is the yoga of insignia and limbs, which is twofold in nature: consisting of internal and external wearing of the insignia.

The vision of the nature of Brahman is enjoined as something to be practiced. The statement that "it was not, nor is it" should be understood as intended to bring about the cessation of ego-identification and, consequently, the cessation of all activities prompted by it and all suffering; it does not, however, imply an absolute non-existence like the disappearance of objects in a dream.
This is because, in this system, such falsity is not admitted regarding the world, as the intention is merely the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); enough of this.
Thus, having established by means of Vedic statements that the wearing of the *liṅga* is a duty, [the author now shows] that the Smṛti also...
He states this to show that it must be performed: "The mantra is in the mouth.

Now, one might object: here, by referring to all Brāhmaṇas in general, the possession of the sixfold duties—such as the recitation of mantras, meditation, and the wearing of sectarian marks—is being enjoined.

If it is argued that this contradicts established custom because some lack both the wearing of the *liṅga* and the smearing of ashes, while others lack the wearing of the *liṅga*, we say no; for [the scripture states]: "Having transgressed my day of death, they become outcastes (*caṇḍāla*) for ten million births."

And that is contrary to established conduct; the sense is that among the many Brahmins who follow the Śruti and Smṛti and are devoted to the lifelong performance of the Agnihotra sacrifice, the wearing of [ascetic] marks and so forth is not observed. He demonstrates this very point with the words "in some," etc. He provides the resolution: "on the anniversary of death..."
By the words "having transcended," etc., [it is meant that] on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*),

which is the day of the passing away, if one omits the *śrāddha* for the deceased performed on the day of death for the sake of any Brāhmaṇa whatsoever, there is a statement prescribing a fault; [this applies] to the eleventh day and so forth.
A certain auspicious night attends upon those whose eyes are wide awake and vigilant.

Having passed over—meaning without performing—the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha on the day [of death], which according to different opinions may be either for a single deity or the *pārvaṇa* for three deities; here, "destruction" (death) should be understood as that of both father and mother, because the annual śrāddha for them alone is mandatory.

Regarding the phrase "by the followers of Ānandatīrtha": when they encounter the occasion for performing a *śrāddha* on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*), they do not perform it out of fear of violating their vow. This is done in accordance with the prohibitory statements found in Vaiṣṇava texts.

In the statement that makes known the fault of transgressing the *śrāddha* rites, this restriction should be understood as applying to cases other than those for the sons of a father who died on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*)—specifically, excluding the particular Vaiṣṇavas.
"Rātri is Śiva": a certain Śaiva encourages his own eyes to keep vigil on the night of Śivarātri.
Before long, someone of similar character will become a friend to you both.

Just as the statement enjoining the practice of keeping vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) is intended for all people and thus has as its scope those other than the followers of the Rāmānuja school, so too this [practice] has as its scope the Brāhmaṇas who wear the *liṅga*. Furthermore, regarding the wearing of the *liṅga* on the head...

Because the word *brāhmaṇa*, although denoting a general category, culminates in a specific instance due to the presence of words that terminate in a particular [meaning], it refers specifically to the *liṅga-aṅga-brāhmaṇa* (the Brahmin who is both the emblem and the body).
"Śivarātri" means a night consisting of auspiciousness (*śiva*); that [night] is present, meaning it exists nearby. On this night—
"Both of you, being vigilant and attentive, remain awake; do not fall into negligence or sleep—this is the meaning.

As for what the fruit of this is, he says: 'samāna...'. A friend, a companion of equal nature to both of you, that is, a third eye, shall appear from your presence, from your vicinity, in no long time."

The purport is that by keeping vigil during this night, a human being becomes manifestly Śiva himself, the Three-eyed One. From this, the injunction is obtained that one must perform the vigil on Śivarātri for the sake of attaining the state of Śiva.
Even this injunction, however, [is rejected] by followers of certain Vaiṣṇava traditions.

Even so, some do not accept that *brāhmaṇatva* (the state of being a Brahmin) is defined by the sixfold duties such as mantra-recitation and meditation prescribed for those characterized as Brahmins by means of gender (*liṅga*) and bodily marks (*aṅga*), either because they follow the literal wording of the texts or due to dogmatic attachment to specific passages. The same applies to the injunction regarding the wearing of the *liṅga*.
This should be understood as referring to Brahmins who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgadhārī-brāhmaṇas). In reality, however, even though there is no restriction regarding unenjoined actions,
the intended meaning is that the defining characteristic of Brahmins who possess the marks and their bearers is their possession of the sixfold dharma.
Even if certain injunctions are not performed by some due to a deficiency in ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and so forth, there is no impairment whatsoever of those injunctions.
The statement regarding this restriction here, however, is made by way of a concessive argument (*abhyupagamavāda*).
In that very same [text]:
All the powerful sages, beginning with Akṣapāda,
joyfully bear the Śiva-liṅga upon the tips of their foreheads day and night.
Thus, in the *Manusmṛti*:
"For one who is liberated from all ritual actions and devoted to the yoga of meditation,
neither cremation nor the offering of rice-balls and water should be performed."

He states that the wearing of the *liṅga* is also established by the scriptural statement prohibiting cremation and other rites for one devoted to the yoga of meditation—beginning with the words "for one liberated from all actions. In response to the inquiry, "Who is this one devoted to the yoga of meditation? [the text continues:]

In this context, because of the presence of the particle *ca* (and), which indicates a conjunction, both "being devoted to meditation and yoga" (*dhyānayogarata*) and "liberation from all karma" (*sarvakarmavimukti*) are presented as the primary objects of reference.
Consequently, when the inquiry arises—"Who is this one devoted to meditation and yoga?"—it is stated:
"Having become devoted to the meditation on Śiva, and being united with the body of the Śiva-liṅga..."
One who abandons all that is inauspicious is called a practitioner of meditative yoga.
Just as men perform worship after meditating upon Śiva externally,
so too is he called a yogi of meditation if he is serene within his heart.

Since it is stated in that very [text], the accomplishment of wearing the *liṅga* is established by prescribing the absence of cremation and other rites with reference to the Lord of Ascetics (*yatīśvara*), who is indicated by the term "liberated from all ritual actions" (*sarvakarmavimukta*), and the wearer of the *liṅga*, who is indicated by the term "yogi of meditation" (*dhyānayogin*). In the *Bodhāyana-smṛti*:
For one who has desisted from all attachments and is devoted to the practice of meditation,
there shall be no cremation, no impurity, and no water-libation rite.

It demonstrates the characteristic of one devoted to the yoga of meditation as being established in mindfulness: "Having become intent on the meditation of Śiva, united with the body of the Śiva-liṅga, and having abandoned everything other than Śiva—he is called a yogin of meditation. In this very manner: "For one who has desisted from all attachments and is devoted to the yoga of meditation."

In the case of the *Bodhāyanasmṛti* as well, the establishment of the wearing of the *liṅga* is achieved through the aforementioned direction indicated by the phrase "one devoted to the yoga of meditation.
In the *Śātātapasmṛti*:
One should cast the corpse of a forest-dweller, a yogin, one who bears a single sectarian mark, a mendicant, or an ascetic— among these belonging to the four stages of life— into the Rasa river.

In this context, since the act of digging is enjoined with reference to the wearing of the *liṅga*, the wearing of the *liṅga* is established as a qualification of the subject matter (*uddeśya-viśeṣaṇa*).
Now, by means of this collection of cited scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti-kadamba*), [it is shown that...]
It has been stated that because the wearing of the *liṅga* and its worship are obligatory, they must persist for as long as one lives, being common even to women and children; however,
this is untenable in the case of menstruating women and women who have recently given birth, who are unfit for seeing, touching, conversing with [the deity], and so forth.

This is because [the practices of] maintaining [the fire] and performing worship are utterly incompatible [with that state]. If it is argued that this is proven by the *Śātātapa-smṛti*, which states, "In that regard, the forest-dweller, the yogin, the mendicant, and the ascetic [share] a single emblem (*liṅgaikya*"), then it should be understood that "single emblem" refers to the attainment of being composed of the emblem through the application of intense meditation.
Since the wearing of the *liṅga* is obligatory for all people alike, including women and children,
those who are menstruating— even though they have become utterly impure—
perform its wearing, worship, and other such rites.
In that case, due to contact with the impure body, the *liṅga* would also attain impurity;

consequently, even after bathing, it would follow that worship and other rites could not be performed. For at that time, no further consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *liṅga* is performed, as that would contradict your own established doctrine.
Furthermore:
One should completely avoid Śaivas, Pāśupatas, those who bear the sectarian mark (liṅgin), those under religious vows (vratina), those who act like cats (viḍālavratina), and heretics (pāṣaṇḍas).

Upon seeing a heretic, an outcast, a degraded person, one who bears the mark of a sectarian, a wearer of false emblems, or likewise a temple-attendant (devalaka), one should enter the water with one's clothes on.
Upon seeing one who bears the discus or the sectarian mark (liṅgin), one should perform a bath with one's clothes on;
likewise for that twice-born man whose body is marked with heated discs and other such signs.

He should be known as ineligible for rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, and so forth. [One should ask: "How should it be performed? [The answer is: toward the Śaivas, the Pāśupatas, those who bear the *liṅga*, and likewise those who observe vows.
The food of a sage should not be eaten, nor likewise that of those who bear the marks of yogis.

If it is argued that, because it is prohibited by the scriptures, the wearing of the *liṅga* must certainly not be performed, and that the previously cited *śruti*, *smṛti*, and other texts should somehow be interpreted as being intent on internal contemplation (*antar-anusandhāna*), do not say so; for [the scripture says]: "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone some..."

"they attained immortality" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.3), and "human beings do not find liberation anywhere other than through the renunciation of karma"— even though such passages establish that [renunciation] produces liberation, the most highly esteemed and primary goal of human life— nevertheless...
One should not harm any living beings, nor should one eat meat;
one should not give the remains of food to anyone, nor should one eat between [meals]. One should not overeat, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from eating. (2.56)
And how is the prohibition of wearing such marks to be reconciled, even though [the practice] is forbidden by such scriptural passages as the Śruti and the Manusmṛti,
and even though [acts such as] the slaughter of animals, the eating of meat, and the drinking of Soma are contradicted by direct perception? These doubts are addressed in succession.
He refutes this with the words "Not so," and so forth.

For [the path of action] is characterized by violence, as evidenced by such scriptural passages as: "Neither by ritual action nor by progeny [does one attain immortality]; let him not harm any living beings; let him not eat meat" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.13).

Just as the general prohibition is restricted by the scriptural injunction for the immolation of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, so too is the statement indicating the impurity of a woman during her menses restricted by the following texts:
"One should sacrifice with Soma," "One should [drink] the remnant with Soma," and "One should immolate the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma."

Just as there is the necessity of performing various specific duties prescribed by particular injunctions such as these, so too, by the perpetual injunction stating "one should install all [types of] lingas" and so forth,
the lifelong obligation to wear the linga and perform its worship is established; in whatever house...
For a woman who has given birth, there is no *sūtaka* (impurity) here;
nor is there *sūtaka* for a woman engaged in the worship of the *liṅga* during her menstrual period.
Likewise, for a woman who has recently given birth, *sūtaka* does not exist at all. (9.44–45)
A woman devoted to the worship of the Liṅga who is in a state of birth-impurity or menstruating [is likewise purified].
Like the sun, fire, and wind, it is pure and possesses millions upon millions of qualities;
by wearing it, women and those afflicted by birth-impurity and the like are liberated from their condition.

Thus, due to the restrictive application of the statement from the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi-vīrāgama*, "For a woman devoted to the worship of the Liṅga, there is no *sūtaka* during her menses," and other such passages, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. Furthermore, there are many other restrictions regarding impurity (*aśauca*) found in the *Dharmaśāstras*.
For just as iron becomes nothing but fire through the penetration of fire,
even so, by my presence, they are no longer mere humans by nature.
Cotton mixed with oil likewise [becomes a lamp] from contact with light;
and for one who is anointed with oil and possesses true devotion, the state of being a *liṅga* arises through contact with the *liṅga*.
According to the statement in the *Śivarahaṃsya* of the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"For one who performs the worship of the Śaiva Liṅga, for one who maintains the sacred fire (*agniparigraha*),
and for forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and ascetics (*yati*), there is no ritual impurity (*sūtaka*) in their bodies."
Thus, according to the *Parāśarasmṛti*, there is no contradiction in women who are menstruating or in similar conditions performing the wearing [of the image] and its worship;
he shows this by way of an illustration: "In the Pauṇḍarīka and Dīrghasattra..."

This very statement was commenced prior to the period of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*). This is because the vow of wearing the *liṅga*, which is relevant to the present context, is considered "commenced" by virtue of its being resolved upon as a duty to be performed for the duration of one's life;

for, according to the rule "the resolve constitutes the commencement of a vow or a sacrificial session," such a resolve is understood to be the very form of the commencement. Thus, [the impurity] does not apply.
Just as an iron ball [is not consumed] by entering fire,

and furthermore, just as the wife of a sacrificer initiated into long-term sacrifices such as the Pauṇḍarīka is not subject to impurity and the like arising from childbirth, because there is no absence of an exception [to the rule], due to the lack of [the necessary] substance.
Or, due to the influence of other obstacles, if a girl remains unmarried for as long as twelve years,
what do the ritualists do when she has reached puberty, or when it is seen or heard that she has attained it?

It is not merely composed of the common [elements]; rather, the meaning is that at that time it becomes composed of fire (*agnimaya*). Likewise, by virtue of the presence of Sadāśiva, those who wear the *liṅga* do not become ordinary human beings; this is the intended sense.
When the ritual for marriage has been spread out and the time for the fire-oblation has arrived,
what do the performers of the sacrifice do upon seeing that the bride has reached her menses?

To this question, [the answer is]: having bathed the girl with the mantra, "These waters are rich in oblation; the divine sacrifice is rich in oblation" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.3.12.1), and having adorned her with two new garments, [he offers] two oblations with the verse, "Yoking first the mind... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.1.1.1).

This is because it has been established in Bhaṭṭoji’s *Vivāhakhaṇḍa* that one should perform the oblation (*juhuyāt*), and because in that context, the impurity (*āśauca*) of a woman in her menses does not constitute an exception to the initiation for marriage (*vivāhadīkṣā*). Furthermore, regarding the paternal *śrāddha* and similar rites,
even if impurity arises after the offering of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins invited as the ancestors (*pitṛ*), [the rite is not invalidated].
Having burnt away the three impurities (*mala*) residing in the three bodies by means of the three initiations, this Guru taught the three *liṅgas*.
For as long as you live, do not separate this emblem from your body.

Regarding the phrase "pertaining to the three bodies": the three impurities (*mala*) residing in the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*), the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), and the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*) are of three kinds due to their being the three substrates. [The impurities are] physical, vocal, and mental.
Thus, for one who has received the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of wearing the *liṅga* performed by a Guru, one should always, with vigilance, [place it] on the tip of one's own left hand.

Regarding the injunction "one should worship," since the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for such worship must persist as long as one lives, it must be accepted that in the case of such initiation, impurities such as those caused by menstruation do not constitute an exception [to the rules of purity].
For this very reason, Kauśikāditya, in the *Ṣaḍaśīti-smṛti* which was composed for the purpose of determining the rules regarding impurity (*āśauca*), stated:
For those who have completed funeral rites, for those who are outcastes, regarding paternal property,
and for the king and his emissary in matters concerning the protection of the land.
For one who intends to wander for the sake of destroying sins from birth onwards,
and for the purpose of being authorized to perform rites for the deceased as well as ancestral rites, [one should perform this].
In the case of the rites for departing the body (utkrānti) and crossing the Vaitaraṇī river, as well as the offering of water for the deceased (pretodaka),
and other such prescribed ceremonies, there is neither impurity (āśauca) nor birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Ritual actions must indeed be performed; he is just like one who has merit.
However, a vow that was commenced for many days prior to the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) [must be completed].
One should perform that [rite] with the body, but not through giving, worship, or recitation.
Forest-dwellers, ascetics, and celibate students are considered pure;
others also are always pure when engaged in their prescribed duties.
Having stated by such means that among those who have commenced the performance of vows (vratas), even if impurity (āśauca) or similar obstacles should occur,
those respective rites must indeed be performed, [the author] addresses the inquiry as to which rite constitutes the commencement of which specific action:
In a sacrifice, the commencement is the selection of the officiants; in the case of a vow or a long-term session (sattra), it is the formal resolve;
in marriage and similar rites, it is the Nāndīmukha ceremony; and in a śrāddha rite, it is the taking up of the cooking materials.
Thus it has been stated.

The passage beginning with "for those who have completed the rites for the deceased" (*pretakāryanivṛttānām*) is clear. And its meaning is as follows: the selection of officiating priests (*ṛtvigvaraṇa*) in a sacrifice, such as a domestic sacrifice (*gṛhayajña*), and so forth.

The commencement (*prārambha*) [is defined as follows]: in the case of a vow (*vrata*), such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*, a pilgrimage to a sacred site (*tīrthayātrā*), the wearing of a sectarian mark (*liṅgadhāraṇa*), or worship (*pūjā*), it is the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).

In the case of a sacrificial session (*satra*), such as the long-term *pauṇḍarīka* sacrifice, it is the resolve. In the case of marriage and similar rites, it is the *nāndīmukha* ceremony; in the case of a funeral rite (*śrāddha*), the act of cooking is the commencement.
Thus, even during a period of ritual impurity (aśauca), these specific rites must indeed be performed immediately after such an undertaking.
And so it is said:
"The vow known as the wearing of the *liṅga* is called Māheśvara."
As long as one lives, one should worship this beloved liṅga which has been given.

According to the method stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa* and other sources, since the vow of wearing the *liṅga* and its worship is also conceived for the duration of one's life at the time of initiation performed by a guru, there is parity [in the argument]: if there is complete purification regarding the aspects such as wearing the *liṅga* during the intervening period, then there would likewise be complete purification even in other ritual acts.

Some, however, argue that even though one is pure for the recitation of mantras and so forth when the mouth has been purified by means such as brushing the teeth or rinsing with water, one remains impure with respect to other acts, such as spitting from the body.
They say that although there may be purity regarding matters such as wearing [the liṅga] and worship, there is an absence of it in other activities.
As it has been said: "Due to contact with the impure body, the liṅga also becomes impure"—this is utterly unattractive. Even though this is so...
According to the method of the statements found in the *Parāśara-smṛti*, the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, and other such works,

since the body lacks impurity in respect to the aspect of wearing [the marks], the possibility of the *liṅga* becoming similarly impure through contact with it is far-fetched; nevertheless, this is refuted even by way of a concessive argument (*abhyupetyavāda*).

In that regard, [is the objection] concerning the impure body—or concerning the *liṅga* which has become that body? Not the first, because it has been stated [in the scripture]: "That which is partless, actionless, and tranquil," and so forth, regarding the claim that [impurity arises] from connection with the impure body.

This is the intended meaning of this section of the *Samādhāna*: first of all, according to this view, just like one who has renounced the body upon attaining supreme dispassion (*paravairāgya*), there is no impurity whatsoever in a body that has attained its true nature as Śiva; this is established by relying on other philosophical systems.
Even if one accepts the impurity of that body,
[the Self remains] "faultless and stainless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19), and thus it is said, "Therefore, Śiva is all-pervading" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.11).

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because it is impossible for the Supreme Lord— the inner controller of all, who is pure by virtue of being understood through scripture as being free from even a trace or fraction of any defect— to incur a defect through contact with an impure body, given his commonality with both pure and impure objects.

Because it is impossible to bring about that [state] even for the *liṅga*, which serves as the substratum for the Supreme Lord as designated by the relationship of indivisibility; if you think that at the time of the initiation of action (*kriyādīkṣā*),

there is the bathing with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), their respective consecrations (*adhivāsa*), the purification of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvaśodhana*), the invocation of the *kalās*, and so forth.
If it is argued that the *liṅga*— which has undergone consecration by the Guru— is destroyed through contact with the impure body,
then that [objection] merely imitates the drinking of the milk of a female tortoise.
Because of such contact, neither impurity can accrue to the *liṅga* nor to the Śiva-tattva which presides over it.

To claim that the Supreme Self is impure would lead only to sin; for the same applies to the *liṅga* presided over by Him— consider, for instance, the sacrifice (*yāga*), which consists of action, desire, and so forth, and is subject to immediate destruction.
Because it would otherwise be impossible for the sacrifice to produce heaven at a later time, the sacrificer and his wife [perform the rite].
Having consecrated the desired *liṅga* given by the Guru, he— being unwearied—
[perceives] the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) through the firm conviction of non-difference from the Supreme Self, which is otherwise inexpressible.
One should constantly worship [it] with mindfulness at the tip of one's own left hand.

Thus, because it is impossible for one whose limbs are conjoined with the *liṅga* established by these words to perform the purposeful acts of daily worship, offerings, and so forth, until the final liberation of the body (*videha-mukti*), that [liberation] also generates a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the abiding power (*sthāyi-śakti*) within the *liṅga*.
For even that [impression] cannot be destroyed through contact with a body subject to intermediate impurity (*āntarālikāśauca*) and the like;

for if destruction were to be postulated even by such means, then [the same would apply to] the impressions of the sacrificer and his wife’s life-cycle rites (*vṛttisaṃskāra*), as well as the various impressions produced by bathing in the Gaṅgā, giving food, and so forth, which would likewise be destroyed by intermediate impurity and the like.

Nor can it be argued that the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by purification and other rites perishes through destruction because of impurity, and that by means of this [perishing] the object attains a state of being unworthy of worship.
For if it were to follow that all actions lack results,
and consequently that the Veda, the Shastras, and other sources of knowledge which teach them would lose their authority, one would fall into the Bauddha doctrine. And it is said:

By reflecting upon the previously cited *Parāśara-smṛti* passage— "For whom there is the worship of the Śiva-liṅga and for whom there is the maintenance of the sacred fire"— it is established that, because impurity does not exist even in the body of the sacrificer (the *liṅgin*), it likewise does not exist in the *liṅga* joined with that body.

Because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) have not ceased. Furthermore, in places such as Śrī Bhuvaneśvara and Puruṣottama, by the mere act of offering, even if one comes into contact with another caste, [one is purified] through the consumption of perfectly pure prasāda, in accordance with the scriptural statement: "My prasāda is supremely purifying, even in a leper’s garden."

Furthermore, since it is accepted that the Vedic tradition endorses [the practice], there is no dispute regarding the fact that the *liṅga*— which is the substratum of the supreme Śiva, who is eternally pure and directly free from the stain of defects— remains devoid of impurity even when in contact with the impure body.

Because it is not observed that the *apūrva* (unseen merit) produced by a sacrifice— which resides in the bodies of the sacrificer and his wife— is destroyed by impurity (*āśauca*), and because impurity is not a cause for the destruction of a consecration (*saṃskāra*).

Nor [is this a problem] even in the case of a stationary object (*sthāvara*), since the impurity arising therein is removed by bathing and touching performed by the preceptor (*ācārya*) at the time of its consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

By the force of the scriptures which enjoin the offering of worship and other rites for as long as one lives in relation to whichever *liṅga* is to be worn, there arises a purificatory refinement (*saṃskāra*) that motivates acts such as worship to be performed at all times, regardless of whether they are pure or impure.
"Even if permanence is postulated,

there is a disparity"— this means between the stationary linga and the living linga. In the case of the stationary linga, regarding the worship performed with the consecration (saṃskāra) that serves as the cause for its being worthy of worship every day:

Because there is no restriction on the agent [of worship], when one person is impure, the worship of that [liṅga] can still be carried out by another person; in that case, the Supreme Lord tolerates contact with the impure. However, in the case of the *prāṇaliṅga*, at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), the Guru bestows a consecration (*saṃskāra*) upon a single person which serves as the cause for its being worshipped by that very person alone for as long as he lives.

Since [the consecration] has been performed, there is no destruction of that [consecration] upon touching the image during a period of ritual impurity (*aśauca*). Furthermore, because lifelong worship (*yāvajjīva-pūjā*) is prescribed for stationary images (*sthāvara*), such [impurity] does not apply to them. For this very reason, one observes the performance of re-consecration (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) and other rites even in those cases;
however, enough of this elaboration.
As for what was stated— that the wearing of the *liṅga* should not be performed because it is prohibited by scriptures such as "the Śaivas and the Pāśupatas," etc.— that too is utterly unconvincing;
for upon a thorough examination of such scriptures, one perceives that [those texts] are intended to show that all [such practitioners] are unworthy of being seen.
"It is not undesirable for us. In that regard, because [the term] "Śaivas" refers to those connected with Śiva,

and due to the fear of violating their vow (*vratabhaṅga*)— which would result in the contradiction [of their status]— it is postulated in this system that such an impression (*saṃskāra*) cannot be destroyed by that [knowledge].

The sense is that it is according to the maxim: "What is undesirable for one side is not [undesirable] for us; when a fault is equal for both sides, the remedy for them is also equal; thus, neither party should be subject to censure in such an investigation of the matter. By the term *śaiva*, derived from the deity Śiva, [the author refers to] the earlier Śaivas who wear sacred ash (*bhūti*) and rudrākṣa beads.
It cannot be said that for the followers of the Smṛtis— who perform worship of Śiva at the time of *pradoṣa* and wear sacred ash—

the term "Śaiva" refers to a Brāhmaṇa who wears the *liṅga* through the process of *yogarūḍhi* (etymological and conventional meaning), because there is no specific word such as *liṅgin* present to denote that [specific group]. Nor is it the case that the word "Śaiva" functions as a qualifier for the word *liṅgin*.

Furthermore, it must be stated that [the term] *pāśupata* is also included, because this contradicts the particle *ca*, which indicates a cumulative conjunction (*samuccaya*) of what has been previously mentioned.

Moreover, the word *pāṣaṇḍa* refers specifically to those who follow the Smṛtis; for according to the lexicon, "Pāṣaṇḍas are all those who bear sectarian marks" (*Amarakośa* 2.7.45), and such marks as the triple-line (*tripuṇḍra*) or the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) belong only to them.

For those who have entered the Bhāgavata path, the various stones, copper images, and so forth— which are the sites of manifestation for their respective deities through the diverse forms of Satyabhāmā, Rukmiṇī, Kṛṣṇa, and others—
are denoted by the term *liṅga*, as in: "Āditya, Ambikā, Viṣṇu, Gaṇanātha..."

Because the worship of the five *liṅgas* as understood from the scriptural statement "Maheśvara" constitutes their Śaiva character as officiants (*kartr-rūpa*), and because this state exists in almost all actual Brāhmaṇas— excluding those who are obstinate Vaiṣṇavas— it would follow that all of them would become untouchable.
It is impossible to claim that [the term] refers exclusively to those who merely wear the sectarian mark (*liṅgin*) by relying on its conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*),

because the word *liṅgin* appears separately in that verse, which would result in redundancy. Furthermore, it is not possible for the word *śaiva* to function as an adjective qualifying others, because of the conjunction "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "Śaivas and Pāśupatas."

Because a collective sense is understood [from the compound]. In the lexicon [Amara-kośa], regarding the term *sarvaliṅgin* in the verse "Pāṣaṇḍas are those who bear all marks" (2.7.45), the word *sarvaliṅgin* is a *karmadhāraya* formed with the suffix *-in*, as in "all those who are mark-bearers. This is because the rule "no possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) after a *karmadhāraya*" is generally applicable; thus, [the possessive suffix] does not apply here. All...

And because it is well-known. Nor should it be said that there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified between the words *pāṣaṇḍa* and *liṅga*; for since Brāhmaṇas who wear [heterodox] marks (*liṅgin*) are included among all those denoted by the word *pāṣaṇḍa* as previously stated, this refers specifically to those who follow the Smṛtis.
The statement that "the food of a sage should not be eaten" does not entail anything undesirable for us, because the sin committed by the donor remains attached to the food;
one should not accept such food even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat.

Thus, since the acceptance of food is prohibited in all such cases; furthermore: "A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice offered by one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), nor at one offered by a village-priest (*grāmayājika*), nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch. (4.205)

The food of a violent person, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, that over which one has sneezed, that which is not formally offered, meat not consecrated by sacrifice, and the food of a woman whose husband is absent; these are forbidden.

One should not accept food from an enemy, nor food that has been shaken off or blown upon; likewise, the food of a slanderer, of a liar, and of one who sells what is forbidden. (4.212–214) One should also avoid the food of a multitude, the food of a courtesan, and that which is censured by the learned.

This is because the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* prohibits the food of various specific individuals— such as "the food of a usurer is excrement" and "the food of a seller of the scriptures is impurity"— yet it does not prohibit the food of those who bear the *liṅga*.
Furthermore, the term *liṅgin* can be analyzed as a possessive derivative (*matvarthīya*) following a *karmadhāraya* compound, meaning "those in whom *liṅgas* exist."
Furthermore, since the word *liṅga*— derived from the etymology previously shown as "that which makes known (*gamayati*) a hidden (*līna*) meaning"—

refers merely to an image that manifests a particular deity, it must be concluded that the capacity to worship all images in a single person is contradicted; therefore, this [qualification] must ultimately apply to multiple persons, specifically in the case of multiple images.

The intention of this text is that all those who worship deities fall into the state of being heretics (*pāṣaṇḍatva*). However, the prohibition "one must not eat the food of a sage" does not render anyone blameworthy, because by the rule "one should not accept food even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat," the consumption of food from anyone at all is prohibited.

In the *Manusmṛti*, within the section enumerating prohibited foods beginning with "the food of the fierce" (*ugrānna*) at 4.205, the fact that those who bear [external] marks (*liṅgin*) are not included among the prohibited foods makes such prohibitions appear as if motivated by hatred. [This is stated: "Having ascertained the conduct of both the one who bears marks and the other... and so forth.

O Great King, they say that what is to be given is indeed [the latter], because in a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, Śruti is more authoritative according to the principle of the section on contradiction (Virodhādhikaraṇa),
as was previously illustrated by all the indicative marks (liṅgas).

Since the wearing of the marks (*liṅga-dhāraṇa*) prescribed by numerous powerful scriptural texts such as "he establishes [it]" and so forth cannot be negated by a mere *smṛti*, it is stated in the Anuśāsana-parvan of the Mahābhārata— which is equal to the Veda:
"O best of the Bharatas, what do the Brahmins call the eternal worthy recipient (*pātra*)?..."
When Yudhiṣṭhira asked, "How should one treat a Brahmin who bears the marks [of an ascetic] and a Brahmin who does not bear such marks? [the Lord replied:
"Having recognized the virtuous conduct of both the one who bears the marks and the other..."
"O Great King, they say that both of these are worthy of gifts;
both of these are ascetics"— by this statement from the *Mahābhārata*,
[the term 'ascetic' applies] to a Brāhmaṇa distinguished by austerity, Vedic study, and virtuous conduct, whether he bears the external marks of his order or not.
"Worthiness as a recipient is understood.
Since this statement by Bhīṣma prescribes that those twice-born who bear the *liṅga* are worthy recipients of gifts,
and since it is impossible for them not to be worthy of being seen, this [text] does not imply the censurability of those who bear the *liṅga*.

However, according to the Śruti: "He who indeed sacrifices beyond his own deity falls away from his own deity; he does not reach the higher one and becomes worse off," it is said: "One's own duty, though deficient, is better than the duty of another well-performed" (Bhagavad Gītā 3.35).
Upon seeing that evil-minded person who, having abandoned his own duty, undertakes another duty, one should perform the rite of gazing at the sun.

From such scriptural and traditional injunctions as, "He who indeed sacrifices beyond his own deity," it is understood that the established doctrine of the scriptures is this: by whichever deity initiation has been received, the primary worship of that deity must be performed by him for as long as life lasts. Such being the case, those who are *liṅgins* (bearers of sectarian marks) for some time [and others for some time]...

Those followers of the Cakrin who, in such a manner, become worshippers of both [deities], must necessarily encounter censure because they contradict the aforementioned established doctrine; this will surely come within the path of experience.
However, those who, from the heart and with true sincerity, [abandon] passion and aversion...
Having abandoned devotion to the one God, with his mind dissolved in that alone,
he who breaks the boundaries of the Vedas regarding his own caste and stage of life,
and takes refuge in extreme doctrines— he is called a heretic (pāṣaṇḍa).
Thus, according to such statements from the Bhagavadgītā and other texts:
"Better is one's own duty, though deficient in merit, than the well-performed duty of another;
for by living by the duty of another, one surely falls from one's caste immediately" (10.97).

Thus, according to the *Manusmṛti* and the statement of the learned, "If one should worship another deity while neglecting one's own, he falls from both worlds and incurs sin," the bearer of the discus (Cakrin) is [praised] because of the censurability of one who abandons his own duty (*svadharma*) to adopt the duty of another (*anyadharma*).

Regarding the phrase "one who possesses the insignia" (*liṅginam*), this refers to one who, having first been a bearer of the insignia, abandons it due to the power of evil karma and becomes a bearer of the discus (*cakrin*), or having first become a bearer of the discus, abandons that and becomes a bearer of the insignia; seeing such a person [one should act].

There is no occasion for their censure. The meaning that must be accepted is this: one should perform a bath with one's clothes on (sacailasnāna) toward such Śiva-yogins who, through supreme meditation day and night, have attained the state of being identical with Śiva. As for [the person] who...

Regarding the phrase "one whose body is marked with signs such as the heated discus" (*santaptacakrādiliṅgāṅkitatanu*), the word *liṅga* here refers to a mark (*lāñchana*). Thus, the meaning is that a twice-born person (*dvija*) whose body is marked by those heated discs and other signs is ineligible for the performance of Śrauta, Smārta, and other rites; this applies specifically to a Brāhmaṇa.

Since the prohibition of being marked with [the signs of] the discus was already established previously by the verse beginning "The body is to be known," if one should happen to see, even through negligence, a Vaiṣṇava whose body is marked with the conch and discus and who is a reviler of Śiva, one should perform the gazing at the sun.

Furthermore, in accordance with such passages as these, if the word *liṅga* refers to the Śiva-liṅga, then one who has first been marked with the heated seal (*taptamudrā*) and subsequently abandons that to become a *liṅgin*, or conversely becomes a *cakrin*, must likewise be excluded, as was stated previously; otherwise—
Animals are superior in intelligence to worms, insects, and moths;
humans are superior even to animals, and among them, the twice-born are the most excellent.
Among the twice-born, the Brahmins are superior; among Brahmins, those of perfected intellect;
among those of perfected intellect, the performers of ritual action; and superior even to them are the renunciants.
Among them, the wise are superior; among them, the worshippers of Śaṅkara;
and among those, O fortunate one, the best are those who are united with my liṅga as their very limb.
A man who possesses knowledge of the six stages (ṣaṭsthala) is superior to those whose limbs are attached to the Liṅga;
indeed, there is no one superior even to him at any time throughout the three worlds.
He is to be saluted and worshipped at all times by those who desire to conquer cyclic existence;
what is the use of much speaking, my child? He himself is I, without a doubt.

These statements have been set forth concerning those who are turned away from the hollow pleasures of worldly objects— starting from worms, insects, and moths, up through the twice-born, and among them, the wise who are attached to the marks and limbs [of renunciation]— and they are worthy of honor.
Thus,
whether on the head, the neck, the hand, or even the chest—
him who is devoid of wearing the *liṅga*, one should abandon like an outcaste.
Upon seeing a *kuṇḍa*, a *golaka*, one who is devoid of the wearing of the *liṅga*,
as well as a temple-priest (*devalaka*), one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
O son, upon seeing a twice-born man who does not wear the desired linga on his gross body, one should immediately perform a bath along with one's clothes.
Upon seeing the wearing of the *aliṅga* on the head, the arm, or the upper part of the forehead, one should look at the sun.
He who does not worship with devotion the Liṅga, the Lord of the three worlds,
is not a recipient of heaven, nor of liberation, nor of sovereignty.
Śiva is eternally present within the body of a Śiva-yogin;
therefore, by worshipping the lord of yogins, Śiva himself is directly worshipped.
Those ignorant ones who hate the yogin, remaining established in all manner of sins—
those who here in this world hate the yogin devoted to the knowledge of Śiva.
Those fools who harbor doubts about the Great-Souled One who bears the Śiva-linga go to the hells along with their ancestors; of this there is no doubt.

These [passages] are to be considered: "In the region of the head, a *kuṇḍa* and a *golaka*; on the thick part of the body, however, an *iṣṭaliṅga* on the head or on the arm-staff"—the purport of these four statements is that one should not harbor hatred toward the worship of Śiva and Śivā. [As it is said: "He who does not worship with devotion..."
The Liṅga is the Lord of the three worlds; he who [neglects it] is not a recipient of heaven, nor of liberation, nor of sovereignty.
It should be understood that this verse conveys the established doctrines of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas. Regarding the body of the Śiva-yogin, it says:
"Those ignorant ones who hate the yogin..."
This is because it contradicts the statements found in the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*, the *Vīrāgama*, the *Mukuṭāgama*, the *Śivadharmottara*, and other such texts.
[Objection: But surely, those who have been arrested by the king somewhere on account of the crime of theft—
And those who entered the wives of others were slain by their husbands out of anger.
Having engaged in conflict with those who are unequal, those of mixed caste, and those such as Caṇḍālas,
and having been slain by them, or having resorted to Caṇḍālas and the like,
these three types of people harbor doubts regarding the Great-Souled One, just as in the previous case of malice toward a Śiva-yogin.

It should be understood that this indicates inferiority. Regarding the phrase "because of the occurrence of contradiction," its connection is with the previously mentioned word "otherwise" (*anyathā*). In that context, "otherwise" refers to prohibitions such as, "Upon seeing one who bears the discus or the sectarian mark, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on," which apply to the subject of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
The meaning is the absence of the state of having as one's object a *liṅga* that is subject to the instability of abandonment and acquisition.
In the preceding text, it was stated that those who, having taken one initiation, abandon it and take another,
and subsequently abandon even that to take a third— such persons have found no footing in the matter of spiritual practice (*upāsanā*).

[These] have been shown as the referents of the term *pāṣaṇḍa*. However, in the *Skanda Purāṇa* and other texts, it is stated: "He who, on this earth, transgresses the boundaries of caste ordained by Śiva should be known as a *pāṣaṇḍa*, excluded from all ritual acts. By this statement, the abandonment of the boundaries of caste is the referent of the term *pāṣaṇḍa*.
He raises the objection that this text is contradictory by saying "nanu" and so forth:
"But [it is said] 'those who are punished by the king,' whereas [the text] states:
'Heretics of cruel intellect, as well as those who inflict bonds, fire, or poison.'"
He who exists on earth transgressing the boundaries of caste as declared by Śiva should be known as a heretic, excluded from all ritual acts.
He who has fallen away from the conduct prescribed for his own stage of life is called "patita" (an outcast).

If it is argued that— based on the definitions of terms such as *pāṣaṇḍa* found in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, *Skandapurāṇa*, and others, which describe those devoted to theft, adultery, and so forth— the term *pāṣaṇḍa* in the passage "the *pāṣaṇḍa*, the outcaste (*patita*), and the *vrātya*" refers specifically to them— that is not so; for the word *pāṣaṇḍa* [does not have that exclusive meaning].

The fact that it has a fixed meaning is established through its various etymologies in the Purāṇas, Dharmaśāstras, lexicons, and so forth; furthermore, according to the direction stated in that very lexicon which determines the primary sense, it is demonstrated that being "possessed of all sectarian marks" (*sarvaliṅgitva*) is the basis for the application of the term *pāṣaṇḍa*. This is because of that [lexicon].
Furthermore, because those who worship non-fixed deities, lay devotees (upāsakas), and followers of the Smṛti have already been established as such previously,

their status as possessing that nature cannot be revoked; moreover, since the rule "upon seeing one who does not wear sectarian marks (aliṅgin), one should look at the sun" and so forth renders them invisible [as objects of ritual contact], this is as firm as adamantine cement.
This should be understood as incidental. He resolves [the objection] with the words "not so" (*na hi*) and so forth;
the sense is that there is no contradiction here because it is observed that words have multiple meanings.
Thus, regarding the prohibitive statements cited previously...

This was said while accepting the premise that [the author] is intent on censure; however, let the actual state of affairs be heard with attention. For instance, regarding such statements as "one who belongs to the heretical sect (pāṣaṇḍa) mentioned in the section on the ascetic order (yatyāśrama) is fallen" and so forth:
Whoever wears on his forehead a *tilaka* that is either square or shaped like the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree from the island [of Śrī], no one shall look upon him except in times of distress.

"One who is devoid of wearing the *liṅga* should be abandoned like an outcaste (*antyaja*)," and so forth— there is indeed no [contradiction] between these passages recited in the context of wearing the *liṅga* and those other passages recited in the context of wearing the discus (*cakra*) which are intended to censure [the former].

According to the maxim that "one who intends to censure actually praises," it must be understood that the intent of these passages is solely to praise the respective matters enjoined in their respective contexts; otherwise, [the following would be intended]:
"One may slay even an assailant who has mastered the Vedāntas."

Having demonstrated his proficiency in investigation through debate with those who hold opposing views—employing both logical reasoning and the method of *abhyupagama-vāda* (provisional acceptance) as appropriate for refuting contradictions—he now states the actual intended meaning of the disparaging statements, based on the principle that "partiality toward the truth is indeed the very nature of the intellect": "The state of affairs, however, is as follows... The underlying intention is this:

Regarding the Vedic statement, "Others than cows and horses are not cattle; cows and horses alone are cattle," although it declares that elephants, buffaloes, and the like—despite being characterized by the quality of being cattle—are not [true] cattle, its purport does not lie in the negation of their status as cattle.
Rather, its intent is to show that such is the greatness of cows and horses that even other animals are [considered] cattle only in comparison to them.

The Mīmāṃsakas postulate that the intent of such statements as "elephants and so forth are called non-animals" is solely for the purpose of praising cows and horses. This is expressed thus: "Indeed, a censure does not intend to censure;
rather, it praises that which is to be praised. By this very logic, [the statement] regarding one who is devoid of wearing the *liṅga* [applies].

Regarding such statements as, "Upon seeing Śaivas, Pāśupatas, heretics, outcasts, those who have fallen from their caste, those bearing the discus-mark, or those bearing sectarian marks— such as the heated discus and so forth— one should not eat the food of a sage," these were made by those who, based on their own respective doctrines, reviled other systems of thought.
In this Kali Yuga, there will be many excellent twice-born men who sell the fruits of austerity and sacrifice, as well as many ascetics.
With white teeth, their senses conquered, shaven-headed and wearing saffron robes,
Śūdras will practice the dharma when the end of the Yuga has arrived.
Thus, according to the statement in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"Those intent on bad food, foul speech, and improper acceptance of gifts;
those of wicked pastimes and evil conduct, corrupted by vain pride."
And ascetics, out of a desire for wealth, will act as monastery superintendents;
devoted to village life, they will be experts in mechanical devices, mantras, and tantras.

Those who delight in the instruction of *raṇḍās* (unmarried women) and are intent on conversing with them should be understood as having their primary purpose in praising their own views according to the circumstances, and not in censuring them;
otherwise, there would be no way for those practitioners who possess true devotion to the Supreme Lord.

How could their censurability be established? For those who practice dharma through hypocrisy are indeed deceivers, and it is for this very reason that they are censured by everyone; thus, since their censurability pertains to them within their own respective systems, there is no occasion for censure regarding those systems themselves.
Consequently, these statements do not contradict one another when taken according to their own intended meanings.
Thus, it is well-established that there is no contradiction [between our position and the scriptures]. Otherwise, regarding the phrase "of the fruits of austerity, sacrifice,

and so forth," the word "otherwise" refers to those statements found in Vaiṣṇava and other texts— such as "the Śaivas, the Pāśupatas," and so on— which indicate that other doctrines are to be rejected.
The meaning is that one accepts [the text] as having the sole purpose of praising one's own doctrine;

the result is the admission that its purpose is for one's own sake. This connects with the phrase "because this would lead to the undesirable consequence of even ascetics being censurable. This is because of the statement by this author:
In this Kali Yuga, many of the best of the twice-born will become sellers of the fruits of austerity, sacrifice, and other such merits, and there will also be many ascetics.
With white teeth, their senses conquered, shaven-headed and wearing saffron robes,
Śūdras will practice the Dharma when the end of the Yuga has arrived.
Devoted to bad food, foul speech, and improper acceptance of gifts;
engaged in evil pastimes and misconduct, they are defiled by vain pride.
And ascetics will assume the position of monastery superintendents out of a desire for wealth;
devoted to village leadership, they will be experts in mechanical devices, mantras, and tantras.
Devoted to instructing widows and intent on conversing with them,
they act as teachers to everyone while being themselves utterly devoid of detachment.
Those who instruct all [others] are themselves devoid of dispassion.
Ascetics will become deceivers with a desire for gold;
driven by craving, they will wander everywhere through cities and other places.
A yogi who daily consumes these— ghee, milk, curd, and rice cooked with milk— becomes intoxicated and falls from his state.
Some here, wearing saffron robes, are libertines amidst the objects of the senses;
they carry single staves or triple staves, have shaven heads, and are deceivers of the world.
Others are devoted solely to their genitals and bellies, while others are addicted to prostitutes;
some are hypocrites and atheists, merely wearing the outward garb in vain.
Some perform service to kings, while others drink blood;
O Indra among kings, they eat flesh and, filled with pride, they drink wine.
"By the mere sight of them, a man incurs sin"—
since such statements from the Skanda and Āditya Purāṇas would result in the condemnation of even ascetics (yatīs). And thus,
[this applies] to those who perform all Vedic rites and are renowned as worthy recipients of gifts and so forth.
Ascetics with golden-like intentions will become beggars for Vaiṣṇavas, Smārtas, and Ānandatīrthīyas— those ascetics who are worshipped by many people—
and they will wander everywhere through cities and other places out of greed.
A yogi who daily consumes these— honey, milk, curd, and rice boiled with milk— becomes heedless and falls from his state.
Some wearers of the saffron robe here are libertines regarding sense-objects;
they carry single staves or triple staves, have shaven heads, and are deceivers of the world.
Others were devoted solely to their genitals and bellies, while others were addicted to prostitutes;
some were hypocrites and atheists, and indeed some merely wore the outward garb [of religion] in vain.
From this, it is understood that sentences teaching prohibited conduct have no *tātparya* (intentional focus) upon their own literal meaning.

However, this is extremely improper, because these sentences do indeed have *tātparya* regarding their own literal meaning. If you argue, "What is the harm if the blameworthiness of many people born in the Kali age is thereby established?"—[we reply: they certainly exist.

Those born in the Kali age are generally blameworthy and of reprehensible conduct; indeed, their sinful deeds will not become meritorious merely by accepting them, for the nature of reality cannot be altered. Nor will association with prostitutes attain the status of dharma simply because many people are attached to them.

Furthermore, if all [beings] were invisible, it would result in the destruction of the boundaries of phenomenal existence (*prapañca*); moreover, it would contradict the Vedas, Śāstras, Purāṇas, Āgamas, and Itihāsas, which enjoin them as performers of various rituals, givers of gifts, and recipients of offerings— so enough of this "digging of a mountain to catch a mouse."

Now, even if it be granted that the wearing of the *liṅga* is not censurable according to the aforementioned Smṛtis, nevertheless, in the section on Brahmins in the *Amarakośa*, it is stated: "A hypocrite is one who makes a living by his [ascetic] marks (*liṅgavṛtti*), while one who has broken his vow is called *avakīrṇī*. Thus, regarding the term *liṅgavṛtti*:

One who has the banner or sign of Dharma—meaning one whose emblem is like that of Dharma itself because it is recited among the prohibited names—is a *dharmadhvajī*. One whose very livelihood (*vṛtti*) consists in the wearing of the outward marks (*liṅga*) is a *liṅgavṛtti*;
this is the name for one whose means of subsistence is characterized by false practice. Furthermore, one who has stumbled or lapsed (*kīrṇa*) from another vow...
Therefore, this text is indeed inconsistent;
nevertheless, because it is impossible to maintain the purpose of all injunctions and prohibitions, [it must now be treated] as requiring expiation (*prāyaścittiya*).
It must somehow be reconciled by interpreting it as meaning that since almost no one becomes liberated, one should simply remain indifferent toward those who follow prohibited conduct.
As stated in the *Amarakośa*: "One who displays the banner of dharma, one who lives for the sake of his outward marks, one who has broken his vow, and one whose observances are ruined" (2.7.54).
By the phrase "one who acts as a *liṅgin*," there is no inclusion of those who wear the *liṅga* out of devotion for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord; rather,
it refers to one whose vow is broken (*avakīrṇin*), that is, one whose observance is impaired (*kṣatavrataḥ*), meaning one whose student celibacy (*brahmacarya*) has been lost.

If it is argued that wearing the *liṅga* (ascetic marks) is indeed blameworthy— because in the *Liṅgavṛtti* section of the *Bhaṭṭīya*, which serves as a commentary on [the verse] "those who are called by names," the term *liṅgavṛtti* is explained as referring to those who live by false practices— we say no; for in the *Manusmṛti*:

Having disregarded those who are censurable, as described by such passages as: "One who carries the banner of Dharma while always being greedy, hypocritical, a deceiver of the world, one who acts like a cat, violent, and a reviler of all" (4.195).
"He who, being without the marks [of his order], lives off the livelihood of one wearing the marks—
such a person bears the sin of those wearing the marks and is born into the womb of an animal"—
thus, in the immediately preceding Smṛti, even a Brāhmaṇa who merely wears the outward marks [is addressed].

Having heard that he maintains the rule, "I shall give only to those of my own caste food, gold, and so forth," a certain rogue—a follower of the Smṛtis—enters his house in the guise of one wearing deceptive sectarian marks;
having taken the food, gold, and other goods, he lives off them. He arrives at the time of midday.

According to the ancient verse which states that a guest, having eaten food in the house of the host, departs after giving his own web of merit to him and taking away the cage of the host's sins, this man as well,
wearing a deceptive disguise, took upon himself the cage of his [the host's] sins.

Since the word *vṛtti* is well-known in the sense of "livelihood," it would be improper to accept [the gift] solely for the purpose of livelihood by means of indicating a deity; thus he says, beginning with "mā bhūt," and this also refutes the interpretation composed by Liṅgabhaṭṭa.

It goes [to hell] because it causes the violation of a religious observance (*niyama*). Furthermore, since it has been stated that one is subsequently born in the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*), the word *liṅgavṛtti* as read in the *Amarakośa* must necessarily also refer to that same [transgression]. Thus, it is not [the case that the word refers to something else].

This refers specifically to those Brāhmaṇas who wear the *liṅga* obtained through initiation (*dīkṣā*) performed by a Guru; for this very reason, the commentary composed by Liṅgābhaṭṭa—that these are names for those whose livelihood is characterized by false practice—is also consistent. As for the statements in the Purāṇas:

Some statements from the Skanda Purāṇa and the Liṅga Purāṇa have already been cited as supplements to Vedic texts such as "He establishes all forms" (*sarvaliṅgaṃ sthāpayati*). Other injunctions prescribing the wearing of the *liṅga* are also quoted here. Among them, first, in the Padma Purāṇa:

In the Śivagītā Upaniṣads, when the Blessed One, the beloved of Lopāmudrā, had approached Rāmacandra— who was overwhelmed by the separation from Sītā— the sage, having saluted him, [described] the means for pacifying the suffering born of separation from one's beloved,
as well as the severing of the throat of the Ten-necked one (Rāvaṇa), who was surrounded by a host of younger brothers such as Kumbhakarṇa.

Having stated that [liberation] depends upon the grace of Paramaśiva, and having performed the initiation of Manu for the sake of obtaining that grace by means of the *Śivasahasranāma*, the essence of the Vedas,
Mahādeva was directly perceived while being worshipped with these names.

By the concluding passage, "He will grant you divine missiles, weapons, and the like; therefore, unite with him," the sentences are of clear meaning and thus are not further explained. Furthermore, [the text] states that having spoken, "Having slain Rāvaṇa, you shall recover Sītā," he vanished.
Then the joy of the Raghus, together with his younger brother, desired to give up his life;
the husband of Lopāmudrā, having perceived this, arrived at his presence.
Beginning with "Having spoken thus," and continuing until "when that best of sages had gone to his own hermitage," and then stating in the subsequent chapter:
"Then Rāma, on the holy mountain of Rāmagiri, on the bank of the Godāvarī..."
Having installed the Śivaliṅga and having performed the initiation according to the prescribed rule.
With all his limbs adorned with sacred ashes and endowed with ornaments of rudrākṣa beads,
he was consecrated with the holy waters originating from the confluence of the Gautamī and the Sindhu.
Having worshipped him likewise with wild flowers and wild fruits as well,
he remained seated upon a tiger-skin seat, covered in ashes and sleeping upon ashes.
Reciting the thousand names day and night with undistracted mind.
Having thus described the power of the asceticism of the son of Daśaratha with these and other words, [the text] immediately thereafter states:
"Then, on the holy Rāmagiri, on the bank of the Godāvarī, Rāma,
having installed a Śiva-liṅga and having performed the initiation according to the prescribed rites..."
With all his limbs adorned with ashes and equipped with ornaments of rudrākṣa beads,
he was consecrated with the holy waters originating from the confluence of the Gautamī and the Sindhu.
Having worshipped him with wild flowers and likewise with wild fruits,
covered in ashes, sleeping on ashes, seated upon a tiger-skin seat,
he recited the Thousand Names day and night with undivided mind.
Thus, due to the power of the difficult penance performed by Agastya— which was the cause for Rāmacandra’s asceticism as shown in the *Śivagītā*— the Supreme Śiva appeared in person,
bestowed upon him divine weapons and missiles such as the Pāśupata, and gave instruction in the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
Thus it was stated. And so, following the demonstration of the path of devotion (*bhakti-mārga*) as the unique cause of liberation in the *Śiva-Rāghava-saṃvāda*, [it is said]:
"O best of the Raghus, I have thus proclaimed the yoga of devotion; act accordingly."
Since I grant all desires, what else do you wish to hear from me?
When Paramaśiva had spoken thus—
on the occasion of defining who is qualified and who is unqualified following the instruction bestowed by the Blessed One— it was said:
"The ignorant person and the non-devotee are objects of ridicule regarding the wearing of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads."
And those who hate the bearer of the insignia (liṅgin) are not at all qualified for this.

Thus, by stating that those who hate the wearing of the *liṅga* are ineligible for the *pāśupata* initiation, the greatness of the *liṅga*-wearing and of its practitioners is established by implication. Furthermore, in the description of Rāmacandra’s asceticism, it is said,
"having installed the Śiva-liṅga," meaning that he established that liṅga in the middle of a sand altar.
Rāvaṇa:
O Blessed One, this path to liberation has been correctly expounded by you. Tell me who is qualified for it; regarding that, I have a great doubt.
Thus, in response to Rāma’s question: "Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and women are eligible for this;
likewise, whether one is a student (brahmacārī), a householder (gṛhastha), or even a twice-born man who has not yet been initiated."
Whether dwelling in the forest or not dwelling in the forest, the ascetic is one who observes the Pāśupata vow.
What is the use of saying more here? Only he who possesses devotion to the worship of Śiva is qualified for this, and never anyone whose mind is directed elsewhere.
Having thus considered the [lack of] eligibility, he immediately thereafter— though dull-witted, blind, deaf, mute, impure, and devoid of ritual action—
worshipped the Lord of Gaurī with flowers scented by oblations; so says Vālmīki.

Those who mock the ignorant, those who lack devotion, those who harbor hatred toward the wearer of the *liṅga*, and those who mock the wearing of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads— these have no qualification for this practice.

Thus, in the determination of those who lack qualification for liberation, by demonstrating that those who disparage the emblem (liṅga) and the wearer (aṅgin) lack the qualification for liberation— and by showing that those who revile the emblem and the wearer likewise lack qualification—
it follows by implication that those who wear the emblem and whose minds are devoted to it possess the qualification for liberation.
It should be understood that this is established (*siddham*).

Furthermore, according to the maxim "the path is that which has been traveled by the great," [this is confirmed] by the assembly of great sages such as Kaśyapa, Atri, and Bharadvāja, as well as Hiraṇyagarbha, Nārāyaṇa, and others.
Since the assembly of deities, headed by the great powers Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, as well as other highly esteemed beings,
have practiced the wearing of the Śiva-liṅga, its acceptance by Vedic people follows even against one's will.

This is one's own duty. For instance, in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*, the very act of installing [the Liṅga] on a pedestal and so forth is shown, just like the installation of Śiva performed by Rāvaṇa as demonstrated in the *Rāmāyaṇa*. However, the statement "and whoever hates the possessor of the Liṅga" necessarily implies the existence of the Liṅga.
In this way, the great sages such as Kaśyapa, Atri, Bharadvāja, Gautama, and others,
always wear the *liṅga* especially upon their heads.

The passage beginning with "ityādi" and ending with "tribhuvaneśvaram" is a statement from the *Liṅgapurāṇa*. Likewise, [the passages] beginning with "tathoraḥsthale harirliṅgam" and "dhṛtvā mūrdhni pitāmaha" refer to the great sages such as Kaśyapa, Atri, Bharadvāja, Gautama, and others.
They always bear the emblem especially upon their heads.
Even the Lord Nārāyaṇa and the faultless gods, beginning with Brahmā,
wear the flawless Śiva-liṅga upon their heads.

"Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and the other principal goddesses, with vigilance, bear upon the upper part of their own foreheads the Liṅga that is the Lord of the three worlds. Thus it is stated in the Śaṅkara-saṃhitā of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Hari, having placed the Liṅga upon his chest, and Pitāmaha, having placed it upon his head,
both attained their respective stations after propitiating me who resides within the Liṅga.
Having placed my male organ upon their heads and other limbs, the gods, led by Śakra,
worshipped me situated within that linga and returned each to his own abode.
"Having respectfully worn my liṅga upon their own bodies, the goddesses, headed by Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, attained supreme bliss through absorption in it.
Thus [it is said] in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*.

"The gods, such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and the sages, such as Gautama and others," together with Śaṅkara— these two statements from the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, beginning with "The gods, such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and the sages, such as Gautama and others" (6.55), constitute three sentences.
Even in the absence of words that explicitly enjoin the rule, they indicate the duty of wearing the *liṅga* by observing the conduct of great people: "Having worshipped Raudra,
they always wear the *liṅga* upon their heads, especially so."
"All powers, such as Lakṣmī and the others, being permeated by devotion to Śiva, bear the Śivaliṅga upon the tips of their foreheads day and night. (6.55–56).
And in this regard: "Either on the head or on the neck..."

The wearing of the *liṅga* by the celestial sages (*devarṣis*) is clearly established by such statements, which first demonstrate the specific locations for wearing the *liṅga*. In the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*:
"Having first worshipped a beautiful stone *liṅga* of Rudra with his own devotion, Hari..."
He has indeed attained that supreme state, the foremost and most difficult to reach, belonging to Viṣṇu.
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"Brahmā constantly worships the auspicious linga made of stone;
by the worship of which alone the supreme state of Brahmahood was attained."
Śakra, the king of the gods, also constantly worships the auspicious linga made of jewels with devotion; by that, he attained the status of Śakra.
Viṣṇu always worships a linga made of sapphire;
by that means he attained the state of Viṣṇu and the eternal Vaikuṇṭha.
Soma [worships] a liṅga made of pearls; Dhanada, a liṅga made of gold;
Vāyu, a liṅga made of bell-metal; and the Vasus, a liṅga made of bronze.

For, according to such passages from the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa* and other texts as "In the beginning, Hari [worshipped] a beautiful stone *liṅga* through his own devotion," there is liberation through the worship of a stone *liṅga* or a sapphire (*indranīla*) *liṅga* of Rudra; through the worship of a stone [image] of Viṣṇu;
through the worship of a gem-encrusted [image] of Brahmā; and through the worship of a pearl [image] of Śakra.
From the worship of the Moon with a golden image, from the worship of Kubera with a stone image,
from the worship of Śiva’s liṅga, from the worship of Vāyu with a bell-metal liṅga, and from the worship of the Vasus with a crystal liṅga.
The Aśvins and the Maruts [worship] a crystal liṅga with devotion;
Divākara [worships] one made of copper, and the Pannagas one of coral.
The Asuras [worship] a phallic emblem made of black iron, and the Piśācas likewise one made of straw;
in this manner do the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
"They always worship the Liṅga of Īśāna, the leader of the gods.
Thus [it is said]. In the Parāśara Purāṇa:
"Mahāviṣṇu, with devotion, [worshipped] a pure Liṅga of Rudra made of stone."
Having worshipped Cārucitra, he attained the supreme state.
