In the Droṇaparva of the Mahābhārata:
"The God of gods, whose nature is inconceivable, the invincible and imperishable Viṣṇu,
having recognized Bhava as the form of all, worships that Lord in the liṅga."
"In him, the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) bestows exceeding affection.
Thus [it is said]. In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "The agency of creation belongs to Brahmā; the crushing of the Dānavas belongs to Viṣṇu."
"Indra obtained sovereignty over heaven from the worship of the Śiva-liṅga;
the Aśvins [obtained it] from the worship of one made of copper; Divākara from the worship of a coral liṅga;
the Pannagas from the worship of a liṅga made of black iron; and the Asuras from the worship of a liṅga made of mercury."

By means of making known to the Piśācas the attainment of their respective offices, it is indicated that all the gods are worshippers of Śiva in their respective Śivaliṅgas, and that they possess proximity to their desired Śivaliṅgas.
Likewise, the statement found in the Droṇaparvan of the Mahābhārata, beginning with "having known the origin of all beings from Bhava," and so forth, [confirms this].
This must be explained. Now,
it may be argued that here, according to the statements of the *Mahābhārata*, *Brahmavaivarta*, *Āditya Purāṇa*, and other texts,
all the gods and others [are established] specifically in the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth for the sake of attaining their respective fruits.

If it is argued that since the worship of the Śiva-liṅga has been prescribed, how can those scriptural statements be intent upon the worship of a liṅga worn on the body? This is not so; for in the Skanda, Liṅga, and other Purāṇas, the various locations for wearing it—such as the head, the neck, and so forth—are first demonstrated.
Furthermore, because the worship of the hand-throne (*karapīṭha*) by those who bear the *liṅga* has been established through the injunctions for wearing the *liṅga*,
it is impossible for statements in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts to refer to the worship of the Śiva-liṅga on a wooden throne or similar supports, as that would contradict such injunctions.

"Only on the seats (pīṭha), etc."— in reality, it is appropriate to accept this [interpretation] there, because there is no fruit in the audacious attempt to consolidate all the expressed meanings found in the eighteen Purāṇas and the Itihāsas such as the Mahābhārata into a single meaning. There are many statements...
There exist many [texts] proclaiming the majesty of the jyotirliṅgas, such as Somanātha, Mallikārjuna, and Kedāreśvara;
there are also many that teach the majesty of worshipping Śivaliṅgas installed on altars (vedi).
To establish that all of these concern one's chosen liṅga (iṣṭaliṅga) would result in the invalidation of the proponent.

Therefore, since this very point is established by the statements of the *Liṅgapurāṇa*, the *Kāmikāgama*, and other scriptures as enjoining worship with the hand as the locus, the proof that Nārāyaṇa, Indra, and others wear the *liṅga* becomes as firm as adamantine cement.
Moreover,
I bow to that Lord,
whose linga the hosts of Maruts, with Indra as their chief, worship day and night together with their wives.

Thus, by the statement from the *Cidambarasaṃhitā* in the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*, the wearing of the *liṅga* by Indra and the other gods is established directly as well. In that regard, according to the rule "the root *yaj* [is used] in the senses of sacrificing, worshipping a deity, forming an alliance, and giving" (*bhvādi* class, 1002), from the verbal root *yaj*:

The meaning is that the gods, the hosts of Maruts headed by Indra (indrajyeṣṭhā indrapramukhā), together with their wives, generate— that is, they maintain through an inseparable relationship— the *liṅga* which constitutes the body of Śiva, for the purpose of establishing a connection characterized by [the nature of] relation (*sambandha-rūpa-saṅgati-karaṇārthatvena*).

It is appropriate for the authors of the scriptures to establish this. Indeed, there are more than a thousand scriptural statements regarding the methods of worshipping Śiva in the form of the Liṅga; thus, no one has any dispute on this point.
In this very way— I bow to that Lord,
whose linga the hosts of Maruts, with Indra as their chief, worship day and night together with their wives.

Thus, even the recourse to the laborious effort of establishing that the root *yaj* in the statement of the *Cidambarasaṃhitā* has the sense of "conjunction" (*saṅgati*), based on the entry in Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha which shows the meanings of the root *yaj* as "sacrifice," "worship of the gods," "conjunction," and "giving" (*yajadevapūjāsaṅgatikaraṇadāneṣu*, 1002, *bhvādi*).

For those who possess discernment, no conviction arises regarding the meaning "they worship" for the phrase "they sacrifice in vain"— an interpretation that would be more consistent with the extremely well-known sense of "they revere"— because there exist many other sentences that establish their own literal meanings,
and because interpreting a single sentence in such a strained manner [would undermine them].
Furthermore, there is no purpose in establishing that [the Lord] is suitable for one's own worship.
Now, even so, in the case of Indra and others, during the time of worshipping a *liṅga* made of jewels and the like upon a golden pedestal,
there is even an occasional connection with the application of sandalwood paste and so forth.

If it is asked how the meaning "they maintain" is established through an inseparable connection, given that the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) has as its primary sense the performance of an action, [the answer is: because of the words *ahar*,
which denote the duration of the day, and *niśā*, which denotes the time of night alone.

Because, in the context of the verbal root *yaj*, once the accomplishment of perpetual retention is established, that [retention] is established precisely through an inseparable relationship; and even if the root *yaj* has the sense of "forming a connection," although it is established that such a connection lasts for the duration of day and night, one continues to sacrifice internally.

In the same way, one might raise the objection that when a Śiva-liṅga made of jewels and so forth is worshipped by Indra and others upon a golden pedestal and the like, the inseparable relationship [of the deity] cannot be established because the meaning of connection denoted by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is fulfilled through the application of the hand and the anointing with sandalwood paste. Anticipating this, he says: "Day and night."

Since the word *ahaḥ* (day) within that compound denotes a full day and the word *niśā* (night) denotes a full night, the meaning must be accepted as "in the case of time or distance, when there is uninterrupted connection" (*kāladhvanor atyantasaṃyoge*). Consequently, the wearing of large thumb-marks (*sthūlāṅgaliṅga*) by them is not established [by this rule].

The word "antaḥ" (inside) must be supplied [in the compound], because its presence is not observed in the actual statement, which would otherwise result in the fault of *adhyāhāra* (unnecessary supplementation); for instance,
in the phrase "having placed my emblem on a limb such as the head," the word "antaḥ" serves to provide the specific locative qualification.
And because of the requirement of those [scriptural] statements:

as for the scriptural statements enjoining the wearing of the *liṅga* and the performance of worship for as long as one lives, some have already been cited; others are likewise to be sought within the scriptures beginning with the *Kāmika* and ending with the *Vātula*. They are not presented here for fear of prolixity.
They are written as follows:

by virtue of the second case (*dvitīyā*) prescribed by the rule *dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.5)— which signifies "extreme connection" (*atyantasaṃyoga*)— it serves to convey the sense of being the substratum for the life of the devotee, thereby establishing the pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) of that state throughout both day and night.
If it is objected: "Since the scriptures (āgamas) lack authority, how can the wearing of the *liṅga* and other practices taught by them possess authority?
We reply: No. One who asserts the lack of authority of the scriptures must be asked:
Is it the lack of authority of all scriptures without exception, or only those beginning with the *Kāmika* and ending with the *Vātula*?
By the statement "the Śiva-āgamas are proclaimed by Śiva," the lack of authority of the twenty-eight Śaiva Āgamas— well-known as being composed by Paramaśiva— is [asserted],
as is [the lack of authority] of the sacrificial violence performed by Buddhas and others who are specific incarnations of Nārāyaṇa.

It cannot be the first [reason], because of its being a means for accomplishing *adharma*; and also because of such statements as: "There is no mantra higher than the Gāyatrī, no mantra other than the Aghora, and there is no reality higher than the Guru" (*Mañjūṣāsārasaṃgraha* 35).

The resolution is that through the constant performance of great mantras such as the Gāyatrī, the Mother of the Vedas, and so forth, and through worship in the form of establishing a connection [with the deity], an inseparable relationship is established; furthermore,

this serves as the resolution for the suspicion that [the goal] might be accomplished otherwise by the wearing of internal marks (antarliṅgadhāraṇa), which would involve the fault of supplying missing words (adhyāhāra).
It must be understood that the proponent who asserts the invalidity of scripture (āgama) should be questioned. Here,
the intention of the text— which introduces three alternative positions (vikalpa) before presenting its own conclusion— is as follows:
In all the imagined kalpas, there is a lack of authority for all the scriptures;
thus, [the sequence is] birth, life, and thereafter striking and awakening,
then consecration, purification, and nourishment.
Satisfying (tarpaṇa), kindling (dīpana), and concealment (gupti)—these ten are the consecrations of mantra.
[The mantras] ending with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* correspond to the heart and the other limbs.
These are the "sprouts" (pallavas) of the mantras.
The "sprout" of the mantras is said to be the foot, and the "head" is the *praṇava*.
A mantra joined with its head and sprout bestows the desired fruit.
One should place the *ṛṣi* on the head, the *chandas* on the mouth, and the *devatā* on the heart;
one should place the *bīja-śakti* on the *ādhāra* and the *kīlaka* on the two feet.
Mute, asleep, dead, naked, devoid of potency,
fruitless, like a serpent, pinned down, or empty— mantras such as these are fruitless.
Without the ritual placement (nyāsa), one becomes mute; without the seat (āsana), one is as if asleep;
without the "sprout" (pallava), the mantra is proclaimed to be naked.

A mantra devoid of its head is said to be dead; a mantra without a guru is useless. A mantra bereft of its seer (ṛṣi), deity (daivata), and meter (chandas) is a mere serpent. Furthermore, there is the invalidity of the Kalpas—the scriptures beginning with the Kāmika and ending with the Vātula—and such is the nature of the Kalpa.
No believer whatsoever can deny the following, which have been accepted as authoritative by the entire community of believers:

the rule for the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) of mantras such as the *Gāyatrī*; the rule for initiation (*dīkṣā*) involving *tāntrika* mantras; and the technical terminology found in the *Āgamas*, such as "head" (*śiras*) and "sprout" (*pallava*), which constitute parts of the mantra.
Because it is being examined,
there remains that which is given to a wicked person after death, as well as that which is devoid of potency and has extra syllables.
When the interval is pervaded by more than one seed-syllable, it is said to be "pinned" (kīlita).
A mantra which another person hears while it is being recited is said to be "void" (śūnya).

By these and other [passages], [the text] establishes the rituals for birth, life, and so forth; the consecrations (*saṃskāra*) such as *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*; the "sprouts" (*pallava*) of mantras; the defects of mantras such as muteness and dormancy; the means of removing those defects; and the purification of the seat (*āsana-śuddhi*), and so on.
If the words contained within those respective Āgamas were invalid,
then the constant practice of great mantras such as the Gāyatrī, as well as rites like the *punar-caraṇa*, would be unestablished;
nor is the second [alternative] tenable.
And for those virtuous ones who possess knowledge and dharma and have undergone the Śiva-consecration,
the Śaiva [tradition] is declared and remembered as having twenty-eight divisions.
Kāmika, Yogaja, Cintya, and likewise Ajita as the cause;
Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Aṃśumat, and Suprabhedaka.
And likewise Vijaya, Niśvāsa, Svāyambhuva, and Anala;
as well as Vīra, Raurava, Makuṭa, and Vimala.
The Candrajñāna, the Bimba, the Prodgīta, and likewise the Lalita;
the Siddha, the Santāna spoken by Śarva, and also the Pārameśvara.
The Vātula and the Kiraṇa—these are the twenty-eight Saṃhitās.
Thus, in the Āgamas, the Vedas, and the Vedānta Upaniṣads,
the great Dharma of liberation pertaining to Maheśvara has been proclaimed according to the scriptures.

Thus, according to the method taught in the Vīrāgama, if the Śaiva Āgamas— which are renowned as the means to liberation— were invalid, then [so would be] Śiva, the Śaiva Āgama, the Śaiva dharma, the acceptance of Śiva, the living liṅga (jaṅgama),
the identity with the prāṇaliṅga, and the worship of the Śivaliṅga, O Guha.
In all the abodes of Śiva, such as Vārāṇasī and others,
he whose intellect becomes perverted is a man who remains outside.
For that fool who is intent on reviling Śiva and who censures the scriptures of Śiva,
no expiation has been seen anywhere, even in any scripture, by anyone.
Thus,
by such statements from the *Skānda*, *Śivadharma-Uttara*, and other texts which indicate expiatory rites (*niṣkṛti*) such as penance ending in death,
it is not appropriate to raise objections against the censure of matters that lack authoritative basis.
Furthermore,

regarding the twelve purificatory rites (saṃskāras) to be performed at the time of the consecration of both stationary and mobile liṅgas— the construction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the pavilion (maṇḍapa), as well as each of those respective purificatory rites— [these are described here].
There shall also be worship of the site (vāstupūjā) and an oblation (havana) established within the offering-pots (pālikās).
In the specific locations such as the lower plank (*adhaḥpaṭṭikā*) and so forth, up to the *ājyapratārikā*, there are worlds [of the Rudras];

if those [texts] were not authoritative, then due to the absence of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth prescribed therein, the daily obligatory duties (*nitya-karma*) of all Vedic people would be lost.
Furthermore, in the commentary composed by the venerable Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya:
Having thus distinguished Paramaśiva as an ocean of jewels consisting of an infinite multitude of auspicious qualities such as limbs and parts, this text asks, "What are those limbs? and answers:
"Omnipresence, contentment, beginningless consciousness, absolute freedom, and eternal imperishability."
And the infinite power of the All-pervading One—those who know the ritual rules call these the six limbs of Maheśvara.

Knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, austerity, power, forgiveness, fortitude, the capacity for creation, self-awareness, and indeed the state of being a presiding controller. (Vāyu Purāṇa 12.31; Kūrma Purāṇa 2.8.13)
These ten indeclinables always abide in Śaṅkara.
Thus,

through the statements of the Śaiva Āgamas defining the limbs and members [of the mantra], as found in works such as the *Prapañcasāra* composed by Śaṅkarācārya, the six-syllabled mantra of Tryambaka— *oṃ tryambakaṃ yajāmahe*... [is established].

Furthermore, since the determination [of this matter] has already been accomplished by the words of the scriptures themselves, it would result in contradiction with them; for the authors of the Bhāṣyas do not cite statements that lack authoritative foundation. Thus, [regarding the views of] Vyāsa, Manu, and others:
"Among humans, I am a Brāhmaṇa; I am a Brāhmaṇa."

Furthermore, because the authority of the Āgamas composed by Paraśiva— who is renowned as a Brahmarṣi in the passage "Rudra, the great seer, superior to all" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.4)— and who is established as eternal in the passage "faultless and stainless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19), cannot be set aside.
The last alternative is not tenable,
because at the time Viṣṇu assumed his world-deluding form, he possessed the quality of deluding the entire universe,
and furthermore, even in his own nature, he experienced the bewilderment born of separation from Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa during his incarnations as Rāma and others.
Regarding the lack of authority of those scriptures that deceive others, which claim to be incarnations of the Buddha and contradict the Vedas, we accept the consequence as desired (*iṣṭāpatti*).
Now, [it may be argued] in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
Thus urged by Mādhava, the enemy of Mura, Rudra composed the treatises on delusion; and Keśava, likewise impelled by Śiva, did the same.
"The Kapāla, Lākula, Śākta, Bhairava, Pūrvapaścima,
Pāñcarātra, Pāśupata, and likewise thousands of others"— thus,
by establishing that both Śiva and Keśava are the authors of delusive scriptures (*mohaśāstra*), as well as others...
By the word "thousands," the Śaiva Āgamas are also included; for it was previously stated by me: "The auspicious Pāśupata vow was indeed established by me in the past.
The third section [concerns] the lack of authority of the scriptures composed by the circles of atheists, such as the Buddhas, Jinists, and others.
In this regard, just as it is for you, so too for us there is simply the acceptance of the fact that even though the Buddhist and other scriptures lack authority,
the Śaiva Āgama is more secret than the secret, subtle, the essence of the Vedas, and leads to liberation.
"This Pāśupata conduct is to be practiced by those seeking liberation" (2.37.141,
143). Having thus established the Vedic authority of the Āgama which expounds the Pāśupata vow consisting of the wearing of Rudrākṣa beads and the Liṅga;
"Indeed, other Śaiva scriptures in this world are delusive;
they have been spoken by me alone, for they are contrary to the teachings of the Vedas.
Having said this—
"The Vāma, Pāśupata, Sauma, Lākula, and Bhairava—these are said not to be practiced, as they are outside the Vedas and otherwise [heterodox]. (2.37.146).
"Whatever various scriptures are seen in this age,"
For their adherence to practices contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti is indeed of the nature of darkness (tāmasī).
"The Kāpāla, Pāñcarātra, Yāmala, Vāma, and Ārhata—such scriptures as these are for the purpose of delusion. (1.11.272–273).
Thus, it is because [the author] accepts the lack of authority specifically for those works that contradict the Śruti and Smṛti.

This is because it is precisely the Śābara-tantras composed by the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) while wearing the guise of a Kirāta, and the Buddhist and other Āgamas composed by the incarnations of the Buddha, that are being referred to here by the term "others.
If it is asked, "In that case, how can the Śaiva Āgamas be said to consist of the essence of the Śruti and Smṛti?"—

Because it possesses the aforementioned characteristics, it serves as an injunction for the installation of stationary *liṅgas* that fall within the scope of the practices of Gautama, Manu, and others.
This is because [the opponent's position] contradicts the established majesty of Rudrākṣa as proven by the *Kālāgnirudra*, *Rudropaniṣad*, and other texts;
it contradicts the non-duality of the individual soul and Brahman taught by numerous scriptures such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*);
and it contradicts the manifold meanings [of the term] refuted by scriptures such as the *Chāndogya* and *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*.

Thus concludes the section on the invalidity of the authority of the venerable Nandi— the fierce five-faced lion who shatters the frontal globes of the elephant of Advaita, and who is the essence of the illustrious Vedas, Vedāntas, Purāṇas, Āgamas, and Itihāsas, and the crest-jewel of the illustrious Viśiṣṭādvaita school.
Composed by the Great Mahopādhyāya, Paṇḍita Śrī Śivakumāra Miśra Śāstrin— this is completed.
The Second Part:
Now, even if the wearing of the *liṅga* is established by this much, the cremation rite for a deceased Brāhmaṇa is prescribed [in the scriptures],
whereas your practiced method of burial is not prescribed anywhere.

If it is asked, "How is that established?", it is said: in the *Ṛgveda*, its establishment is through the mantra, "O Kardama, let offspring be born from me; O Kardama, come into being" (*Ṛk Saṃhitā* 5.87.11).
By "Kardama," [is meant] the earth (*pṛthivī*); [from it arise] the various millions of living beings, such as animals, humans, and so forth.

The beings were born. By the use of the word *kardama*, which denotes a lump of clay mixed with water, [the text] begins the discussion on the necessity of wearing the *liṅga* as a subordinate element within the earth, which serves as the primary material cause (*pradhānopādāna*).

In the first part [of this work], many matters have been established, culminating in the authority of the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Āgamas* such as the *Kāmika*, which constitute the foundation for the wearing of the *liṅga*. Now, regarding the funeral rites (*pratipatti*) consisting of the burial of the body in the earth, which are performed according to the doctrine of those who wear the *liṅga* after their passing:
An authoritative source is cited: "By the mud, creatures were born" (Ṛgveda 5.87).

It should be understood that this refers to cooperative agency (*sahakāritva*), because in its absence, mere earth in a solidified state would lack the utility for the construction of a body. With respect to such earth, by means of a deceased person...
It is prayed for thus: "O Kardama, arise within me!"— O Earth, whose nature is that of a moist lump of clay, when my death arrives through the ripening of time,
[arise] within my body situated in the womb, which is known by the alternative name of the thirty-two-jointed *yuk-samādhi*.

The meaning is: having concealed [me] from rebirth and caused me to reach a state of dissolution, please bring about my attainment of the highest world preceded by the cessation of all evil. [And likewise: the goddess Earth, the wife of Viṣṇu, who is undecaying.
By means of the two *ṛg* verses beginning with "The goddess Earth, the wife of Viṣṇu" (*Tai0 Brā0* 3.1.2.6),

and by the mantra recited in the *nakṣatreṣṭi* sacrifice— "We worship her, the western one, with oblation"— the accomplishment of the digging is also effected. Here, the body of the deceased person [is placed] by the performer together with his kinsmen and relatives.

Having brought [the body] near by means of a palanquin or similar conveyance, after performing whatever consecrations (*saṃskāra*) are to be done there, this verse is employed for the act of entering the pit; its meaning is: "We worship this Goddess Earth with an oblation (*havis*) consisting of the body of the deceased person. And likewise in the *Agni*[-purāṇa]:

Just as an oblation such as the *puroḍāśa* cake or clarified butter being offered is consumed, so too there is the possibility that the body, once cast into the cavity of the earth, would simply dissolve right there;
and since such dissolution is untenable unless it is concealed within *samādhi*, this constitutes "accomplishment" (*siddhi*),
which is required by all verbal means of knowledge— including *śruti*, *smṛti*, and so forth— as the basis for grasping their conventional meanings.
Furthermore, its establishment is achieved through the ultimate purport even of the well-known statements in the *Nighaṇṭu* regarding intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*).
For instance, it is said that for a body composed of the five elements, "the law of time is dissolution into the fivefold state" (*pañcatākāladharma*);
thus, the body is initiated by the encapsulation (*saṃpuṭīkaraṇa*) of the five elements, and [its end occurs] by virtue of the ripening of time.
When the state of dissolution into the five [elements] occurs, it is necessary to unify the five members within the five gross elements (*pañcabhūta*).
In that regard, since air and space are imperceptible, their inclusion is not suitable for practical application; therefore, the conjunction should be performed only among earth, water, and fire.

In that regard as well, since fire and water are supported by the earth, it is necessary to perform the conjunction of the principles (*tattvasaṃyojana*) by depositing them specifically within the earth, which is the support of all. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Parāśarasmṛti*:
"One should unite the body, known as the five elements, with reality through reality; even therein, union within the element of earth is the means to liberation.
Furthermore, at the end [of life], for those who have undergone the consecration by fire, the body remains a confluence of blood and flesh.

Even when the body is being cremated, it is necessary to cast the remaining bodily parts, such as the bones, onto the surface of the earth or into the waters of the Ganges with the mantra "Go to the earth" (pṛthivīṃ gaccha). Thus, while one part is combustible by fire, the remainder is disposed of in the earth, water, and so forth.
If this were accepted, it would result in the absurdity of meaninglessness; therefore, one must simply cast [the body] upon the earth, which serves as the support for all.
As it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Even when the body has been burnt, that remainder of the limbs is cast either upon the ground or in the water."
"Therefore, the rule of disposal is more powerful because it leaves nothing remaining and there is no further injunction.
Thus, the *Parāśara-smṛti* and other texts stating that "the body is called the five elements" are cited as authoritative evidence.
Furthermore, having raised the objection regarding contradictions with the *śruti* passages and others recited in the section on the *Pitṛmedha* (ancestral rites), [the author proceeds].

Since the cited *śruti*, *smṛti*, and other texts pertain specifically to the case of a Brahmin who has come into contact with the body of the deceased, they do not prescribe a covering of the body in all instances;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the *śruti* passages recited in the *Pitṛmedha* and other rites which enjoin cremation.
It should not be argued that this leads to the consequence of [the injunction] being without a valid object (*nirviṣayatva*),

because— following the authority of the previously cited statements from the *Padmapurāṇa*, Śātātapa, Manu, and other Smṛtis— the general injunctions prescribing digging are [to be understood] according to the "goat and animal" logic (*chāgapaśunyāya*).

Having accepted that the subject matter [of the injunctions] concerns Brāhmaṇas who possess the *liṅga* (signs) and the body [of the deceased], there is no obstacle to restricting the injunctions prescribing cremation to those other than such Brāhmaṇas; otherwise,
[there would be a contradiction with] the injunctions prescribing two separate rites.
Because both would result in being non-Vedic due to their mutual contradiction, the Pitṛmedha passages are established as having a scope distinct from those passages concerning digging,
for there can be no determination of mutually contradictory statements without such an arrangement.
Because the establishment [of the distinction between valid and invalid cognition] is necessary due to the impossibility of [universal] validity;
for this very reason, it was stated by the preeminent knowers of Brahman-vidyā regarding the acceptance of the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman: [in the mirror...]
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree.
One of them eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.6).
"Two Brahmans are to be known: the higher and the lower. (Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad 6.22).

Thus, in the event that difference is accepted despite the contradiction with statements establishing non-difference, he briefly explains even the doctrine of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*) as an incidental digression here, beginning with the words "for this very reason, like a mirror," etc. He says, "because there is no contradiction," referring to such passages as "Two birds, inseparable companions... and so forth. Two...

The meaning is "the two birds" (*suparṇau*). The dual ending is replaced by *ḍā* according to the grammatical rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), and so forth. Here, because the body is described as a tree in passages such as, "They speak of the Aśvattha tree as having its roots above and branches below" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.1), it is the body itself [that is meant].

It is expressed by the word "tree. Just as with worldly birds, the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) are described as birds because they reside within the tree that is the body; thus it is said, "They both embrace the same tree. Both the individual self and the supreme self [embrace] one and the same [tree].
They have taken their stand upon the tree whose form is the body.

Between those two—the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)—it is the other, namely the individual self, who eats the sweet fruit of action; this is an illustration, for according to its own respective karma, it consumes what is either sweet or not sweet. The other...

The Supreme Self, not eating, is unattached to the attributes of the body because its power of consciousness is undiminished due to the absence of ignorance. Thus, being free from the bondage of karma and not experiencing the fruits of karma—neither pleasure nor pain—it shines forth intensely, "abhicākaśīti. In this scriptural passage:
Thus, a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established. Likewise, in the passage "Two Brahmans are to be known:
the higher and the lower," as well as "There is no diversity whatsoever here" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.19), and "Rudra is one alone; he did not stand as a second."

Furthermore, because both [the Smṛti and the Śruti] would consequently result in being invalid due to their contradiction with such scriptural passages enjoining non-duality as: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else, that is the Infinite" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1), and "Where one sees nothing else... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.2).

"Brahman is one only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1); "There is not any diversity here whatsoever" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19); "Other than this, there is no seer; other than this, there is no hearer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23); and so forth, as well as in passages such as "where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).

And since the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established [in other texts], there is a mutual contradiction between the Śrutis; therefore, neither dualism (*dvaita*) nor monism (*advaita*) alone can be accepted, but rather the position of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*) must be maintained.
Its meaning is as follows: "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) and "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*)—the two qualified entities; the non-duality (*advaita*) of the two qualified entities.

Regarding the term *viśiṣṭādvaitam* (qualified non-dualism): here, Brahman qualified by the subtle power of the *cit* (conscious) and *acit* (non-conscious) manifold is denoted by the single term "qualified.
Only the position of qualified non-dualism (*viśiṣṭādvaitapakṣa*) is to be accepted; for in that system, [the relationship between] the gross and subtle conscious and non-conscious...
Because there is no contradiction, as the authority of even dualistic statements is established by taking into account the distinction between the qualifier and the qualified.
Nor should it be said that burning has fire as its object, while digging has a different class of entity as its object.

Since they lack the qualification for performing rituals prescribed by the Vedas, it would result in the absurdity of digging being intended for Brahmins and cremation being intended for other castes;
furthermore, the contradiction with established custom is equal in both cases, so let this suffice. Now, as for the mantras cited:
This very [Brahman], even when characterized by the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*) expansion of consciousness and unconsciousness (*cid-acit-prapañca*), is so described.
When characterized by the power of the gross expansion of consciousness and unconsciousness, it is denoted by the term "non-distinct" (*apara-viśiṣṭa*).
The established conclusion (*siddhānta-svarūpa*) is that there is identity between these two. That is to say, [the identity] of that which has attained the state of grossness.

And for that which has entered into a subtle state, there is only one internal controller (*antaryāmin*), the supreme reality of the Lord (*parameśvara-tattva*), who is the primary regulator. Since He exists in the form of the conscious internal controller of conscious individual souls (*jīvas*),
in relation to Him, [scriptures] state, "There is no other seer than He," and so forth, as well as, "He hears nothing else," and so forth.

The scriptural statement is thus justified. Just as the common usage "Devadatta alone is now at his own home" proceeds even though he is characterized by a multiplicity of things such as body and senses, so too is the teaching "Brahman is one only, without a second" established. As for the verse "Two birds," it is naturally consistent [with this view]; therefore, there is no contradiction for anyone.
He states that there is no contradiction with the Śruti, saying: "Because there is no contradiction.

Hereafter, the author’s intention will be briefly demonstrated regarding the subject of the final rites (*antyakṛtya*), concerning the relationship between the Śruti and Smṛti texts pertaining to the *Pitṛmedha* and the statements of other Śaiva Āgamas and similar works.

If it is argued that, although digging might appear to be applicable at first glance due to the distinction of caste, it lacks the status of a mandatory rite (*vaidha*) because there is no injunctive statement (*vidhi-vākya*) such as "one should dig up a dead man," we say: not so; for there is the injunction, "one should cremate the deceased."

Even in the absence of an explicit injunction, just as one infers an injunction such as "one should cremate the deceased" based on the fulfillment of the requirements for an injunction through the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the various mantras recited in the *Pitṛmedha* and other texts, so too here,
an injunction is inferred due to the fulfillment of the requirements for an injunction by means of the indicative marks of the numerous mantras cited previously.
"Because it is appropriate to assume an injunction stating that 'one should dig up a dead man'"; however,
in reality, after prescribing the wearing of the *liṅga* in the *Sadānanda Upaniṣad* with the words "The *śaiva-liṅga* should be worn on the chest by a Brahmin" (7–8), [the text] states directly:

A definitive rule cannot be established because, in the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*), the opposite could equally be suspected. It should not be suspected that no injunction containing the term "digging" (*khana*) is observed;
for digging is indeed enjoined: "One should cast the pure, stainless bodies into a pit" (10).

The meaning is that one should cast those bodies belonging to Śiva—which are of the nature of the Liṅga—into a pit after death, that is, one should perform the act of digging a grave for them. As stated in another Upaniṣad: "As long as he lives, he dies; then they place him in the earth."

By the word "haranti" (they carry away), digging is prescribed. As long as the living being who is a devotee of Śiva remains alive, he is a *jīva*; then, after death—that is, once he has become dead—one should carry this devotee to the *avanī* (the earth).
The meaning is that, having performed the rite of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) within the womb of the earth, one should effect the removal of the devotee’s body.
Thus it is said. Nor should it be argued that in the passage "they carry [the fire] to the *avani*," the meaning could not be "they carry [it] with fire upon the *avani*";

for this is because [the injunction] "one should give a cow to a Brahmin" and "one should not give a gift to one of one's own lineage" is inferable from the *Smṛtis* and other sources, and there is also an explicit injunction in the *Sadānanda Upaniṣad* and elsewhere.

In the statements of the *Śivadharmaśāstra* and similar texts, just as the Brahmins and others are the recipients (*saṃpradāna*) of the gift of a cow and so forth, this very dative case is employed [to denote the recipient]— as in:
"One should cast the body upon the earth for the sake of the devotees who are Śiva-yogins."
If one performs cremation without knowing [the proper procedure], he falls into hell.
A wise man should not burn the body of anyone who is a devotee of Śiva;

For one who is a devotee of Śiva and has died, there is no cremation or such rites;
for that which is already burnt requires no further burning, nor does that which is already cooked require further cooking.
For those whose bodies have been consumed by the fire of knowledge, there is neither cremation nor ritual action.
Thus, according to the statements of the *Śivadharmaśāstra*, after prohibiting the cremation of devotees, [it prescribes] burial:

This is because it conforms to the statement in the *Vātulāgama*, and because it is appropriate that the body and the *liṅga* dissolve right there, given that both have earth as their material cause (*prakṛti*). Nor should it be argued: "Since the body consists of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*), why could its removal not occur in fire alone? What is called natural death does not occur by one's own will;

For those desiring to abandon their own bodies, the first method is that of the forest, the second consists of fire, and the third is the method of invisibility.
Non-seeing is the best; the non-separation of the limbs and the sexual organ is likewise best. Similarly, digging is best when it is pure within the cavity of the earth.
In the absence of those two, there is combustion, like the union of fire and camphor.

"One who is desirous, capable, learned, whose sons have been born, and who has black hair, shall establish the sacred fires" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*...).
For a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with the means prescribed by such scriptural passages as Bhāṣya 6.1.5,

the performance of sacrifice— which serves as a means for attaining the status of a Brāhmaṇa according to the Śruti text, "By sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22)— is an obligatory duty.

Because the state of being an *āhitāgni* (one who has maintained the sacred fires) is established in the context of defining the wearing of matted hair (*jaṭā*) and sectarian marks (*liṅga*), and because we observe that even among certain modern Pūrvaśaivas who possess the aforementioned means of accomplishment, there is the maintenance of the sacred fires; therefore, this applies to them as well.
If it is argued that since cremation is prohibited [for the liberated soul],

this would contradict the *Kalpasūtra* statement, "Those who have maintained the sacred fires cremate [the deceased] with the sacrificial vessels," because that text prescribes cremation for anyone who has maintained the fires at the time of death using the vessels of the *vaitāna-agni-hotra*, we say: do not think so.

In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*, beginning with the passage "The great sages Kaśyapa, Atri, Bharadvāja, Gautama, and others," it is stated that the great sages such as Kaśyapa and the rest possess the characteristic of wearing the *liṅga* upon their bodies. Furthermore, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* of the *Śivapurāṇa*, it is stated that Kaśyapa and the others were maintainers of the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). In that regard...
As for the deliberation that the ritual procedure must be followed:
"A twice-born man who knows the Dharma should cremate a deceased wife of the same caste who died before him with the Agnihotra fire and the sacrificial implements."

"Having first given the fires to his wife who has died in the forest, he should perform the rites for the final end [of her life], and then perform the marriage ceremony again and the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*) as well. (Manusmṛti 5.167–168).
Thus, according to the *Manusmṛti*, in the event that the wife of a sacrificer dies first—

Regarding the Agnihotra vessels, since their cremation along with [the wife] is prescribed by rule, even if the sacrificer should die prior to the second marriage, because those vessels have already been employed for their previous purpose, in that regard—
Because the impermanence of the cremation fire— performed using sacrificial vessels prescribed by the *Kalpasūtras* for the *agnihotra*— is admitted;

and because the *Kalpasūtra* provides an option with the words "or with sacrificial vessels," it follows that there is no requirement for a fire [to be maintained] in vessels other than those such as the *araṇi*.

Furthermore, one should not perform cremation together with the forest fire and so forth after generating the fire again; for since those sages remain until the end of the kalpa, there is no fruit in such an investigation. Beyond this, the position of excavation is established by refuting all possible doubts.

It should be stated that [the body] is placed upon those [embers] touching the Śivaliṅga; for, according to the *Manusmṛti* (5.167), "The knower of dharma should perform [the cremation] with sacrificial vessels," it is not understood from this that the cremation is to be performed with vessels other than those specifically designated as sacrificial. Nevertheless, by means of the *agnihotra* fire used in sacrifice, for the sacrificer—
Furthermore, because the impermanence of the ritual acts prescribed in the *Kalpasūtras* cannot be avoided by means of cremation; and moreover:
"Having performed the *Prājāpatya* sacrifice with his entire property as the sacrificial fee, and having consigned the sacred fires into himself, a Brāhmaṇa should renounce from his home. (6.38)

Thus, according to the *Manusmṛti*, when a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) reaches the time for undertaking the fourth stage of life (*turyāśrama*), he is enjoined to perform the *Prājāpatya* sacrifice, effect the internal consignment of the fires (*agnīnām ātmāropaṇa*), and depart from his home as a wandering mendicant; and of such a person, who has desisted from all ritual actions—
Furthermore, because of the prohibition of cremation for one devoted to the yoga of meditation— as seen in the previously cited scriptural passages—
and because of the impermanence [of the body] even in that regard;
nor, even in the absence of cremation for a renunciant sacrificer, does [the duty] extend until the end of his wife's body.
It must be stated that at the time of death, having collected the ritual vessels, cremation is indeed performed with those vessels;

for this is necessary to account for the masculine gender found in the Vedic text, "They cremate the one who maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni) with his fires," by interpreting the term *āhitāgni* as referring to the sacrificer (*yajvan*).

For if there is an absence of burning, impermanence cannot be avoided. Nor should it be argued that, by changing the gender of the word, the term *āhitāgni* is accepted as referring to his wife; for the ritual acts prescribed by the *kalpasūtras* for the *agnihotra* performed at the sacrifice would necessarily be impermanent [in that case].

In the view that one who has performed sacrifices renounces at the very same time as the formal installation of the fires (*agnyādhāna*), because there is no burning of the sacrificial vessels due to their absence even when they would normally accompany [the fire]— owing to circumstances such as the reversal of place and time—
one first burns the vessels separately and then renounces.
And also because of the absence of sacrificial vessels until the death of his wife’s body.

And that which is the offspring of offspring itself—then one should take refuge in the forest.
Having renounced all village food and every possession,

According to the Smṛti (Smṛti 6.2–4, 9), for a householder— whether a performer of sacrifices or otherwise— it is prescribed that he should become a student (*brahmacārī*),
having been a householder (*gṛhī*) he should become a forest-dweller (*vanī*), and having been a forest-dweller he should renounce (*pravrajet*).

Thus, having entered into the formal bond of the forest-dweller stage (*vānaprastha-āśrama*) as prescribed by the injunctions governing the sequence of the stages of life (*āśrama-krama*), if he has himself maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), he should perform the *prājāpatya* sacrifice, consign the fires into his own self, entrust his wife to his son or other relative, and enter the forest. Nor should it be argued that even in the absence of cremation, his vessels and other implements are set aside until the end of his wife's life and then disposed of along with them; for since he entered the stage of life together with his wife, she too is a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and thus cremation is not applicable to her.
