If one performs the cremation rite for the subtle body (liṅgadeha) without the purificatory rites for the subtle body (liṅga-saṃskāra),
both [the performer and the deceased] will suffer destruction in hell.
"He who, having been initiated by the *liṅga* of breath (*prāṇa*), should initiate another bearer of the *liṅga*,
shall go to the terrible Raurava hell due to the burning of that [other's] body.
Thus it is stated in the Śivarahasyakhaṇḍa.

One who possesses the knowledge of Śiva, being of the nature of Rudra, burns away [the sins] of those whose bodies are attached to the *liṅga* by means of the ritual mantra; thus, there is no hell for them as long as time endures.
Those who bear the *liṅga*, sacred ash, and *rudrākṣa* upon their bodies—
that body, being endowed with the *liṅga* in every limb, is said to be Śiva himself.
"Then hell burns that body of the agent for an inexhaustible time.
And likewise: "One should perform the *agnihotra* as long as one lives; one should worship the *sandhyā* every day.
[The daily duties are: bathing, *sandhyā*, recitation (*japa*), fire-offering (*homa*), Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), and libations to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*)."
Hospitality and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice are virtuous rites to be performed day after day.
One should offer the Śrāddha daily to the ancestors, bringing them satisfaction.

Having abandoned all obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, which must be performed as long as one lives and which produce sin (*pratyavāya*) when not performed as prescribed by such scriptural injunctions as "thus," etc.—

In the Kali age, one should avoid these five: the sacrifice of horses, the sacrifice of cows, renunciation (of worldly life), the ancestral rite involving meat, and the procreation of offspring by a brother-in-law.

Thus, even though there exists a scriptural prohibition, when Brāhmaṇas who are devoid of the wearing of [Śaiva] marks perform various virtuous acts such as sacrifices, bathing in the Gaṅgā, and the distribution of food, and subsequently renounce the householder's stage to adopt the ascetic order;

Does the *apūrva* (unseen potency) produced by various virtuous acts performed during the householder stage of life reside within that person’s self, or not? In the first case, since sacrifices and the like perish immediately,
the *apūrva* must be postulated as the necessary explanatory principle (*anyathānupapatti*) for how such acts can produce heaven at a later time.
If one were to accept even those [works] that have been renounced as causes for attaining worlds dependent upon karma,

then the statement of the established doctrine— that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is for the sake of liberation through union (*sāyujya-mukti*)— would be untenable. Nor can it be argued that because the performance of works done without desire (*niṣkāma-karma-anuṣṭhāna*) is a means to liberation, [one may perform them] while desiring heaven (*svarga-kāma*).

Regarding the word "svarga" (heaven) in the injunction "one should sacrifice": that pleasure which is unmixed with pain, not followed by subsequent suffering, and brought about by one's desire— that is the referent of the term "svarga."

It should not be argued that, because the word *svaḥ* (heaven) denotes liberation (*mokṣa*)— the very nature of bliss as understood from such scriptural passages— there is no loss of liberation even if the latent impression (*apūrva*) produced by actions performed while in the householder stage (*gārhasthya*) persists within the self of the ascetic; for if that were so,
liberation would be established merely through the performance of actions done without desire (*niṣkāma*).
Because there is no purpose in adopting an *āśrama* after first abandoning those various duties that must be performed as long as one lives.
Nor is it the case that—“Men do not find liberation elsewhere than through the renunciation of action; not by action [alone].”

It should not be argued that the adoption of the ascetic order (*yatyāśrama*) is mandatory because liberation is shown to be attained solely through the renunciation of ritual action (*karmasaṃtyāga*), as in the passage beginning with *na prajayā dhanena tyāgenaike amṛtatvamānaśuḥ* (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.3), for such statements refer to [the seeker] who has realized that very [Self].
Having known [the Self], one transcends death; no other path exists for the journey (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8);

"The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3); and "Liberation comes from knowledge alone"—in accordance with such passages, since knowledge is understood to be the direct cause, [liberation] occurs through that [knowledge], and not by means of ritual actions.

The intended meaning here is that [the performance of obligatory and occasional rites] is not a cause of liberation directly; it is not, however, that its being a cause [of liberation] through the medium of knowledge is non-existent. Otherwise, [it would contradict the following]:
"By performing only the obligatory and occasional rites, one effects the destruction of evil."
"And purifying knowledge, one should ripen it through practice. Thus it is said:
"Through practice, a person attains discriminative knowledge and liberation;
from dharma come happiness and knowledge, and from knowledge, liberation is attained."
"For by action alone did Janaka and others attain perfection" (Bhagavad Gītā 3.20).

A wise householder who has acquired wealth through righteous means, who is established in the truth, who is fond of guests, who performs ancestral rites, and who speaks the truth, is liberated even while remaining a householder.

Otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with such statements as "Liberation occurs through death at Kāśī," because those types of statements teach that actions produce liberation by means of knowledge (*jñāna*).
In the second case [if one holds that the unseen potency is destroyed], there is the [destruction] of the unseen potency (*apūrva*) produced by those respective actions.
There would be the consequence of contradicting the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) which maintains that [the body] persists until the emergence of the fruit;

furthermore, there would be the impossibility of Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and others resorting to renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) for the sake of liberation from obligatory and occasional duties (*nitya-naimittika*), and so forth— despite the existence of such logical sublation (*yauktika-bādha*).

In accordance with such scriptural passages as, "One should listen to the reality... those ascetics whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta, being of pure nature by means of the yoga of renunciation" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.3),
Śaṅkarācārya established [the necessity of this] during the Kali-Sandhi by means of hundreds of oaths.

The fourth stage of life (caturthāśrama) is accepted. And just as, although the cremation rite is prescribed for any Brāhmaṇa by means of numerous mantras recited in the *Pitṛmedha* and other texts—[as it is said]:
"Having bathed, the householder, with a purified soul, should perform the consecration for the ascetic"—
And the disciples, having gazed upon him for a long time, adorned him with perfumes and flowers.
It was then nourished by dances, songs, and the like, by saffron and other substances, by water mixed with kusha grass, by shouts of "Victory!", and by the sound of kettledrums.
Having gone toward either the eastern or the northern direction, the wise man should dig there;
once a pit has been cleared from the earth, he should deposit the body of the ascetic.
According to the method stated by Aṅgiras, when death occurs among ascetics (*yatins*), no ritual touching (*spṛṣṭi*) or similar rites are required.
If a man, having bathed with the notion that there is impurity (*aśauca*), should set out on a journey toward the cardinal directions;
If the death of a wandering mendicant occurs among one's kinsmen, sons, or wives, there is indeed no impurity for them; however, they should not even perform a ritual bath.
Upon the death of a Parahaṃsa, cremation should never be performed;
instead, burial should be carried out for him, and there is neither impurity nor the offering of water libations.
One should first perform the ritual of digging for other monks as well.
In accordance with such statements from the Manusmṛti and the Sūtasamhitā,

even their digging [of the earth] and other rites are accepted; and likewise, at the end of life, for the Mahāpāśupatas who wear the *liṅga* and possess the knowledge of the identity (*sāmarasya*) of the *liṅga* and the body.

Since digging is prescribed by numerous Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and other texts, and since the cremation rites for the deceased— which serve a future purpose by way of securing the status of being a father and so forth— are not required of them according to the method previously stated,
we consider it logical that the act of digging, which serves a present purpose, alone should be performed.
However, this is the distinction: for the Mārgaśaivas (the Pūrvaśaivas),
after performing the *ātma-āropaṇa* of the fires belonging to the *prājāpatyeṣṭi* until the end of their lives, the act of digging [the funeral pit] is carried out.

If one has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), that rite is performed according to the method prescribed in the Śaiva Tantras. However, for certain unmarked (*aliṅgin*) Brāhmaṇas, there is no sin of omission for failing to perform it throughout their lives, and thus they do not accept [the performance of] this rite.
Therefore, for those Mahāpāśupatas who have received initiations such as *vedha* through the compassionate glance of their teacher,

and who contemplate the identity between the *liṅga*, the body, the sacred site (*sthala*), and the reality (*tattva*), no rites such as *sapiṇḍana* need be performed upon the exhaustion of the body through the ripening of time, because these are merely funeral rites for the deceased.
For this is the purpose of establishing sapinda-relationship: since, upon the abandonment of the body by the father and others,

there is no attainment of the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka) without the cessation of their state as a preta (ghost), and consequently no liberation through that means, it is for the sake of bringing about that cessation.
For the sake of ending the fourth [state], through the cessation of the state of a preta,
the fourth ceases after the joining of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).

In accordance with this statement, on the twelfth day, the *dīrghapreta-piṇḍa* (the long-lasting preta-oblation) is divided into three parts and joined with the three piṇḍas of the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) and others, who have been established as the deities; by this joining of the preta-water with their water, the state of being a *preta* comes to an end. And of that...
Because of entering into the position of the great-great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*), there is also the cessation of that [status].

This being so, in the *Pūrvatantra*: "For him, one should offer this *prājāpatyā* [oblation] consisting of a hundred *kṛṣṇala*s"—that is, the *prājāpatyā*, which has Prajāpati as its deity, consisting of a hundred *kṛṣṇala*s.

The subsequent portion of the text establishes that for those who have attained union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*) by casting off the function of fire while in contact with the body of a Śiva-liṅga, there is an absence of the state of being a *preta*; therefore, even the *sāpiṇḍya* rites and others intended to terminate the state of a *preta* need not be performed. In this very context, [it addresses] the former system...
He presents the section on the sublation of threshing in the case of *kṛṣṇala* beans, located in the tenth chapter, as a supporting argument, saying: "This being so...
In the context of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it is heard thus: "For him, this [offering] dedicated to Prajāpati..."
"One should offer one hundred *kṛṣṇala*s. Here,

in the context of the specific *iṣṭi* sacrifice based on the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, which involves offering a *caru* of gold fragments (*suvarṇaśakalā*), [the rule concerns] that which is useful for a specific type of sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

Since threshing is already established for the rice used in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices by the rule, "One threshes the rice" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 1.19.11), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that— according to the principle of extension (*codaka*) that "the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) should be performed like the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*)"— threshing must indeed be performed even upon the pieces of gold.

However, since it has been established as a settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) that threshing is useful for producing rice by means of removing the husk— and thus, although threshing applies to rice for the purpose of removing the husk, it does not apply to fragments of gold because the mediating factor is absent— so too, in the present case, it does not apply to those who have attained identity with Paraśiva.
For all those great Pāśupatas, Brahmins who bear the *liṅga*, and for all ascetics who bear the *liṅga* who die in Kāśī,
divinity alone is attained; the state of being a progenitor (*pitṛtva*) does not exist at all.

According to this statement from the *Skanda Purāṇa*, because he lacks the state of being a *preta* unlike ordinary people, he is referred to by the word "Kṛṣṇa" [as one who is] made of gold, like a grain of rice. A sacrificial oblation (*caru*) made of gold is prescribed for his sacrifice. Since this sacrifice is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the modification must be performed according to the model of the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Since the procedure for the Darśapūrṇamāsa is extended [to the Kṛṣṇala sacrifice] by means of the injunctive statement (*codakavākya*), the act of threshing— prescribed by the sentence "He threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*)— would also apply to the *kṛṣṇalas*. However, because threshing has the purpose of removing the husks, and since there are no husks in the *kṛṣṇalas* (which consist of gold needles), [threshing is not performed].

Just as threshing is set aside due to the absence of a purpose, so too here, for those who have attained union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*) and whose bodies are joined with the *liṅga*, there is no state of being a ghost (*pretatva*); thus, because there is no purpose, the *sāpiṇḍya* rites and so forth do not exist—this is the sense.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Skanda Purāṇa* regarding those who die in Kāśī: [text continues]

According to the maxim that "only what is possible can be prohibited," since there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*), there would be no purpose in performing an expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) to remove it; therefore, [the text] speaks of removing their state of being a ghost (*pretatva*).
Now, one might object: even if there is no state of being a ghost for those Brāhmaṇas who possess the marks and limbs [of their caste] at the end of the body, ignorance (*avidyā*)...

Because it is impossible for a deceased person to attain identity with Īśvara or Sadāśiva, they cannot enter the three categories [of ancestors]; consequently, since there is no cessation of the status of the great-great-grandfather (vṛddhaprapitāmaha) for that person's son...
If it is argued that there would be no inclination toward performing the monthly *śrāddha* and other rites intended for the three groups [of ancestors],
listen with careful attention:
"For the sake of the cessation of the fourth [group], through the cessation of the notion of being alive..."
For all ascetics who bear the outward marks [of their order], there is only the status of a deity; the status of a progenitor (pitṛtva) does not exist at all.
Thus it is recited.
Regarding the phrase "by the absence of the cessation of the great-great-grandfather," this appears to be the intended meaning here:
[the status] of a deceased person...

Even though both the state of being a *preta* and the state of being a living being have ceased, and [the deceased] has attained identity with the Lord (*Īśvara*), Sadāśiva, and Paramaśiva, together with his father, paternal grandfather, and paternal great-grandfather, the son—who is the performer of the rite—by including his own father, establishes the status of the "triad of ancestors.
Consequently, the paternal great-grandfather becomes distinct from that group. Therefore:

From that time forward, as long as he lives, that man performs the *śrāddha* for his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather alone; he does not include the great-great-grandfather in that ritual offering. This is because, upon his death, the state of being a living person ceases for him.
Since it is impossible for there to be an identity between the three persons consisting of Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Paramaśiva,

and since there is no separate existence of the great-grandfather apart from him, the performance of *śrāddha* for one's own father, grandfather, and great-grandfather on behalf of a living person would not be possible.

He provides the resolution: "Because such a category is simply unestablished"—for the sake of the cessation of the fourth [category], through the cessation of the notion of being a living soul (jīva);
after the application of the principles (tattvas) and so forth, even the fourth ceases.
Thus, there is the cessation of both according to the method taught in the *Makuṭāgama*. To explain:

in the phrase "after the conjunction with the principles (*tattva*) and so forth," the word *tattva* refers to the thirty-six principles, and the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the thirty-eight *kalās*. And so it is said:
On the eleventh day, having performed the sixteen-fold rites and others for the clay figure with a single dedication, when the twelfth day arrives,
one should invoke the deceased person into that single [clay figure].

To his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather— Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Paraśiva— one should offer [oblations] to the thirty-six principles (tattvas) presided over by them and the thirty-eight kalās,
either in all the Maheśvara [sections] or in some where the category of non-existence (abhāvapakṣa) occurs: *oṃ hāṃ*.

"I invoke the earth element, oṃ hāṃ; I invoke the water element, oṃ hāṃ; I invoke the fire element, oṃ hāṃ; I invoke the air element, oṃ hāṃ," and so forth, beginning from the earth element up to the Śiva element, [reciting] "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" (Īśāna is the lord of all sciences).
"I invoke Śaśinī; even the Lord, though the fourth of all, desists. This is the meaning:
after joining the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) and the thirty-eight digits (*kalās*) in the manner that will be described, [the following occurs].

When the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*) ceases, even the fourth ancestor—the great-great-grandfather—ceases; he becomes separate from that group. The actual reality of the meaning of this section can only be determined by consulting the *Makuṭāgama*, so we shall desist here for fear of excessive writing.

The meaning is: "among the three Vīraśaiva Brāhmaṇas" who are conceived as being identical with Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Paramaśiva—those counted as a triad among the Māheśvaras; or "in some cases," which refers to the alternative when Vīraśaivas are not available at the time of the Śrāddha.
One should invoke [the deities] with the mantra beginning, "I invoke Bhūtāṅgadāmā," "Brahmādhipati, Adhipati of Brahmā, Brahmā...

and so on, up to "I invoke Jvalinī," starting from the digit Śaśinī and ending with the digit called Sthiti, using bilva leaves along with unbroken rice (*akṣata*). Thereafter, one should [invoke] the forms of the principles (*tattva*) and digits (*kalā*) belonging to the Ādyeśvaras.
Having performed the worship of the feet of the Brahmins, preceded by the offering of seats and other honors,
[I offer this] for my father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather, through the cessation of all states of existence, so that they may attain the nature of Śiva, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva.
One should form the resolution (saṃkalpa), thinking "I shall do it. Then, with the mantra beginning: "Oṃ hāṃ, I unite the earth-element;
Oṃ hāṃ, I unite the water-element; Oṃ hāṃ, I unite the fire-element; Oṃ hāṃ, I unite the air-element; Oṃ hāṃ, I unite the ether-element," and so forth.
I join Śaśinī-kalā, the sovereign of the thirty-six principles up to the Śiva-principle; I join Aṅgadā, the lord of all sciences and of all beings.

The meaning is "among the common Śaivas. Regarding the phrase "by means of the cessation of the state of being a living soul": here, having performed the invocation of the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth and the digits (kalās) beginning with Śaśinī within the mantra demonstrated for the Māheśvara Brāhmaṇas, [one performs it] in the Śaiva person—that is, in the deceased person who has been invoked and established in proximity—[the offering] of those principles and the aforementioned digits.

When the union has been performed with the final mantras ending in "I join [them] again with what has been displayed," there occurs the attainment of fatherhood preceded by the cessation of the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*).
"Brahmādhipati" means the lord of Brahman; "I join him who is established in Brahman"—may Śiva be mine.

By means of the five Brahma-mantras, beginning with "Let there be Marīci, I unite Sadāśivā" and "I unite Jvalinī," and so forth, one proceeds from the digit Śaśinī up to the digit Sthiti, [attaining] the eightfold [powers] through the cessation of the state of being a living soul (jīvabhāva).

When there is an identity between Śiva, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva with one's father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, the sacrificer achieves the successful performance of the monthly *śrāddha* and other rites intended for the three ancestral groups, through the cessation of [the status of] the great-grandfather.
Now, at the time of initiation obtained through the grace of the Guru for those belonging to the Mārgaśaiva tradition, during the ritual of initiation (kriyādīkṣā),
there occurs the attainment of liberation from the mass of flesh born from the womb of the disciple’s mother,
as well as the separation of the great-great-grandfather from that group.

Regarding the methodology of the Śaiva Āgamas: the realization of these principles will come only through the thorough study of the Kāmika, Vātula, and Makuta Āgamas; therefore, it should be undertaken from those very sources.

Now, regarding the term "Mārgaśaivas": because they have already attained identity with Śiva by virtue of possessing initiation obtained through the grace of their guru, [the ritual] is performed for them— specifically by means of the initiation called *svastikārohaṇa*, which is included within the category of ritual initiation (*kriyādīkṣā*)—
for the purpose of removing the defects associated with the mother's womb.

If it is argued that because the *piṇḍotpatti* (emergence of the body) of the mantra occurs again through the process of re-creation (*utpattikrama*) by means of performing the deposition of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvanyāsa*), and because of the subsequent conjunction of the *tattvas* and *kalās* performed therein, there is an absence of the cause for achieving identity with Śiva— this is not so;

for even in the case of a devotee who has not previously received initiation, when he is connected to the *piṇḍa* through mere contemplation (*bhāvanāmātra*), for him it remains just as much [as before].

"Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf," so too for one who has attained the state of *jīvanmukti*— as taught in such scriptural passages as "For a long time I shall not be liberated; then I shall be fully realized" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2)— the fivefold sheaths (*pañcakośa*) born of ignorance do not adhere.
Due to the occurrence of hunger, thirst, and so forth, which necessitate the maintenance of that [body], and due to the possibility of passion, aversion, and so forth,
there arises an obstruction to the performance of all obligatory and occasional rites;
thus, even for one who has attained the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of action, it is like gold whose nature is overwhelmed by its earthly form.

It should not be thought that there is no requirement for the application of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), the principles (*tattva*), and the creative energies (*kalā*) due to the absence of a cause— namely, the natural dissolution of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the performance of ritual acts— even though that [state] has reached the stage of liberation while living (*jīvanmukta*).

Just as there is a connection between a lotus petal and water, since some form of connection with the body necessarily exists, and because [the self] is overwhelmed by that [connection] such that hunger, thirst, and so forth remain unmanifest, [this state persists] immediately after the end of the body.
This is because the accomplishment of the manifestation of identity with Paramaśiva— the supreme Śiva whose other names are Śiva, Maheśvara, Sadāśiva, and Supreme Kaivalya— is attained.
Nor should it be said that the physical body (māṃsapiṇḍa) ceases to exist at the very moment of initiation.
For, just as the arising of the mantra-body (*mantra-piṇḍa*) is accessible through meditation alone, so too is its cessation; however,

like those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) such as Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and Durvāsas, the connection with a body composed of the five elements for the followers of the Mārga-Śaiva is exactly like water on a lotus leaf, and not otherwise.
The wise should reflect that this is similar to the connection with the bodies of ordinary people; however,
the statements that establish this meaning are found in the *Paitṛka-prakaraṇa* contained within the *Makuṭa*, *Candrajñāna*, and *Vīrāgama*, and they are cited below.
—These are the points to be joined. Some examples are cited from the *Makuṭāgama*:
"By virtue of the union with the Śiva-liṅga-body obtained through initiation by the Guru..."
By the analogy of the bee-insect, the twice-born attained oneness with Śiva.
When one who has touched the limbs of the *liṅga* dies and the twelfth day has arrived,

[this rite] is necessary for the purpose of ceasing the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*) through the conjunction with the principles (*tattva*), the powers (*kalā*), and so forth, which reside in Śiva, Maheśvara, Sadāśiva, and Paraśiva, and for the purpose of attaining oneness with Śiva.
The intention of the concluding portion of the text is that it must be reflected upon. Within this section,

in the passage beginning with "Vasiṣṭha-Viśvāmitra," it is indicated that because Vasiṣṭha and the others are eternally perfected (*nityasiddha*), they have no requirement for any ritual action whatsoever.
He presents scriptural statements as authoritative evidence for his own established doctrine, beginning with the words:

"By means of union with the Śiva-liṅga obtained through the initiation of the Guru," and so forth, up to "the oneness with Śiva [attained] from the state of being a living soul. This refers to the elision of the suffix *lyap* (i.e., it means "having attained").
Sapiṇḍana must not be performed for a sage, because of the absence of the state of being a preta.
Those expert in the Śaiva Āgamas declare that the unity with Śiva, which was attained at the time of initiation, becomes manifest through the state of being a living soul (jīvabhāva).

Having gathered the *kalās* corresponding to the principles (*tattva*) from the ancestors who are non-different from Sadāśiva and the others, and having worshipped them elsewhere according to the prescribed rule;
"For the sake of ceasing the state of being a living soul, for one who is attached to the limbs of the sign of the dead,
the son should join the principles (tattvas) and so forth, in order to achieve the unification of the three groups. Thus it is said in the *Candrajñāna*.

When the twelfth day has arrived, one should perform the conjunction with the principles (tattva-yojana) and so forth for those whose bodies still bear the signs of death, in order to bring about the cessation of the notion that they are living.
"One should not perform the *sāpiṇḍya* rites and so forth for one who has died while in physical contact with the *liṅga*.
By the very union with the *tattva*, the state of being a living being ceases. Thus it is said in the *Vīrāgama*.
The principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva are, in their respective order:
the word "thou" (tvaṃ) is the principle of Ātman, and "art thou" (asi) is the principle of Vidyā.
That state is the Śiva-tattva, which is again of the nature of the Ātma-tattva;
it consists of twenty-five principles as well as ten principles.
The principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) is known as Śiva; it is remembered as the single principle. Maheśa, who is Sadāśiva, should be known as the lord of these principles.

The meaning is as follows: Śiva, who is indeed higher than the highest, having caused the state of being a *jīva* to cease within Śivā—the supreme cause—there arises the unity with Śiva obtained at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
"Equal in number to the *tattvas*" means numbering twenty-four; namely, those called Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.

And "the principles (tattvas) in their proper order" refers to the threefold division of the principles: the principle of the self (ātmatattva), the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), and the principle of Śiva (śivatattva). Here, the knowledge produced by the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi) is called the principle of knowledge; the referent of the term "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha) is called the principle of the self; and the referent of the term "that" (tatpadārtha) [is the principle of Śiva].

It is called the Śiva-tattva. Herein, the Ātma-tattva consists of twenty-five [categories], the Vidyā-tattva consists of ten, and the Śiva-tattva consists of one. These very [categories] previously mentioned are [bestowed] by the Guru according to the three modes of initiation (dīkṣā), as follows:
Furthermore, what purpose would there be in the *sāpiṇḍya* relationship for a devotee who has attained oneness [with the deity]?
Therefore, the Lords of the Principles (*tattveśvaras*) should be properly worshipped in their proper sequence.
"When the twelfth day has arrived, which is auspicious for the Śiva-yogin.
Here, in the phrase "the lords of the principles" (*tattveśvarāḥ*), the word *tattva* (principle) is also an indicator for the *kalās* (phases).
Thus, by means of the worship of those whose forms are the *piṇḍas*, the *tattvas*, and the *kalās*, as well as the ancestors who are the lords presiding over them, etc.
The intended meaning should be inferred as follows: "The conjunction with the [deceased's] true essence (tattva) and so forth must be performed. As stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:

"Because the existent one possesses the characteristic of the space within the heart (*daharākāśa*), and because of the characteristic of yoga and so forth, since he consists of the nature of the subtle body (*liṅga-bhāva-ātmaka*), there is no need for funeral rites (*pretakārya*) and the like."
Even according to other schools of thought, the *sāpiṇḍya* and other such relations are indeed non-permanent;
for in the event of the death of a father or others occurring after they have already entered a religious order (*āśrama*),
there is a prohibition of the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), water, and so forth, by means of the previously cited Smṛtis of Śaunaka, Manu, and others.

Because of the impossibility of performing the *sāpiṇḍya* rite [in those cases]; for even if the father remains a householder, if the grandfather and others have become renunciants (*saṃnyasta*) and have thus attained union with Brahman (*brahmībhūta*), there is an absence of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) intended for them, and since the joining of the *preta*-rice-ball is impossible therein, that [joining] is likewise absent in those instances. However—
The thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) are said to belong to all [the ancestors], beginning with the father and grandfather. Their intermediate names are to be understood from other texts.
Likewise, regarding "of the devotee of oneness" (*aikyasya bhaktasya*): of the devotee of oneness with Śiva, within one's own self through faith.

"For one who meditates on that unity. Therefore, the Lords of the Principles (*tattveśvara*) should be properly worshipped. The meaning of "Lords of the Principles" here is the Vīraśaiva Brāhmaṇas who have been meditated upon as being identical with the Lord of the Principles, Sadāśiva.
Regarding "at the auspicious [occasion] of the Śiva-yogins": the meaning is at the time of the festival of attaining liberation, which is the auspicious state of the Śiva-yogins.

Alternatively, this is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*); that is, "in the auspicious," meaning for the sake of the auspicious. This refers to the mark of Brahman within the small space—that is, the mark of Brahman residing within the heart-lotus—which exists as uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time and is indicated by such marks as yoga.
In cases where death occurs specifically among householders, the performance of *sāpiṇḍya* must also occur there; thus, its non-obligatory nature (*anityatva*) is indeed unavoidable.
Even though—

One who has attained union with the body of the Śiva-liṅga should not perform rites such as the ancestral offerings (śrāddha), nor the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), nor the water-libation; he should not perform the Pārvaṇa and other such ceremonies.
Every year, one should feed devotees of Śiva in honor of him;
for the food given to those devotees is indeed offered to Śiva himself.
This statement regarding the prohibition of all *śrāddha* rites applies [only to those who have not yet attained the state of *atyāśramī*]; for it is said:
"The *atyāśramī* should carry a jar of ashes associated with the *prāṇaliṅga*, a patched garment, a water-pot, an alms-bowl, and a staff."

Thus, having abandoned wife, children, and so forth, preceded by the relinquishment of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rituals as understood from such scriptural statements, and having attained the state of being a *śivaliṅga* by virtue of possessing the nature of the *liṅga* (the subtle body),
the impermanence [of those who have taken up the stage of renunciation] is unavoidable for all schools of thought regarding their fathers and other relatives.
Thus, because of the non-performance of *sāpiṇḍya*,

he considers [the lineage] to culminate in the *nirābhāra-vīraśaiva*. Otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with the cited statements found in the *Kuṭāgama* and *Vīrāgama*, which prescribe the necessity of performing the conjunction of the *tattvas* and *kalās*.

From them [arises] the "burden" (*ābhāra*), consisting of worldly anxieties, which has departed from them. However, for the *liṅgins*— the householders who are solely devoted to the knowledge of Śiva,
specifically the *viśeṣa-vīraśaivas*— even in the absence of funeral rites, rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), and so forth:
When one who was attached to the *liṅga* and its limbs has died,
the disciples, sons, and others should perform the subsequent rites prescribed in the Śaiva Tantras within the home.

Thus, in accordance with the statement from the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*, all concluding rites must indeed be performed according to the method prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*; therefore, everything is entirely consistent.

Since such a Vīraśaiva is devoted solely to Him (Śiva), the scriptural statement prohibiting the performance of *śrāddha* rites for them should be understood as referring only to that [specific case]; for, by being established in Śiva, who is the embodiment of unsurpassed auspiciousness, they have no dependence on external ritual acts.
May there be peace! (*iti śivam*)
For one in whose speech the auspicious name "Śiva" proceeds,
all blessings are indeed held within the palm of their hand.
Having meditated with some effort in my mind upon that God who is the very nature of Śiva, and upon that Goddess who is the source of all auspiciousness, I bow down to them again and again.

In the illustrious Vikrama year calculated as nineteen hundred and sixty (1960), during the summer season on the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śuci, on the day of the Lord of Speech (Thursday),
he sat upon the throne in the lofty monastery of the Kāśī-jaṅgama-vāṭikā.
The illustrious Rājeśvaravid composed this commentary named Śarad.

Thus ends the second part of the *Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā*, composed by the illustrious Nandīśvara, who is renowned throughout all the scriptures— including the Śruti, Vedānta, Smṛti, Purāṇas, Āgamas, Itihāsas, and all other treatises—
and who is the grandson of Basaveśvara and the son of Maheśācārya.
The Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā was composed by Nandīśvara.
The Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā is complete.
That non-duality of Maheśvara, who is qualified by Śakti, which exists within the entire phenomenal world—
this was indeed made manifest in former times to people by those who were experts in the essential truth of the Kāśmīra Śaiva Āgamas.
Desiring to proclaim for the benefit of the world the profound essence of his own established doctrine,
Nandikeśa indeed composed that *Liṅgāśrayacandrikā* in ancient verses.

When the divine lotus-feet of the Lord Śambhu— the ocean of compassion— are being incessantly worshipped with words by Brahmā and the other gods, Gaurī’s Lord spreads throughout the world a joy born of affection.
She is exceedingly respectful, for she performs her duties even toward those dear to Śiva with a sense of awe, as if they were the moon.
Having observed her supreme devotion to the lotus feet of the Lord of the Universe, I, Śivakumāra, have joyfully composed this commentary; may it be auspicious.
Śambhu is auspicious, Gaurī is auspicious, Śeṣa is auspicious, and the Moon is auspicious;
Gaṇapati is auspicious—therefore, this book is auspicious in every respect.
The commentary on the work titled *Śarad*, composed by the great professor and scholar Paṇḍita Śivakumāra Miśra, resident of Kāśī, the illustrious holy field, is hereby completed.
